items.body:
*By Megan Sumeracki*

This semester, I’m teaching a hybrid class that only meets on Thursdays. Because of this, we have met every week up until this week. However, with Thanksgiving break, my students will have a two-week gap right at the end of the semester. We will return from Thanksgiving break in early December, with the final exam looming around the corner.

These are particularly extreme circumstances, and some students will only have a few days off this holiday. Still, it’s common to come back from Thanksgiving break to hear “I can’t remember.” Or, even more concerning, the “wait, when did we learn this?” question.

As a cognitive psychologist specializing in learning, I’m not overly concerned. It’s counterintuitive, but forgetting is actually an extremely important part of remembering. It’s easier to understand why when we consider how forgetting occurs over time, and how spaced practice works.

In the 1880s, Hermann Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve *(1)*. He showed that forgetting tends to happen very rapidly at first, and then slows down. He also showed that spreading out repetitions was more efficient than massing them, or cramming. We know from a wealth of research in the last 140 years that spaced practice slows the rate of forgetting. This research has confirmed, many times over, that cramming does not work in the long run. Instead, spacing practice leads to much more durable long-term learning and remembering *(2)*.

Why does spacing help? When we review information after some time has passed, it has started to fade. When we revisit the information—or better yet, when we retrieve the information—it takes effort. That effort is sometimes called a desirable difficulty, and it helps produce durable learning *(3)*. Each time we successfully retrieve something, it becomes easier to retrieve the next time, and it is forgotten more slowly afterward. In other words, a little forgetting sets the stage for more durable remembering.

Having a break for Thanksgiving provides a natural space to let students forget a little bit, and then give them a boost upon returning. The figure below shows curves that illustrate the general pattern reported in research on forgetting (e.g., *1, 2* ).

These curves are a simulation, not real data. They illustrate the general pattern reported in research on forgetting and spacing (Ebbinghaus, 1885/1913; Cepeda et al., 2006): memories fade over time, retrieving them brings them back, and each retrieval slows forgetting. The specific values were chosen for illustration and are not predictions.

There are other benefits too. Spacing out practice shifts the context in which the material is being practiced, which may also help produce durable learning and remembering *(4)*. It is also important to take breaks in general. Stress can tax our cognitive resources and make it harder for us to retrieve what we know *(5, 6)*. Sleep also plays an important role in consolidating new memories. If the break provides opportunities to catch up on sleep and destress, it can be beneficial for learning upon return as well. See this post on [The Importance of Sleep for Memory and Cognition](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2016/7/14-1) and this post, [When Do the 6 Strategies for Effective Learning Work Best?](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2017/4/20-1)

Of course, there is a limit to how much space we should put in between review or retrieval attempts. If the space is too long, and the information is completely forgotten, then students may need to relearn it. Likely there will be savings in relearning—i.e., it won’t take as long to learn it again as it did the first time *(1)*. However, the benefits from spaced practice will likely be much less than they would have been, or possibly eliminated. The goal is to retrieve or at least review older material before it is completely forgotten to get the boost. Check out this post, [Optimizing Your Learning Schedule](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2018/7/5-1), to learn more about this.

items.body:
Kaum ein Abiturthema zeigt so deutlich wie dieses, dass es ihn gibt: einen modernen Deutschunterricht, der die Aufgabe ernst nimmt, jungen Menschen Orientierung in einer digitalen Gesellschaft zu ermöglichen. Ein Kommentar.

Es gibt Abiturthemen, bei denen man als Lehrkraft erst einmal Überzeugungsarbeit leisten muss. Bei denen man vor einem Kurs steht und begründen muss, warum es sich lohnt, sich mit etwas zu beschäftigen, das auf den ersten Blick weit weg ist vom eigenen Leben. Ich habe solche Stunden oft genug gehalten. Und ich habe auf diesem Blog auch schon [dafür gestritten, dass man sie halten sollte.](https://bobblume.de/2019/10/06/diskussion-sollte-goethes-faust-teil-des-lehrplans-sein/)

„Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ gehört nicht dazu. Der sperrige Titel täuscht. Denn worum es hier geht, tragen die Schülerinnen und Schüler jeden Tag in der Hosentasche mit sich herum.

## Wo das Thema im Abitur 2027 eine Rolle spielt

In Nordrhein-Westfalen, Berlin und Brandenburg, Hessen, Niedersachsen und Schleswig-Holstein ist das Themenfeld im Abitur 2027 ausdrücklich als Schwerpunkt ausgewiesen, mit leicht unterschiedlichen Akzenten. Mal geht es um politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation zwischen Verständigung und Strategie, mal um den Sprachgebrauch in unterschiedlichen Medien, mal um Rhetorik und Medienwandel. In den übrigen Ländern, etwa in Baden-Württemberg und Bayern, sind genau die Aufgabenformate gefragt, an denen sich das Thema hervorragend üben lässt: die Analyse pragmatischer Texte, die Erörterung und das materialgestützte Schreiben.

Mit anderen Worten: Es ist eines der zentralen Felder des Deutschabiturs.

## Worum es eigentlich geht

Wie wird Sprache eingesetzt, um zu überzeugen, zu mobilisieren, auszugrenzen? Wo legt jemand seine Gründe offen, und wo will er bloß wirken? Diese Fragen konnte man früher an Bundestagsreden und Leitartikeln stellen. Das fällt nicht weg, aber es kommt auch etwas hinzu: Die politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation, die Jugendliche tatsächlich erreicht, hat nochmals völlig andere Formen und Kanäle: ein KI-generiertes Video, das Empörung erzeugt und am Ende einen Shop verlinkt. Ein [Finanzpodcast, der von „Systemmedien“](https://www.t-online.de/leben/kolumne-bob-blume/id_100330412/finanz-influencer-und-podcasts-werden-jugendliche-zum-rechtsruck-verleitet-.html) spricht und damit mehr transportiert als eine Meinung. Eine Kommentarspalte, in der niemand den Text gelesen hat, über den alle streiten. Ein Feed, in dem auf das Kriegsvideo der Tanzclip folgt.

Das ist politische Sprache. Nur eben nicht mehr im Plenarsaal, sondern zwischen zwei Wischbewegungen. Und wer diese Sprache nicht durchschaut, wird von ihr beeinflusst oder [im schlimmsten Fall manipuliert.](https://substack.com/@netzlehrer/p-211289258)

## Kein Entweder-oder

Nun könnte man einwenden, das sei die übliche Anbiederung an die Lebenswelt. Ein bisschen TikTok, damit es sich zeitgemäß anfühlt. Den Einwand muss man ernst nehmen, ich habe ihn selbst oft genug erhoben. An anderer Stelle habe ich beschrieben, dass Deutschunterricht auf [drei Ebenen zur Teilhabe an Kultur](https://bobblume.de/2021/05/31/diskussion-was-soll-und-kann-deutschunterricht/) befähigt: durch basale Grundfertigkeiten, durch die Auseinandersetzung mit Alltagskultur und durch die Hochkultur. Die mittlere Ebene ist diejenige, die sich am schnellsten verändert. Gerade deshalb darf man sie nicht dem Zufall überlassen.

Und es geht nicht um ein Entweder-oder. Wer Kleist liest, lernt etwas über Macht und Sprache vor Gericht. Wer ein Empörungsvideo analysiert, lernt etwas über Macht und Sprache im Feed. Beides schärft denselben Blick. In der Diskussion um den Faust habe ich geschrieben, dass man Kompetenzen an unterschiedlichen Inhalten lernen kann, aber nur an bestimmten Inhalten unterschiedliche Kompetenzen. Die Sprache der digitalen Öffentlichkeit ist ein solcher Inhalt. An ihr lernt man zu analysieren, zu urteilen und selbst zu schreiben. Und nebenbei etwas, das in keinem Erwartungshorizont steht: den Schritt zurück.

items.title: Listen to the Music of the Ancient World: From 40,000-Year-Old Flutes to Ancient Greek Songs
items.subtitle: There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world.

items.body:
There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world. We can learn its languages, at least the ones that have left behind decipherable writings; we can behold its artifacts; we can visit its ruins. But nothing gets us quite as close to entering the consciousness of our distant forebears as hearing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In [the new Archaeologist’s Notebook video above](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2nWf_OXdKz8), Giselle Király gives us a tour through ancient musical history, explaining the instruments of those times that survive in one form or another today. That tour begins at a much earlier point than many would expect: 40,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when humans were already punctuating their struggle for survival with organized sound.

As evidence, Király points to the “tiny, exquisitely crafted flutes carved from animal bone and mammoth ivory” discovered on cave floors around Europe. Surprisingly, when played in replica form, these vulture- or swan-bone flutes actually sound somewhat Middle Eastern. But whatever the stylistic traits of the music their original players produced, that music had the potential to confer benefits beyond immediate pleasure: “It would’ve connected people, built cohesion within the community,” and maybe even bridged “the land of the living with some spiritual world.” Each of the other discovered or reconstructed instruments, like swingable “bullroarers,” bone rasps, and lithophones (of the kind [previously featured here on Open Culture](https://www.openculture.com/2019/09/watch-an-archaeologist-play-the-lithophone.html)) would have played its own sonic part to that end.

Király also discusses the lavishly decorated Lyres of Ur, the world’s oldest surviving stringed instruments; a 3,500-year-old Egyptian long-necked lute with a guitar-like fingerboard; and a set of 65 Chinese *bianzhong * bells covering a five-octave range. But music isn’t just about the objects it’s played with. Also important are the means of recording it, an ancient example of which Király cites in the [Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal](https://www.openculture.com/2023/03/hear-the-oldest-song-in-the-world-a-sumerian-hymn-written-3400-years-ago.html) inscribed on a clay tablet around 1400 BC, the oldest known complete musical notation. Centuries later, in the Greek-speaking world — and in the more monumental form of a marble stele — a man named Seikilos recorded an epitaph to which we now refer by his name. The lyrics of this [oldest completely preserved, fully playable musical composition](https://www.openculture.com/2015/05/hear-the-seikilos-epitaph-the-oldest-complete-song-in-the-world.html) exhort the listener: “While you live, shine. Have no grief at all.” For “life exists only for a short while,” and “time demands its toll.” The ancients needed to hear this no less, perhaps, than we do.

**Related content:**

[What Did Music in Ancient Rome Sound Like?](https://www.openculture.com/2023/06/what-did-music-in-ancient-rome-sound-like.html)

[What Ancient Greek Music Sounded Like: Listen to a Reconstruction That’s “100% Accurate”](https://www.openculture.com/2024/12/what-ancient-greek-music-sounded-like-listen-to-a-reconstruction-thats-100-accurate.html)

[Hear the Oldest Song in the World: A Sumerian Hymn Written 3,400 Years Ago](https://www.openculture.com/2023/03/hear-the-oldest-song-in-the-world-a-sumerian-hymn-written-3400-years-ago.html)

[Hear the World’s Oldest Instrument, the “Neanderthal Flute,” Dating Back Over 43,000 Years](https://www.openculture.com/2025/06/hear-the-worlds-oldest-instrument-the-neanderthal-flute-dating-back-over-43000-years.html)

# Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion | Cleveland Museum of Art

## Artwork Page for Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion

### Details / Information for Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion

### Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion

c. 1230–40

#### Italy, Pisa

Mediumtempera with gold on panelMeasurementsFramed: 186.6 x 160.7 x 12.7 cm (73 7/16 x 63 1/4 x 5 in.); Unframed: 185 x 160 x 10.2 cm (72 13/16 x 63 x 4 in.)Credit LineLeonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund 1995.5You can copy, modify, and distribute this work, all without asking permission. Learn more about CMA's Open Access Initiative.Location100 1916 LobbyArtLens AppPrint?

#### Did You Know?

Although the artist did sign this panel at the bottom, the signature is illegible, his first name perhaps being Michael.

### Description

Large painted crucifixes dating from the 1100s and 1200s are among the earliest surviving Italian panel paintings. Large crosses, like this beautiful example, were typically suspended high above an altar in the main apse of Italian churches. Smaller crosses were placed on or just above altars in small side chapels. Such crosses served as the visual focus for devotion and symbolized the Eucharistic sacrament performed by the priest on the altar below. This crucifix shows Christ alive on the cross as the triumphant savior of mankind. Smaller images on the "apron" represent images of Christ's Passion (to the left) and his death and Resurrection (to the right). On the far left terminal appear the mourning Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist, while on the right the viewer is shown Saint James Major and Saint Bona, patroness of the city of Pisa. The concluding event, the Ascension of Christ, once appeared on the upper terminal, just above the Virgin and Apostles. The figure of Christ is painted in a severe and hieratic style suggestive of medieval Pisa's artistic and commercial links with the Byzantine East. The appearance of Saint Bona on this cross may suggest that it was made for the Church of S. Martino in Pisa, where Franciscan nuns tended the holy woman's relics.

### Crucifix with Scenes of the Passion

c. 1230–40

items.body:
### “A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader.”

*“All attempts at gaining literary polish must begin with judicious reading,”* H.P. Lovecraft [advised aspiring writers](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/11/h-p-lovecraft-advice-on-writing/). We’ve already seen that [reading is a learned skill](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/01/09/best-books-on-writing-reading/) and an [optimizable technique](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/16/how-to-read-faster-bill-cosby/), and that [non-reading](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/06/15/how-to-talk-about-books-you-havent-read/) is as important an intellectual choice as reading itself, so it follows that reading, more than the mere monolithic act of ingesting text, comes with degrees of mastery. But what, exactly, does it mean to be a *good* reader?

**Vladimir Nabokov** (April 22, 1899–July 2, 1977) was a man of [wonderfully opinionated insights on literature and life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/18/vladimir-nabokov-james-mossman-interview/). He was also, it turns out, equally opinionated in his criteria for what constitutes a good reader. In his collected [Lectures on Literature](http://www.amazon.com/Lectures-Literature-Vladimir-Nabokov/dp/0156027755/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/lectures-on-literature/oclc/6357239&referer=brief_results)), Nabokov offers the following exercise, which he posed to students at a “remote provincial college” while on an extended lecture tour:

> Select four answers to the question what should a reader be to be a good reader:
> The reader should belong to a book club.
> The reader should identify himself or herself with the hero or heroine.
> The reader should concentrate on the social-economic angle.
> The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.
> The reader should have seen the book in a movie.
> The reader should be a budding author.
> The reader should have imagination.
> The reader should have memory.
> The reader should have a dictionary.
> The reader should have some artistic sense.
> The students leaned heavily on emotional identification, action, and the social-economic or historical angle. Of course, as you have guessed, the good reader is one who has imagination, memory, a dictionary, and some artistic sense–which sense I propose to develop in myself and in others whenever I have the chance.

He goes on to consider the element of time in reading, making a case for the value of rereading:

> Incidentally, I use the word reader very loosely. Curiously enough, one cannot read a book: one can only reread it. A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader. And I shall tell you why. When we read a book for the first time the very process of laboriously moving our eyes from left to right, line after line, page after page, this complicated physical work upon the book, the very process of learning in terms of space and time what the book is about, this stands between us and artistic appreciation. When we look at a painting we do not have to move our eyes in a special way even if, as in a book, the picture contains elements of depth and development. The element of time does not really enter in a first contact with a painting. In reading a book, we must have time to acquaint ourselves with it. We have no physical organ (as we have the eye in regard to a painting) that takes in the whole picture and then can enjoy its details. But at a second, or third, or fourth reading we do, in a sense, behave towards a book as we do towards a painting. However, let us not confuse the physical eye, that monstrous masterpiece of evolution, with the mind, an even more monstrous achievement. A book, no matter what it is—a work of fiction or a work of science (the boundary line between the two is not as clear as is generally believed)—a book of fiction appeals first of all to the mind. The mind, the brain, the top of the tingling spine, is, or should be, the only instrument used upon a book.

…

items.body:
**STUTTGART. „Vielfalt stärken – Zukunft gestalten“ lautete das Motto des Jahreskongresses Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026, zu dem am 26./27. November in der IHK Region Stuttgart rund 400 Ausbilder:innen, Schulleitungen und Lehrkräfte zusammenkamen.**

Dr. Christoph Franz, Dr. Benny Pock, Andrea Bosch, Dr. Jens Brandenburg und Andreas Deuschle beim Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026. (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

Mit **Andreas Deuschle, Staatssekretär im Ministerium für Kultus Baden-Württemberg**, wurde heute der Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026 in Stuttgart eröffnet. Deuschle vertrat Kultusminister Andreas Jung, der in diesem Jahr erstmals die Schirmherrschaft des Kongresses übernommen hat. Jung bezeichnete die berufliche Bildung kürzlich in einem Interview als „Flaggschiff“, „Aushängeschild“ und eine Basis des wirtschaftlichen Erfolges seines Bundeslandes. Entsprechend wurde auf die duale Ausbildung im Koalitionsvertrag von BÜNDNIS 90/DIE GRÜNEN und CDU ein besonderer Schwerpunkt gesetzt. Im Begrüßungsgespräch mit der stellvertretenden Hauptgeschäftsführerin der IHK Region Stuttgart, Andrea Bosch, ging es darum, wie das Kultusministerium dieses Vorhaben gemeinsam mit dem Wirtschaftsministerium in Schulen und Betrieben mit Leben füllen will. Deuschle betonte dabei, dass es gelte, „gemeinsam Perspektiven zu schaffen“.

**Austausch über Zuständigkeiten hinweg**

Dass diese politische Zielsetzung nur gemeinsam gelingen kann, spiegelte das Teilnehmerfeld des jakobb 2026 wider: Als Plattform für die berufliche Bildung versammelt der Kongress einmal im Jahr alle Schlüsselakteure an einem Ort. Von der Berufsschullehrkraft bis zur Personalleitung mittelständischer und globaler Unternehmen nutzten die Entscheidungsträger den Austausch in Stuttgart, um Weichen für die Ausbildung von morgen zu stellen.

**Dr. Christoph Franz**, Vorsitzender des Berufsschullehrerverbands Baden-Württemberg (BLV), und Mitveranstalter des jakobb, zum Konzept: „ Wir erleben täglich, unter welchem Druck die berufliche Bildung steht: Fachkräftemangel, Transformation der Wirtschaft, Digitalisierung und KI, Integration und zunehmend heterogene Klassen. Diese Aufgaben kann niemand allein lösen. Der jakobb bringt Lehrkräfte, Schulleitungen, Wirtschaft, Verwaltung und Wissenschaft an einen Tisch. Genau diesen Austausch über Zuständigkeiten hinweg brauchen wir jetzt. Gleichzeitig zeigt der jakobb, was die beruflichen Schulen in Baden-Württemberg leisten. Sie sind kein Plan B, sondern ein Erfolgsmodell und das Rückgrat der Fachkräftesicherung im Land.“

Der jakobb bringt die Akteure der beruflichen Bildung miteinander ins Gespräch. (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

**Raus aus dem Tagungsraum, rein in die Praxis**

Ein weiteres Alleinstellungsmerkmal des Kongresses ist die konsequente Verbindung von Theorie und Praxis: Wenn die Fachvorträge und Diskussionsrunden enden, öffnen regelmäßig am zweiten Veranstaltungstag Spitzenunternehmen sowie innovative berufsbildende Schulen in der Region Stuttgart ihre Türen für exklusive „jakobb-Führungen“. **Dr. Benny Pock**, Geschäftsführer von Klett MEX und Mitgründer des jakobb, unterstreicht die Bedeutung dieses Formats: „ Der jakobb belässt es nicht beim theoretischen Diskurs. Unser Ziel war von Anfang an, die beiden Lernorte der dualen Ausbildung – den betrieblichen und den schulischen Teil – nicht nur an einen Tisch zu bringen, sondern vor Ort erlebbar zu machen. Die Exkursionen bieten Ausbildungsverantwortlichen und Lehrkräften die Chance, voneinander zu lernen, Best Practices im laufenden Betrieb zu studieren und frische Impulse direkt in die eigene Ausbildungspraxis mitzunehmen.“

…

items.body:
# Intellectual telescopes

This is a post from Robin Sloan’s lab blog & notebook. You can visit the blog’s homepage, or learn more about me.

## Intellectual telescopes

November 25, 2026

In a pre­vious post, I tried out an analogy for AI-assisted work: the pantograph, a once-ubiquitous tool for trans­forming human draw­ings vastly larger or minutely smaller, allowing human-sized hands to per­form nimbly at dif­ferent scales.

Here’s another analogy from the com­ments sec­tion on Scott Aaronson’s blog:

In any case, I recently saw this num­ber­phile video on the Rie­mann hypoth­esis with Jon Keating. At some point, Brady asks him some­thing like “Is it pos­sible that the proof of the Rie­mann hypoth­esis is some­thing that no human can understand, that our hardware, our brains, just can’t process?”

And Keating replies “Yes, that is pos­sible. Humans have faced this before. If I want to see the stars, I would quite like to see them with my own eyes. But there are cer­tain things in the uni­verse that the Hubble space tele­scope can see that my eyes can’t see. And I am pre­pared to accept that the Hubble space tele­scope does a better job than my eyes. And I just look at the pic­tures it pro­duces, in wonderment”.

I like this a lot. Although, it’s impor­tant to say the formal math lan­guage Lean is as much “the space tele­scope” here as the AI lan­guage models; they wouldn’t be able to pro­duce any­thing leg­ible or ver­i­fi­able without it.

Finally, it strikes me that this kind of work is very impor­tant — it’s the equiv­a­lent of actu­ally ren­dering space tele­scope “images” (which are just streams of numbers) into pic­tures, very prob­ably false-colored, that humans can con­sider and appreciate.

P.S. Of course, you could also use another analogy, emphasis mine …

As long as there are prob­lems to solve, and as long as we bring some­thing to their resolution, I think we should ride the AI dragon. We should enhance ourselves, move up in abstraction, and let the dragon deal with what it does better than us. [ … ]

I doubt that riding the dragon can be a pro­gram for the steady-state ASI sce­nario (if there is one), but it can be a pro­gram for now. The dragon is get­ting bigger every three months. It may ride itself at some point, but so far few can ride it properly. Those who do not ride it now may never be able to ride it in the future, at least not to find new things.

… which, from the title of this blog, you already know I love🤓

items.subtitle: Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten.

items.body:
Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten. Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel.

Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem [Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück *und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht.*

**Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?**

**Markus Weißkopf** ist Redakteur des Research.Table bei Table.Media. Er war Geschäftsführer von Wissenschaft im Dialog und hat dort unter anderem die Plattform Wissenschaftskommunikation.de aufgebaut. Foto: WiD

Markus Weißkopf: Kurz zuvor hatten Wissenschaft im Dialog und der Bundesverband Hochschulkommunikation gemeinsam die [Leitlinien zur guten Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/leitlinien-zur-guten-wissenschaftskommunikation-85129/) veröffentlicht. In dem Zuge hatte die Community viel über gemeinsame Werte, aber auch über die Professionalisierung der Wissenschaftskommunikation diskutiert. Wissenschaftskommunikation.de sollte unter anderem eine Plattform für diese Themen bieten.

Annette Leßmöllmann: Die Plattform sollte zeigen: Wissenschaftskommunikation bedeutet mehr als nur Pressemitteilungen und Hochglanzmagazine. Mir war es ein Anliegen, Forschung und Praxis zusammenzubringen und somit die [Vermittlung der Wissenschaftskommunikationsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/kategorie/forschung/) voranzutreiben. Zum einen, um praxisrelevante Ergebnisse bekannt zu machen, zum anderen, um die theoretische Weiterentwicklung, die Interdisziplinarität und die Selbstreflexion des Forschungsfeldes zu zeigen. Gleichzeitig sollten Praxisfragen für die Forschung nachvollziehbar werden, um neue Forschung anzustoßen.

**Annette Leßmöllmann** (@annetteless.bsky.social) ist promovierte Linguistin und hat am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* den Lehrstuhl für Wissenschaftskommunikation mit dem Schwerpunkt Linguistik inne. Sie lehrt in den Bachelor- und Master-Studiengängen „Wissenschaft – Medien – Kommunikation“ (@WMKstudium).

**Welche Fragen oder Konfliktlinien aus der Gründungszeit beschäftigen die Community bis heute?**

Weißkopf: „Als Anlaufstelle Nr. 1 hat sich das Online-Lexikon Wikipedia im Internet längst etabliert. Die Wissenschaft sollte das Potenzial von Wikipedia für die Vermittlung fundierten Wissens ernsthaft prüfen.“ Das hat eine Pressesprecherin [im Rahmen des ersten Schwerpunkts „Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation“](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/blick-nach-vorn-wie-sieht-die-wissenschaftskommunikation-der-zukunft-aus-5-13517/) geschrieben. Natürlich ist das Prüfen wissenschaftsimmanent. Aber im Bereich der Kommunikation können wir es uns nicht erlauben, jahrelang zu prüfen. Die Wissenschaft hat nun ein Engagement bei oder für [Wikipedia](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/format/wikipedia/) so lange geprüft, bis es zu spät war. Nur einzelne Einrichtungen wie die Universität Innsbruck bilden hier Ausnahmen. Da würde ich mir manchmal mehr Mut zum Experimentieren wünschen!

Leßmöllmann: Was sich bereits vor zehn Jahren angekündigt hat: Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden. Dass sie in Interessenslagen und Machtstrukturen eingebettet ist und dass es als machtvoller kommunikativer Akt angesehen wird, wenn jemand „bestimmt“, was wahr oder falsch ist – das war damals eher ein Gedankenexperiment, ist heute aber deutlich als Konflikt zu spüren.

…

items.body:
# Injured Ukrainian soldiers learn to use their new limbs | Psyche Videos

https://player.vimeo.com/video/1238020752

### Far from home, Ukrainian soldiers relearn to inhabit their bodies

It’s estimated that as many as 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers and civilians have lost a limb since Russia began its full-scale invasion in 2022. At the Protez Foundation in Oakdale, Minnesota, such patients are fitted with state-of-the-art prosthetics free of charge and are taught how to use their new limbs. However, as the stirring short documentary Liminal captures, the process is far more than just physical.

For the film, the director Brennan Vance profiled a group of Ukrainian soldiers who, injured on the front lines, came to Minnesota to recover far from the brutal war that had defined their lives for years. Yet, despite their life-altering injuries, most were still eager to continue fighting, especially as the US commitment to the cause seemed to be waning. With the encouraging guidance of Yakov Gradinar, the Ukrainian-American chief medical officer at the Protez Foundation, the young men learned not only how to be in their bodies once again, but also how to inhabit the world. Poignant and inspiring, Vance’s documentary is both a unique window into the ongoing conflict and a powerful portrait of what it means to suffer a profound loss and yet still find a way forward.

items.body:
The great Danish philosopher and religious writer Søren Kierkegaard was born at the beginning of the 19th century and died at age 42, suddenly, on the street one day. He was educated at the University of Copenhagen, where he later completed theological seminary to prepare for the Danish Lutheran priesthood, but—being perhaps too stubborn and uncertain of himself—he never ordained and never held a pulpit, though he remained a passionate Christian throughout his life and is considered one of the great Christian theologians. Kierkegaard was certainly an extreme and unusual person: a brilliant thinker and writer whose opinions were often as obscure as they were vehement. Internally fixated, he was equally a social person; he spent long hours each day roaming the streets of Copenhagen, stopping to chat with passersby about anything and everything, a practice he called “people-bathing.”

The central event of Kierkegaard’s life was his strange, brief engagement to Regine Olsen in 1840. Kierkegaard was apparently deeply in love with this attractive young woman, but as soon as they became engaged, he realized that an ordinary life of marriage and household would be impossible for him, and he would do her a great disservice by attempting it. So he broke off the engagement. Regine was devastated, and the more Kierkegaard demurred the more she wanted him. Eventually he attempted to dissuade her by pretending to be a terrible cad who was playing philosophically and experimentally with her affections (which he actually believed), but this did not work either. Eventually he had to move to Berlin to escape the emotional entanglement and the public ridicule all this brought on him. His profound reflections about this love affair—which for him involved the questions of what love actually is or isn’t, what a person is or isn’t, and what commitment, eternity, and religious faith are—never left off and may well have been the source of his creativity and the genesis of his ideas. He wrote about the affair in his work *Repetition*, which is a sort of novel about the complex and philosophical therapeutic relationship between a psychologist and a young man in love (whose circumstances are more or less identical to those of Kierkegaard).

During the decade that followed this event, Kierkegaard published an astonishing number of nearly unclassifiable works, many under pseudonyms—spanning philosophy, psychology, aesthetics, literary criticism, devotional works, fictions. No one seems to have a handle on exactly what his point of view was, because he was against systematic thinking (his works are full of passion and range all over the place) and because of the pseudonyms. Kierkegaard never straightforwardly stated his positions, so it’s unclear to what extent the pseudonymous works represent his own point of view and to what extent they espouse ideas he wanted to satirize. This is not surprising: He wrote his doctoral thesis on the use of irony in the Socratic dialogues, so irony—getting at meaning by not saying what you mean and possibly meaning many things at once, or not meaning what you mean or meaning what you do not mean—was central to his literary impulse.

To the extent his ideas can be characterized, we could say he emphasized the complexity of subjectivity, the awesome responsibility of every individual to their eternal inner nature, and the need for each person to become free of social norms and the tyranny of the crowd so as to find the true path for themselves. I have often thought of Kierkegaard as the ultimate Protestant—one who could accept no religious authority other than his own private and not-communicable relationship to himself and to God: an inherently terrifying and lonely path.

The titles of two of his greatest books tell the story: *Sickness unto Death*, and *Fear and Trembling*. Some call Kierkegaard a Christian existentialist, forerunner to 20th-century existentialist philosophers like Martin Heidegger and Jean-Paul Sartre.

items.body:
Can a fort be an instrument?  In the hands of Dick Raaijmakers, Horst Rickels and Walter Maioli, it can be, and is.  Constructed in the 19th century, Fort Asperen has become the “outer shell” for a series of mechanical installations designed to bring the fort to sonic life.  These instruments channel wind, amplify vibrations and create natural percussion, making the fort a living thing:  FORT KLANK.

The 24-minute track operates as a virtual tour of the facility.  One is free to imagine the fort’s history, from protector of the realm to tourist destination.  When a gong is struck, one thinks of kingly processions; vast metallic scrapes come across as anachronistic heaters and boilers, reminders that when the fort was created, steam power was in vogue.  Various sounds skitter around the background like wild mice no one has been able to eliminate, while the louder squeaks of doors and creaks of hinges suggest the ghosts of those who may have died there.

A massive blast in the fifth minute comes across as a furnace of sound: a call to arms, perhaps, or the heart of the Industrial Revolution.  Were forts always this loud?  If so, how did anyone sleep?  Today’s unmanned forts could benefit from more such installations, which return a sense of their original mystery.  After the blast comes near-silence and a snipping like embroidery; perhaps there were conjugal visits.

Large metallic dragging sounds occupy the center, a reminder of how hard it is to move large machinery.  The gong returns before the density increases again.  The very presence of a fortress implies the possibility of battle, which seems to break out in the eighteenth minute: all hands on deck!  The internal mechanisms are howling, the outer walls are in in danger of being breached, and the cacophony alone is intense enough to strike fear into the hearts of siege makers and those under siege.  Watery sounds join the fray, implying boiling, heating and the use of force. Then it is quiet again: the threat has passed, history has left the fort behind, and visitors are free to travel its corridors, wondering at its walls, its foundations, and most of all its sounds, as strange as the passage of time.  (Richard Allen)

items.title: Laurie Spiegel’s cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth
items.subtitle: Earlier this month, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled beyond 25.902 billion km from Earth, a distance light would travel in 24 hours.
items.feedText: # Laurie Spiegel's cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## Laurie Spiegel’s cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth Peter Kirn - November 26, 2026 Add comment Earlier this month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled beyond 25.902 billion km from Earth, a distance light would travel in 24 hours. Now is a great time to listen to Laurie Spiegel’s contribution to that record — a dizzying sonic model of Kepler’s Harmonice Mundi. An Earth day is essentially meaningless now that Voyager 1 is far from its home planet, but suffice to say the spacecraft is now, in our scale, really far away. It’s a reminder that this whole project was an interstellar equivalent of tossing a bottle into the ocean, with no real chance of ever passing into another star system, let alone being found. So the project, in the words of Carl Sagan at the time, “says something very hopeful about life on this planet.” It’s a reflection on Earth’s life as much as the near-void around. Voyager’s Golden Record would seem a little anachronistic to young humans now if they were to find it.
items.body: # Laurie Spiegel's cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## Laurie Spiegel’s cosmic sounds of Kepler passed one light day from Earth Peter Kirn - November 26, 2026 Add comment Earlier this month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft traveled beyond 25.902 billion km from Earth, a distance light would travel in 24 hours. Now is a great time to listen to Laurie Spiegel’s contribution to that record — a dizzying sonic model of Kepler’s Harmonice Mundi. An Earth day is essentially meaningless now that Voyager 1 is far from its home planet, but suffice to say the spacecraft is now, in our scale, really far away. It’s a reminder that this whole project was an interstellar equivalent of tossing a bottle into the ocean, with no real chance of ever passing into another star system, let alone being found. So the project, in the words of Carl Sagan at the time, “says something very hopeful about life on this planet.” It’s a reflection on Earth’s life as much as the near-void around. Voyager’s Golden Record would seem a little anachronistic to young humans now if they were to find it. It comes with instructions and a handy accessory pack including a needle and cartridge — we are literally talking a phonograph record here, albeit one printed on copper. Laurie Spiegel’s own composition, then, is both the least-mentioned detail of the record, and perhaps the most forward thinking. I actually wonder if it was fully appreciated by Sagan’s committee at the time; I understand just an excerpt made it on the record. And maybe the reason it doesn’t get mentioned in NASA’s music section is that a lot of 1970s ears didn’t really consider this music. And yet — give it a listen. Kepler’s Harmony of the Worlds is a hypnotic, sonic expression of geometry. (The re-release is sold out as physical, in case you had a spacecraft you wanted to glue it to, but is available as digital download.) It’s an exquisite piece of code and composition. The Expanding Universe by Laurie Spiegel The music collection is compelling — maybe more creative in its non-Western choices. (Kudos to Carl Sagan for the breadth of ideas here, though; that kind of spirit is something we could use more now!) The sound choices, from humpback whale song to a kiss, are to me the most fun to listen back on, a 1970s sound portrait of humanity. And that’s ultimately the thought experiment, asking us to consider our place on a cosmic scale. It’s not the Total Perspective Vortex — more like a reflection on an Earth perspective. NASA · Golden Record: Sounds of Earth The greetings are sweet: NASA · Golden Record: Greetings to the Universe The ISS crew sent a message to Voyager 1, leaving that spacecraft a little less alone: The original press release: Voyager Will Carry Earth Sounds Record And more, from NASA/JPL: What are the contents of the Golden Record? Where are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 Now? And Smithsonian Magazine: What Is on Voyager’s Golden Record? And of course, let’s hope this doesn’t happen. Uh, sorry — spoilers. I guess. (You’ve had since 1979; too late. See, maybe if they’d done what the ISS did in the movie, they wouldn’t have had this catastrophe.) Previously on CDM: > Free sounds are a window into space exploration on Earth > Get a free sampled drum kit made in a spacecraft test facility > Three years of solar flares transformed into music: ESA x Maple Pools Photo at top: NASA/JPL. items.body:
The [campaign to secure land for the Uganda Buddhist Centre](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-seeks-to-save-wetland-build-africas-first-dedicated-retreat-center/) (UBC) has passed $1 million, putting it halfway to its $2 million goal, organizers announced this week. Another $750,000 is needed to complete the land purchase by [the December 15 deadline](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-campaign-secures-land-deposit-sets-new-december-deadline/).

“What we do in the next three weeks decides whether this land is protected forever,” campaign organizer Leslie Booker wrote in the announcement.

### The story so far

Lion’s Roar [first reported on the campaign](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-seeks-to-save-wetland-build-africas-first-dedicated-retreat-center/) in August, as UBC marked its 20th anniversary. Founded in 2005 by Bhante Buddharakkhita, UBC was the first Buddhist center in Uganda and the first in Africa established by an African monk. Its campus in Bulega-Garuga, near Entebbe, includes the Buddhist Peace School, the African Buddhist High School, and a medical center serving the surrounding community.

The campaign aims to buy 13 acres of wetland next to the campus, on the shores of Lake Nalubaale (Lake Victoria), the source of the Nile. Bhante Buddharakkhita plans to build what organizers describe as the first retreat center on the African continent dedicated solely to sharing the dhamma, and to protect the wetland permanently. If the land isn’t secured, it could be sold for a resort or a military base. Organizers warn that either would threaten food and water security for nearby schools, an orphanage, and surrounding villages.

In September, [we reported](https://www.lionsroar.com/uganda-buddhist-centre-campaign-secures-land-deposit-sets-new-december-deadline/) that supporters had paid the $875,000 deposit needed to hold the land, and that the seller had extended the deadline for the remaining balance to December 15.

### “ Halfway home “

The $1.75 million asking price makes up most of the campaign’s $2 million goal. The rest covers surveys and unexpected costs. With $1 million raised, the $750,000 still needed by December 15 would complete the purchase itself.

Booker credited the campaign’s community for the milestone, saying every dollar came “from people like you,” through gifts large and small and through supporters sharing the campaign with others. Organizers are asking for “gratitude gifts” over the Thanksgiving week, whether it’s a donor’s first gift or their fifth. They’re also asking supporters to share the campaign with friends.

### A new film

The campaign has also released a short film, *Find Friends: Bhante Buddharakkhita and the Uganda Buddhist Centre*. It tells the story of UBC, Bhante Buddharakkhita’s vision for the land, and why protecting it matters. The film features Bhante Buddharakkhita and Booker.

“If you’ve ever tried to explain what Bhante means to you and couldn’t find the words, this film does it for you,” Booker wrote.

### How to help

Donations can be made through the campaign’s [Chuffed page](https://chuffed.org/project/201770-expanding-bhante-buddharakkhitas-uganda-buddhist-centre). Gifts are tax-deductible in the US. Donor-advised fund grants and employer matching gifts are also accepted. Supporters can also start a fundraising team with their sangha or friends through the same page.

items.body:
Built in 1840, this one-room School House served as the educational center for all of the first to eighth grade children in the Hockanum area, later serving only up to sixth grade. This was one of several school houses serving small neighborhood communities around Hadley.

A 1647 Massachusetts law required all towns with 50 or more families to hire a teacher to instruct their children in reading and writing. Parents and students contributed to their school in the form of money, goods, supplies, and chores.

These were one-room schoolhouses, on land that was usually donated. Most schools had one book, the "New England Primer," that was used to teach the alphabet, syllables, and prayer.

The last class to go through this school was in 1933. By then, it was more economical to bus students to the center of town than to keep the neighborhood school houses open.

Along with the outhouse next to it, the Hockanum School House was, and still is, taken care of by the Hockanum community.

items.body:
# Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Back to Articles

## Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Published November 27, 2026Update on GitHub Upvote -David CorvoysierdacorvoJingya HuangJingyaSayak Paulsayakpaul

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

A seal dreams of warm sand. Generated entirely on Trainium3.

### Two goals

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

### How it works

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

[{"name":"dream","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, shallow depth of field. A plump seal ... is fast asleep on warm golden sand under palm trees ...","seed":3},{"name":"nap","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... a plump grey seal is fast asleep on a small ice floe ...","seed":1,"to":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":9}},{"name":"iceberg","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... the whole iceberg slowly rolls over ... and washes over the seal. ..."},{"name":"shake","prompt":"Style: cinematic, realistic, wide-angle lens. ... It slowly shakes its head and body ... and flops down on its belly on the floe, ...","from":{"shot":"iceberg","frames":25}}]

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

- from: the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion.
- to: the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it.
A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

# 1909 Chinese provincial elections - Wikipedia

Jump to contentFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopediaFirst Chinese provincial elections

Elections were held in 21 of Qing China's 22 provinces, excepting Xinjiang. Non-provinces are marked in white.

The Qing dynasty held its first set of provincial assembly elections from February to June 1909. Following a lengthy period of political turmoil which included the failure of the 1898 Hundred Days' Reform and the 1899–1901 Boxer Rebellion, the constitutionalist movement gained approval from the imperial court and Empress Dowager Cixi. Seeing local self-governance as a first step towards constitutionalism, in 1907 the Qing Government approved the creation of provincial assemblies. The following year, an indirect election system was outlined to fill these assemblies. They were held in 21 of the country's 22 provinces; Xinjiang elections were postponed due to low rates of literacy in Chinese. Suffrage and candidacy was limited to a small population of wealthy men, most of whom were members of the scholar-gentry. Public attitudes towards the elections were generally apathetic, and corruption, fraud, and vote buying were common across the country. Turnout greatly varied between provinces and regions, but was generally low.

The elected provincial assemblies were composed largely of constitutionalists, who were often divided between progressive and conservative wings. Some assemblymen were clandestine members of the revolutionary organization Tongmenghui. The assemblies agitated for a variety of economic and political reforms, which brought them into conflict with the provincial governors, who held veto power over the bodies. The assemblies participated in parliamentary elections, electing half of the members of the National Assembly. Before another set of elections could be held, the Qing dynasty collapsed in the 1911 Revolution and the Republic of China was founded. The first provincial elections under the new government were held in 1912.

### Background

Further information: Late Qing reformsConstitutionalist leader Liang Qichao, c.1905

Since the Song dynasty (960–1279), scholars were appointed to positions in the imperial Chinese bureaucracy through the imperial examination system.[1] This system was carried through to the late Qing dynasty, although it had come under increasing intellectual opposition during the late 19th century as corrupt and ineffective. As it entered the 20th century, the Qing empire was in social and political turmoil, facing a series of defeats by the Western powers. Despite the repression of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898, the constitutionalist movement continued to advocate for the creation of a constitutional government in lieu of Qing absolutism. The writer Liang Qichao emerged as the movement's most influential leader.[2][3][4]

The de facto head of state Empress Dowager Cixi, previously opposed to the reform movement, had begun to grow sympathetic in the wake of China's humiliation in the Boxer Rebellion and the upset victory of the constitutionalist Empire of Japan in the Russo-Japanese War.[2] The administrative, bureaucratic, and judicial systems were the first major targets for reform; redundant and archaic offices were abolished, the functions of the Six Boards (powerful imperial government agencies) were transferred to a new set of civil ministries, and the three northeastern provinces were integrated into the administrative framework of the other provinces.[5] In June 1905, prominent imperial officials Yuan Shikai, Zhang Zhidong, and Zhou Fu jointly submitted a call for the creation of a constitutional monarchy.[6]

Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly [Opportunities Newsletter](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/newsletter/opportunities/).

**[Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + Photo](https://innovateartistgrants.org)** **Featured**
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.**

**[Bryson County Retreat](https://www.brysoncountyretreat.org/)** **Featured**
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**Open Calls**

**[Wildlife Photographer of the Year](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/wildlife-photographer-of-the-year/competition.html)** *(International)*
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
**Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.**

**[Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art](https://responsafoundation.com/2026/10/13/this-memory-competition/)** *(International)*
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for *This Memory,* a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead.
**Deadline: December 4, 2026.**

**[Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab](https://www.moabarts.org/public-art-application)** (Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.**

**[Material Works Art Award 2026](https://pci.jotform.com/form/262185636090156)** *(International)*
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
**Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.**

**[Call for Mail Art](https://www.hivebookarts.org/exhibitions/call-for-mail-art)** *(International)*
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition *love|mark*, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
**Deadline:** **December 15, 2026.**

# All our models of how the mind functions are missing something

## The energy of thought

### We have an astonishing number of models of how the mind works. All of them neglect something essential

The Moment the Snow Melts (2025), an installation by the Japanese artist Chiharu Shiota, in Milan, Italy. Photo by Emanuele Cremaschi/Getty Images

Listen to this essay

20 minutelisten

Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.

So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?

‘Metabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is important to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

The brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.

A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer: the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

We argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. But that does not require the mind to be uniquely realised by the brain: metabolic constraints narrow the options without settling on a single one. Consider the example of memory storage. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.

So the metabolic constraints on physical systems like brains cannot be ignored when modelling the mind. This means rethinking our stance towards views like multiple realisability and medium independence. Rather than taking them to be firm metaphysical commitments, we should think of them as working hypotheses: great starting points, but open to revision after new research.

Recently, the philosophers Mazviita Chirimuuta, Corey Maley and Rosa Cao have each argued that information-processing in brains depends on signal amplitudes, metabolic molecules and energy supply. This suggests a tight link between mind and metabolism, but it does not decisively rule out multiple realisability or medium independence. Instead, it shows that studying brain metabolism can test how much these hypotheses help us understand the mind. Looking at metabolism is therefore important, even if future science finds out that there is no one-to-one relation between mind and brain, that minds can exist in silicon, or that body and environment are essential for cognition.

Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime

The past 25 years have seen great advances in our understanding of brain metabolism, providing us with a wealth of material for studying metabolic constraints on the mind. We now have detailed energy budgets: the brain devotes about 16 per cent of its energy to generating action potentials, 44 per cent to transmitting these signals chemically at the synapse, and 40 per cent to maintaining and repairing neuron cells. This means that only 60 per cent of brain energy is for signalling, while the rest is spent keeping the neural machinery from falling apart. According to a 2015 paper by the neuroscientists Elisabeth Engl and David Attwell, energy for maintenance and repair ‘must contribute to limiting the cognitive abilities of the brain because the total energy use of the brain constrains the temporal rate at which information can be encoded and processed.’ But budgets like this are too coarse on their own to serve as constraints, especially when modelling individual cognitive capacities. Numerical costs of information-processing, by contrast, are more specific. According to one study by the theoretical neuroscientist Jan Karbowski and colleagues, storing one bit of information in the synapse costs about 500,000 ATP (the ‘fuel’ of the cell).

Return to the example of memory. How can metabolism help us assess whether a model of memory is plausible? The dominant theoretical framework in neuroscience is that memory is stored in synapses: the junctions where signals pass from one neuron another. When a new memory is formed, the synapses change, affecting the signals that are transmitted. One such change is known as ‘Hebbian learning’, named for the neuropsychologist Donald Hebb, whose work is summed up in the slogan (not his) ‘neurons that fire together, wire together’.

Models are useful when they solve a theory’s problems, and the synaptic theory has two big ones. The first, often called interference, is that synapses that change easily are good at storing new memories but bad at keeping old ones. Almost any change in neural firing alters a synapse’s molecular makeup slightly. But then how do new memories keep from overwriting old ones? The second problem is called turnover. Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime. In order to stay alive, neurons must constantly rebuild their decaying parts. A neuron is like Otto Neurath’s ship, rebuilt plank by plank at sea. How does information survive in a system whose every part is being replaced?

In 2016, Stefano Fusi and Marcus Benna published a mathematical model to solve the interference problem. It asks us to imagine the synaptic memory process as a set of beakers – each standing for a chemical process at the synapse – filled with liquid and connected by tubes. The level in the first beaker is the synapse’s strength: adding liquid strengthens it, and removing liquid weakens it. ‘Over time,’ Benna explained in an interview, ‘the resulting flow of liquid will diffuse across the other beakers, corresponding to the long-term storage of memories.’ Because those deeper beakers fill and drain more slowly, they hold a trace of past changes and keep drawing the first beaker back towards its old level. New memories form quickly; old ones fade only slowly, as the levels even out.

However, metabolic constraints render this solution implausible. The beaker model describes a system in which biochemical processes in the synapse even out over time: liquid can flow one way or the other, but it ultimately reaches equilibrium. In biology, settling into equilibrium means death. As the physicist Erwin Schrödinger put it: ‘Living matter evades the decay to equilibrium.’ Neurons must take in and expel ions and molecules to stay alive. A neuron that reaches equilibrium loses its organisation and can no longer perform functions such as storing memories at the synapse. Treating metabolism as a constraint shows us that a linear beaker model does not solve the problem of forming new synaptic memories and keeping old ones. This consequence is easy to miss if modellers do not consider the relevance of metabolism.

Metabolism itself, though, points to a better model. Karbowski has developed a model of synaptic memory in which metabolism takes centre stage. Because living systems are never at equilibrium, he builds his model with the mathematics of nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Unlike the beaker model, this framework describes the resting state of the synapse as not being in equilibrium with its environment, and thus capable of storing memories.

Holding on to old memories costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep them while laying down new ones

The model links biochemical processes at the synapse in cycles rather than in linear sequences (as in the beaker model). ATP powers transitions between states in the cycle, so metabolism is built into the model directly. These transitions represent how the synapse strengthens or weakens to store or erase memories. Because the state changes in the cycle have different rates, they never reach equilibrium. The synapse can form new memories and keep them over time without dying.

Karbowski then combines the cyclic model with the numerical costs of information-processing (such as the ATP cost per bit of memory storage). His calculations show that encoding new memories is energetically cheap, and so is, under certain conditions, storing them for a long time. That may explain why interference doesn’t erase long-lasting memories: holding on to them costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep old memories while laying down new ones. The same picture suggests an answer to the turnover problem: if a memory is held in a state that the synapse actively maintains, rather than in any particular molecules, it can outlast the molecules themselves, much as Neurath’s ship stays afloat precisely because it is constantly being rebuilt.

A second example of how metabolism can inform models comes from research on mental effort. When you start work in the morning, you feel fresh. But as the day grinds on and you’re writing your 700th email and attending your fifth meeting, tasks that were easy become gruelling. This is the cost of mental effort. How can mental effort be modelled? One possibility is the ego depletion model, developed by the psychologist Roy Baumeister and colleagues. It posits that performing effortful tasks depends on a finite resource: glucose in the brain. The decrease in performance is explained by the decrease of the resource.

But the model has been challenged on empirical grounds, such as difficulties with replicating its findings. As a result, researchers such as Robert Kurzban and colleagues have turned towards computational models of mental effort, in which the brain calculates the benefits and costs of staying on task versus switching to another activity. Proponents conclude that computational models are superior, and that metabolism is not relevant to model mental effort.

Yet the opposition between resource models such as ego depletion and computational models of mental effort is false. Ego depletion was undone partly by metabolic evidence: the brain’s glucose use barely changes during demanding tasks, far too little for an afternoon of self-control to run it down. That is metabolism doing just what we have described, ruling out a model the brain could not run. And computational models face metabolic questions of their own, because weighing the costs and benefits of staying on task is itself work that must be paid for. Neuroscientists such as Amitai Shenhav, Matthew Botvinick and Clay Holroyd believe this computational process takes place in a brain area known as the anterior cingulate cortex. We can use evidence about available energy to assess whether models of this process are feasible.

Some researchers already integrate metabolism into their models of mental effort. Alexandre Zénon and colleagues, for instance, posit that effortful tasks require the brain to process more information and therefore use slightly more energy. Since its energy budget has a hard upper limit, the brain needs to spend less energy on other tasks. Zénon and his team explicitly link metabolism to our subjective feeling of effort, which might reflect how fast metabolic changes build up during demanding tasks. Fatigue, in turn, might reflect our expectation that these changes will continue.

Likewise, Holroyd’s ‘controllosphere’ model starts from the theory of how the brain controls behaviour and draws on empirical findings that sustained mental effort produces waste in neurons. On this model, the feeling of effort is a signal to the brain to stop tasks that require high control, so that waste can be cleared before causing damage. Research on mental effort shows that including metabolism into models of the mind is not a mere theoretical possibility. It is already a practical reality.

Attention to metabolism and energy use can improve more than just our knowledge of biological organisms. It can also help our understanding of artificial neural networks at the heart of dramatic advances in artificial intelligence. While the speed of development is new, the link between AI and the brain is old, going back to the first neural network model in 1943, from pioneers such as Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, or ‘the perceptron’ of Frank Rosenblatt in 1958. Recent advances like LLMs (large language models) reignited existential questions about whether AI is really intelligent, or even conscious. Metabolism and energy use should inform how we approach these questions.

The relationship between AI and energy use is largely uncharted territory, and a metabolically informed perspective suggests where to start looking. Hyperscale data centres use a lot of energy, far beyond the 20 watts the human brain runs on. Yet in philosophy and cognitive science, views like medium independence lead scholars to think of AI in abstract, formal terms: while the physical basis of an AI system may vary, the computation, so the thought goes, is the same. This focus on abstract computation leads philosophers such as Luke Kersten and Leonard Dung to argue that AI systems could, in principle, duplicate human minds. But, in brains, energy constraints help determine which computations are performed in the first place. If the same holds for artificial systems, then whether a chip and a brain are running ‘the same’ computation cannot simply be assumed. It has to be found out.

Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows

Our research belongs to a growing discussion of energy use and its role in modelling both brains and AI systems. For example, Cao and the neuroscientist Daniel Yamins have studied how AI models implement a highly abstract version of the mechanism that brains use to respond to novel visual stimuli. Cao and Yamins recognise that brains and engineered AI face different energy constraints, yet they consider energetics only abstractly, in terms of efficiency and optimisation. We propose instead to rethink energy use in AI from the bottom up. How an AI system uses energy is a modelling problem, which depends on scale, training data and details of grid infrastructure, just as the brain’s energy use depends on the details of its metabolism. This crucial parallel between studying brains and AI systems is missed when we focus on task optimisation alone. Modelling AI energy use informs how and when energetic differences lead to computational, perhaps even cognitive, differences.

Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows. AI energy use is a practical problem that the study of metabolism can help tackle. Cognitive scientists such as Megan Peters are already looking to the brain to improve energy efficiency in AI. These projects highlight the practical benefits that come from studying brain metabolism for engineering projects like AI model building. They also have theoretical benefits: projects that include energy use serve as tests of philosophical positions like medium independence.

When it comes to figuring out how to model minds, it is time that researchers take a ‘metabolic turn’, to quote our colleague Patrick McGivern. Taking seriously how systems use energy and regulate themselves gives us new ways of addressing the toughest questions that we face in making sense of the mind.

# Buchkritik zu »Der letzte Akt« - Spektrum der Wissenschaft

## Buchkritik zu »Der letzte Akt«

### Pilgernd zur Macht

### Rasputin als Symbol für den Niedergang der Monarchie

Startseite Kultur Aktuelle Seite: Buchkritik zu »Der letzte Akt« Rasputin gilt vielen als der unheimliche Strippenzieher am Hof des letzten russischen Zaren, und eine Biografie über ihn scheint eine gute Mischung aus »Sex and Crime«, Politik und Verrat, opulent lebendem Adel und darbendem Volk zu versprechen. Das Lied »Rasputin« (1978) der Popgruppe »Boney M.«, das ihn als »Lover of the Russian Queen« betitelt, dürfte zu dieser Wahrnehmung beigetragen haben. Aber was steckt hinter all diesen Mythen, Gerüchten und Berichten über den aus Sibirien stammenden Bauern, der kaum lesen und schreiben konnte, aber einen folgenschweren Einfluss auf die Zarenfamilie und damit auf die Geschichte Russlands gewann? Der namhafte Historiker Antony Beevor beleuchtet in spannendem, erzählendem Stil all die kulturellen und politischen Umstände, die Rasputins Aufstieg ins Zentrum des Zarenreichs und vor allem ins Innerste der Familie Romanow ermöglichten. »Der letzte Akt« ist daher nicht nur für Leser interessant, die etwas über Rasputin erfahren möchten. Das Buch bietet auch tiefe Einblicke in das Russland zu Anfang des 20. Jahrhunderts – und damit kurz vor seinem Kollaps. Pilgernd zur Macht So erfährt der – durchaus überraschte – Leser, welch große Bedeutung Rasputins Religiosität für seinen Zugang zum Adel hatte. Denn seinen Aufstieg begann er als »Strannik«, als mittelloser Pilger, der von Ort zu Ort zog. Stranniki galten als heilige Menschen, die Krankheiten heilen und zukünftige Ereignisse vorhersagen konnten. Auch in den Adelshäusern erfreuten sie sich großer Beliebtheit. Als religiöse Autorität erlangte Rasputin – trotz seines zweifelhaften Leumunds aufgrund seiner Ausschweifungen, die bis hin zu sexueller Gewalt gingen – Zugang zum innersten Kern der Zarenfamilie. Vor allem auf die Zarin Alexandra Fjodorowna hatte Rasputin ungeheuren Einfluss. Sie betrachtete ihn als weisen Freund der Familie, ohne den keine politische Entscheidung getroffen werden durfte. Bald konnte im Zarenreich nur noch ein politisches Amt besetzen, wer Rasputin gegenüber bedingungslose Loyalität zeigte. Dies geschah in einer Zeit, die für die Dynastie der Romanows auch so schon gefährlich genug war. Innenpolitisch gab es massive Unruhen aufgrund der prekären Lage der Arbeiter und Bauern, die der Erste Weltkrieg noch weiter verschlimmerte. Der Adel schwelgte im Reichtum, während Korruption und Misswirtschaft das Land zugrunde richteten. Zar Nikolaus II. war derweil von seinem eigenen Gottesgnadentum überzeugt, zeigte aber keinerlei Mitgefühl für die leidende Bevölkerung. Rasputin als Symbol für den Niedergang der Monarchie Zudem hatte sich Rasputin viele Feinde unter den russischen Adeligen gemacht, die im Zuge seines Aufstiegs an Einfluss bei Hofe verloren hatten. Auch in der Öffentlichkeit genoss Rasputin einen schlechten Ruf: Er wurde zum Symbol für Korruption, Machtmissbrauch und die Schwäche der Monarchie. Das Gerücht, dass Rasputin der Geliebte der Zarin sei, kostete Nikolaus II.
