> [“An appropriately designed critical thinking class can dramatically reduce four common biases in judgment and decision making”](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2027-52606-001) — a newly published study by Michael Bishop, Adam Feltz, and Paul Conway [(previously discussed here)](https://dailynous.com/2026/02/16/crafting-a-critical-thinking-course-that-sticks-with-students-guest-post/)

items.title: Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?
items.subtitle: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association.
items.feedText:
# Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?

Skip to main content

## Why is Fox Newsobsessed with the WNBA?

Fox News

Fox News’ fixation on the league dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t consume Fox News myself.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA.

The first clue came at a family gathering. A conservative relative started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark while parroting right-wing conspiracy theories about Black players. This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

Background graphic pulls out and plays four videos with chyron headlines: “Why does the left hate Caitlin Clark?”, “Flagrant fouls against Caitlin Clark continue”, “ WNBA suspends Thomas 1 game after punching Clark”, and “Critics say Caitlin Clark is being snubbed by the WNBA.”

The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, I was recommended more. That made sense. But then stories from, of all places, Fox News started appearing in my feed.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about the WNBA.

Headline after headline pitted Clark, the league’s white, straight-coded star, against other players, almost entirely Black and queer women.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Caitlin Clark. Three headlines are pulled out: “Caitlin Clark fans unload on WNBA, Thomas after violent sequence leaves Fever star battered,” “WNBA star who hurt Caitlin Clark’s eye calls for league to take action against Trump administration policies”, and “Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese a jacka– for jealousy of Caitlin Clark in response to ESPN analyst.”

Fox News also singled out specific players, framing Angel Reese as “entitled” and “laughably bad,” despite Reese being named the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year and reaching the Finals in her third year (notably, before Clark).

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Angel Reese. Four headlines are pulled out: “Angel Reese embarrasses herself with cringe video, needs to get a grip: WATCH”, “Why does Angel Reese get a pass for acting like an entitled brat over her dumb Caitlin Clark comment?”, “Don’t be fooled, Angel Reese was laughably bad in another blowout loss”, and “Angel Reese dangerously peddles racist conspiracy theory after WNBA coach calls her two words.”

When it comes to sports, there are, at least seemingly, facts. This team won, and this team lost. This player scored a lot of points. You would expect a lot of similar coverage. But this was different. On their website, Fox News even elevated the WNBA right alongside… literal war.

A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026.

To measure just how deep this obsession ran, I turned to data.

I analyzed over 30,000 WNBA-related articles from 2019 to 2026 across Fox News (and its sports arm OutKick) against six peer outlets: the Associated Press, CBS (Sports + News), ESPN (+Andscape), The New York Times (+The Athletic), USA Today, and the Washington Post.

To see what was happening on television, I also analyzed thousands of cable news chyrons — the banners running across the bottom of the screen — from Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC (now MS NOW) dating back to 2017. See more in the methods.

on the web

### Which players get an outsized share of Fox News’ attention?

Compared with

on television

### The words used in television chyrons

Cable news chyrons, September 2017–November 1, 2026, from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye.

Let’s look at online headlines first. The center line here represents an equal balance. If Fox News and other outlets devoted the exact same percentage of their WNBA coverage to Clark, she would sit right in the middle.

A dot plot showing the share of coverage by players including Sophie Cunningham, DiJonai Carrington, Angel Reese, Caitlin Clark, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner, Aliyah Boston, Paige Bueckers, Alyssa Thomas, Kelsey Mitchell, A'ja Wilson, Breanna Stewart, and Napheesa Collier. The X axis ranges from 15× bigger share for other outlets (left) to equal (center) to 15× bigger share for Fox News (right).

Instead, Clark pulls a 3.5× larger share of Fox News’ WNBA headlines than she does across all other outlets combined (the further right a player is, the more heavily they over-index on Fox News).

Clark’s dot moves right to 3.5× bigger share for Fox News.

Other players get an outsized share of Fox News’ attention, too — but largely when they can be plugged into the network’s culture-war machinery.

All other players’ dots move. Sophie Cunningham, DiJonai Carrington, Angel Reese, Caitlin Clark, Natasha Cloud, and Brittney Griner have bigger shares of coverage on Fox News. Aliyah Boston has equal coverage. Paige Bueckers, Alyssa Thomas, Kelsey Mitchell, A'ja Wilson, Breanna Stewart, and Napheesa Collier have bigger shares of coverage by other outlets.

Fox News champions players who match its base. Sophie Cunningham draws 10× more headline share on the network than across other mainstream outlets, boosted by her public stance against trans inclusion in sports.

Sophie Cunningham’s dot is highlighted showing 10× bigger share of Fox News headlines.

It turns outspoken players into political lightning rods, obsessing over Natasha Cloud’s racial justice activism and Brittney Griner’s Russian imprisonment and gender identity.

srText: Natasha Cloud’s dot (3.1× Fox News) and Brittney Griner’s dot (2.1× Fox News) are highlighted, showing bigger shares of Fox News headlines.

It also inflames on-court tension by weaponizing physical play, framing Black players like Reese and DiJonai Carrington as hostile or violent toward their white counterparts.

Angel Reese’s dot (3.3× Fox News) and DiJonai Carrington’s dot (6.7× Fox News) are highlighted, showing bigger shares of Fox News headlines.

Napheesa Collier’s dot (5.2× other outlets), Gabby Williams’ dot (3.8× other outlets), Breanna Stewart’s dot (3.5× other outlets) and A’ja Wilson’s dot (2.0× other outlets) are highlighted, showing bigger shares of other outlets’ headlines.

But digital headlines are only half the picture. What happens when the lens shifts to prime-time cable?

On television, similar patterns emerge. This ternary plot maps chyron mentions across Fox News (top), CNN (bottom-left), and MSNBC (now MS NOW, bottom-right). The center marks balanced coverage; the closer a dot pulls toward a corner, the more exclusively that single network dominates the conversation.

The dot plot turns into a triangle chart of cable news chyrons, with Fox News at the top, CNN at the bottom left and MSNBC at the bottom right. Sophie Cunningham, DiJonai Carrington, Alyssa Thomas, Gabby Williams, A’ja Wilson and Natasha Cloud are in Fox News’ zone. Caitlin Clark sits on the edge of Fox News’ zone. Angel Reese, Paige Bueckers, Kelsey Mitchell, Breanna Stewart and Napheesa Collier are in CNN’s zone. Brittney Griner and Aliyah Boston are in MSNBC’s zone.

Clark hovers on the Fox News border, with the network accounting for half of her chyron mentions. She serves as an entry point for cultural grievances, especially when paired alongside players who skew even further into Fox News’ territory.

FoxCNNMSNBCFox%

- Fox share:50%
At Fox News’ top apex sits Cunningham, propelled by her public opposition to trans athletes and her reputation as Clark’s“bodyguard.” Fox News routinely pits the two Fever teammates against openly queer Black players like Carrington and Alyssa Thomas, sensationalizing fouls as “cheap shots” or malicious.

Sophie Cunningham, DiJonai Carrington and Alyssa Thomas are highlighted, all in Fox News’ zone.

FoxCNNMSNBCFox%

- Fox share:99%
- Fox share:93%
- Fox share:86%
Fox News routinely bypasses the WNBA’s top talent. The network missed obvious editorial layups: it ignored Napheesa Colliercalling out league leadership — a critique directly aligned with Fox News’ own anti-WNBA talking points — and overlooked Clark’s backcourt partner, Kelsey Mitchell, as she set the all-time single-season scoring record.

Napheesa Collier, Paige Bueckers, Breanna Stewart and Kelsey Mitchell are highlighted in CNN’s zone, and Aliyah Boston in MSNBC’s zone.

FoxCNNMSNBCFox%

- Fox share:0%
- Fox share:0%
- Fox share:0%
- Fox share:0%
- Fox share:0%
An exception among the league's elite is five-time MVP Wilson. Long anchored in CNN territory, her dot swung sharply toward Fox News following an on-court confrontation with a fan during the 2026 playoffs, underscoring how quickly the network tunes in when athletic greatness can be recast as public conflict.

A’ja Wilson’s dot is highlighted, in Fox News’ zone.

FoxCNNMSNBCFox%

- Fox share:57%
### Fightin’ Words

Understanding Fox News’ framing means looking beyond who they cover to how they cover them.

To do that, we applied a text-analysis method aptly called “fightin’ words.” The model pinpoints words uniquely tied to a specific outlet, adjusting for corpus size while deemphasizing commonly used jargon (like “head coach”) and rare, low-signal names (like OutKick writer “Dan Dakich”).

Each term receives a measurement that is standardized as a z-score — what we’ll call a “distinctiveness score” — ranking words by how disproportionately one outlet relies on them compared to the rest.

See how Fox News’ top phrases compare across possible methods.▾RankFightin’ wordsWeighted log odds with an informative prior (z-score)Raw countTimes Fox uses the phraseRate differenceFox’s rate minus others’, per 10,000 phrasesArticle ratioArticles with the phrase, Fox / others1social mediasocial mediasocial mediaDan Dakich2white privilegewomen’s basketballwomen’s sportsstay fearless3black womenwomen’s sportswomen’s basketballpopular because4women’s sportshead coachFever staridentity politics5Fever starnational championshipcollege basketballCari Champion

on the web

### The phrases that define Fox News’ coverage

Compared with1–0 of 0

Fox News: 3,420 WNBA articles; the other outlets: 17,901, April 2023 on. Words ranked by weighted log-odds with an informative prior (Monroe et al. 2008). Tan bars are z-scores under 1.96 (a common threshold). Hover a bar for an example.

Weighted log-odds ratio with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008), using Jack Hessel's implementation, over headlines from April 2023 on. “All outlets” pools ESPN, CBS Sports, USA Today, Just Women's Sports and The Athletic, which together publish far more than Fox — so the horizontal axis, which counts both archives at once, is mostly theirs. Hover any word for the split. The shaded band is |z| < 1.96, where the difference is not distinguishable from chance.

Plotted side by side, WNBA coverage looks like two parallel universes: all other outlets on the left, Fox News on the right.

A diverging bar chart showing the two-word phrases uniquely used by other outlets (left) vs. Fox News (right).

On the left, other outlets focus on actual basketball, emphasizing game strategy with terms like points, rebounds, and free agency.

Basketball phrases are highlighted on the other outlets’ side, such as scored points, points rebounds, free agency, point guard and fourth quarter. None of Fox News’ phrases are highlighted.

Meanwhile, on the right, Fox News’ vocabulary barely touches on-court play. Its coverage is driven by social media reactions and political flashpoints, leaning heavily into conservative buzzwords like “white privilege,” “national anthem,” and “biological men.”

Four of Fox News’ phrases are highlighted: social media (its top phrase), white privilege, national anthem and biological men.

At the center of this framing sits “Fever star” Clark, whom Fox News repeatedly tethers to its conservative agenda.

“Fever star” is highlighted, the 5th phrase on Fox News’ side.

Beyond overarching themes, how are individual players framed? Stars like Clark are often framed very strategically. There is a “fight over Caitlin Clark’s soul,” as professor Kate Starbird, a misinformation researcher and former WNBA player, put it to me. Starbird and collaborators are currently tracking WNBA “outrage bait” on social media, where Clark is often a centerpiece.

When Clark entered the league in 2024, the culture-war media machinery shifted into overdrive (explore our historical network timeline below). Some commentators suggested that conservative audiences embraced Clark partly because of her background as a straight-presenting, white, Midwestern star. As Courtney M. Cox writes in Double Crossover, “It is essential to highlight how basketball, racialized as a Black sport, still privileges whiteness, especially in media coverage and endorsement.”

Starbird notes that Clark isn’t a “stable” figure for the conservative or liberal media. With a few exceptions, Clark is talked about more than she talks — at least off the court, and not to the refs.

To map how those narratives take shape, we applied the distinctiveness model to specific grammatical roles: how players are described, how their play is characterized, what actions they take, and what is done to them.

Sometimes this is Fox News editorializing directly — “Carrington is a dirty player.” Other times, it captures quoted speech or players defending themselves (“DiJonai Carrington sent a message to fans who think she plays ‘dirty.’”) But with “ragebait” media, the distinction collapses: by highlighting Carrington’s claim that she’s not a dirty player, they incite their audience to insist that she is.

Because these player-specific descriptors appear less frequently overall, some carry lower distinctiveness scores that fall below traditionally used thresholds (indicated by tan bars below). They are included because even words used a handful of times (or fewer) can speak volumes. Fox News characterizing Angel Reese’s play as “pathetic” just three times carries immense weight, especially when no other outlets used the word to describe a player (outside quoted speech) across tens of thousands of articles.

You can see the divergent framing even with specific incidents. When Carrington accidentally poked Clark in the eye during a playoff game, The New York Times (via The Athletic) treated the collision as incidental basketball contact. Fox News, meanwhile, opened with a dramatic scene of Carrington sticking her “long fingernail” into Clark’s eye, burying Clark’s comments about intentionality paragraphs later.

vs.New York Times

Caitlin Clark downplayed being poked in the eye by Connecticut Sun guard DiJonai Carrington in Sunday’s WNBA first-round playoff loss, saying her eye “feels good…” “It wasn’t intentional by any means,” Clark said Tuesday. “You just watched the play, it wasn’t intentional.”

Sep 24, 2024 · Article ↗︎

Fox News

Connecticut Sun guard DiJonai Carrington stuck her long fingernail in Caitlin Clark's eye during the Sun's 93-69 win over the Indiana Fever Sunday in the WNBA playoffs… Slow-motion footage showed Carrington bending her hand while coming down from the block attempt, pointing her nails in Clark's face.

Sep 24, 2024 · Article ↗︎

vs.CBS

Cunningham wrapped her up with a hard foul and threw her to the ground, sparking a scuffle between the teams. Cunningham’s foul was upgraded to a Flagrant 2, which comes with an automatic ejection, and Sheldon and Sun guard Lindsay Allen were both ejected as well.

Jun 18, 2025 · Article ↗︎

Fox News

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham received praise on social media Tuesday night as she appeared to defend Caitlin Clark with a hard foul on Connecticut Sun guard Jacy Sheldon… As the Fever put away the Sun 88-71, Cunningham was congratulated for stepping up as the team’s enforcer.

Jun 18, 2025 · Article ↗︎

vs.ESPN

Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas has received a flagrant foul 2 penalty and a one-game suspension for "recklessly making contact with her fist to the throat area" of Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark , the WNBA announced Thursday… "We have a generational talent and WNBA superstar who had two cheap shots [against her] right there that weren't called," White said. "Absolutely unacceptable."

Jun 25, 2026 · Article ↗︎

Fox News

Alyssa Thomas' thug-like play, punching Caitlin Clark in the throat and kneeing her in the groin, is indefensible. The league thought so, and so does the sane general public, who saw the WNBA’s biggest star mugged on the court like she was the victim of some schoolyard bullying... He appears to be implying… that Caitlin Clark receives favorable treatment because she is a generational talent with a massive fan base and because she is white.

Jun 27, 2026 · Article ↗︎

Flip through the coverage to see more diverging moments, including Fox News’ glowing portrayal of Cunningham’s fouls next to their racist description of Alyssa Thomas’s “thug-like play.”

When viewers take that outrage into the real world, the consequences are dangerous. For the league’s predominantly Black players, it has triggered intense harassment, hostile confrontations, and even death threats.

According to The Athletic, players may actively choose to leave or avoid Clark’s team, the Indiana Fever, because of this kind of harmful fan behavior — which actively hurts the game, including Clark’s.

As a white woman, I’ve seen glimpses of this mindset not only from conservative family but from random strangers. For instance, a few months ago, I was waiting at a bus stop, wearing my Seattle Storm jersey and heading to watch a game against the Chicago Sky — Carrington’s team — when a man rolled down his truck window and yelled that he hoped there wouldn’t be any dangerous fouls or funny business. (Uh, go away, sir.) It shows how weirdly pervasive this way of seeing the WNBA has become.

Explore Fox News’ framing by tone, politics, appearance, celebrity, and play more below.

on the web

### How Fox News frames each player in headlines

#### The headlines

Topic Tone Any toneNegativeNeutralPositiveHeadline

### “Rejecting” Identity Politics

While Fox News vociferously rejects “identity politics” in WNBA coverage, they’ve accused outlets like ESPN, USA Today, and The Athletic of being “racial idolaters” and generally injecting left-wing politics about race, gender, and sexuality into their reporting.

Laura Ingraham and Clay Travis, the founder of OutKick, discuss a USA Today column that suggested some of Clark’s fans were racist.

Here’s the irony: Fox News talks more about race, gender, and identity in the WNBA than any other outlet. This year they’ve mentioned race or racial politics in 23% of their WNBA articles, and LGBTQ+ topics in 34%, far more than any other outlet.

Does Fox News simply write more opinion-oriented coverage, while the other outlets stick to sports? I don’t think so, at least not entirely.

For one thing, this comparison includes any opinion pieces or off-court coverage from other outlets, and Fox News does cover actual game play. But the amount of editorializing in Fox News’ reporting is telling in its own right. Few, if any, outlets write about the WNBA quite so much through a cultural and political lens.

A closer look reveals the formula behind that framing.

### Fox News’ framing increasingly relies on “Us vs. Them”

Fox News’ WNBA playbook wasn’t built overnight. In 2019, the network covered the league like everyone else: which is to say, barely at all. Coverage was sparse, mostly confined to the occasional box score, trade note, or injury update, with a few sporadic pieces on players’ activism or politics, like Natasha Cloud’s.

That shifted during the 2020 COVID bubble season when players turned their activism into tangible political power, mobilizing to help unseat Dream co-owner and GOP Senator Kelly Loeffler. Hostility hardened in 2022, during Griner’s imprisonment in Russia. Fox News commentators and conservative politicians often reinforced one another’s framing of the prisoner swap as a weak concession for an “unpatriotic” athlete.

Explore the web of characters mentioned together in Fox News headlines below.

on the web

#### Who Fox News names together

Fox News WNBA headlines, per month

### Race became a Fox News focus when Clark joined the league

on the web

Share of Fox News articles that mention race vs. six other outlets

Share of articles that mention at least one of the following: racism, racist, white privilege, racial, “Black” or “white” + women/girls/players/athletes/stars/community, people/person/women/players/athletes/coaches “of color”.

on television

How Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC split coverage of race in television chyrons

Across mainstream outlets, coverage of race peaked in 2020 during the height of the Black Lives Matter movement. That summer, WNBA players led high-profile demonstrations inside the bubble, walking off the court during the national anthem and wearing “Say Her Name” shirts on national television.

But unlike other outlets, Fox News’ coverage of race didn’t fall off after 2020. Instead, it rebounded and was reframed when Clark entered the league in 2024.

Fox News’ most distinctive race-related phrases aren't about civil rights or systemic equity. They are combative culture-war slogans: “race bullies,” “race idolaters,” and even “race war.”

FOX NEWSMay 2026

### Fox News dramatically accelerated its coverage of LGBTQ+ topics in the last year

on the web

Share of Fox News articles that mention LGBTQ+ topics vs. six other outlets

Share of articles that mention at least one of the following: transgender, trans, gender eligibility, “biological” male/female/woman, LGBT, LGBTQ, lesbian, gay, queer, sexual orientation, same-sex, bisexual, nonbinary.

on television

How Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC split coverage of LGBTQ+ topics in television chyrons

Fox News’ obsessions with race, gender, and the LGBTQ+ community, especially trans women, are intimately connected — a dynamic long unpacked by Black, feminist, and queer scholars through intersectional concepts like “misogynoir” (coined by Moya Bailey) and “transmisogynoir.”

Fox News routinely highlights white players who conform to traditional conventions of femininity — like Cunningham, Kelsey Plum, and Cameron Brink — while denigrating Black players who do not, advancing an ideal of straight, white, femme womanhood. Drawing these boundaries has only one obvious end: hating women, including trans women.

Cunningham reinforced this framing with anti-trans remarks of her own. While she told ESPN that she “got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans” and clarified that “I never once said that,” she repeated conservative anti-trans talking points about “protect[ing] young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men.”

She later doubled down on those comments. And right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates worldwide rallied around her, including Vice President J.D. Vance, J.K. Rowling, and Jennifer Sey.

Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

Trans women’s participation in the WNBA has become a non-stop Fox News preoccupation. On television, they spent more than 13 hours discussing the WNBA in summer 2026 alone. It’s worth repeating: no transgender players are currently in the league.

In our analysis of chyrons from Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC, Fox News was responsible for 96% of the usage of the word “trans” and 90% for “transgender,” totaling over 200 uses.

As Fox News pundit Jesse Watters recently said on air regarding Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve wearing a “Trans Kids Belong” shirt: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”

### Fox News particularly focuses on fouls and “protecting” Clark

on the web

Number of Fox News articles that mention hip-check, poke, punch or throat, or protect (per month)

Number of articles that mention at least one of the following: hip-check, poke/poked, punch/punched, throat, protect/protects.

on television

How Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC split coverage of fouls in television chyrons

One particularly powerful right-wing WNBA narrative — which arguably ties both implicit racism and transphobia together — is about fouls.

From the moment Clark entered the league, conservatives have pushed a story that other players are purposely targeting her on the court, often suggesting it’s because she is white. While Clark has faced real physicality — and calls for better officiating were widespread — the narrative of racialized persecution was pure political spin.

Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner

The Republicans cite, as evidence, the fact that “Clark has been hip-checked, poked in the eye, and struck in the throat during games.” It was an almost verbatim echo of Fox News, who spent months repeating those exact words across more than 200 articles fretting about the need to “protect” Clark.

That fixation on “protecting” Clark easily merged with another familiar right-wing narrative. By casting the WNBA as a hostile environment in need of cultural rescue, commentators tapped into the exact same “protect women and children” playbook long weaponized against trans women.

### This coverage matters

It’s tempting to dismiss this coverage as drivel. But unfortunately, it matters.

Fox News

Fox News anchors a media pipeline connecting prolific right-wing blogs and fringe online content farms directly to Republican politicians, including Donald Trump, who fawned over Cunningham’s looks and castigated the league to loud boos at rallies in the lead-up to the 2026 midterms.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA. Two videos of Trump talking about the WNBA are pulled out.

As their own host Jesse Watters openly said on air, Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. They are exploiting world-class athletes as lucrative ragebait. And it’s working, at least as a business strategy: in August 2026, Fox’s OutKick hit a record 13 million visitors.

Three Fox News clips are pulled out: The Five on a WNBA coach’s “Trans kids belong” T-shirt aimed at Sophie Cunningham, The Big Weekend Show on WNBA Finals ratings amid national anthem drama, and Joe Concha on Cunningham’s post-election message going viral.

The issue isn’t that women’s basketball is being made political — sports are, and have always been, political. The danger is how quickly manufactured panic hardens into policy: Even as the 2026 midterms signaled a broader pushback against anti-trans rhetoric, voters in several states, including my home state of Washington, passed measures restricting transgender students from participating on sports teams that align with their gender identity.

We can’t let the WNBA be weaponized as a Trojan horse for anti-trans politics, or bigotry of any kind. The version of the league peddled by conservative media, the “ragebait W,” is unrecognizable to anyone actually watching the games. So let’s change the channel.

As Roxane Gay argued, the WNBA must match its players’ progressive courage — welcoming trans women while fiercely shielding its athletes from “bad-faith attacks, death threats, harassment, and other racial animus.”

The background switches like a TV changing channels and now shows roughly 40 examples of other outlets’ coverage of the WNBA. Four clips are pulled out: Gabby Williams in an interview, CBS Evening News on the WNBA and players reaching a historic deal, CNN on average WNBA salaries that could rise to over $1 million, and Layshia Clarendon speaking to Andscape.

The W is built different. Inclusivity is in its DNA: from the community in the stands, to beloved non-binary and Black-coded mascots, to the players' relentless push for equity on and off the court. And the basketball is electric. In this pivotal moment of the league’s growth, we need to see the outrage machine for what it is and push back, lest we all get played.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of other outlets’ coverage of the WNBA. Four game clips are pulled out: the Seattle Storm’s in-arena show with its mascot, a moment from a Storm game, and three-pointers from Gabby Williams and Angel Reese.

# Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?

Skip to main content

## Why is Fox Newsobsessed with the WNBA?

Fox News

Fox News’ fixation on the league dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t consume Fox News myself.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ cable coverage of the WNBA.

The first clue came at a family gathering. A conservative relative started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark while parroting right-wing conspiracy theories about Black players. This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

Background graphic pulls out and plays four videos with chyron headlines: “Why does the left hate Caitlin Clark?”, “Flagrant fouls against Caitlin Clark continue”, “ WNBA suspends Thomas 1 game after punching Clark”, and “Critics say Caitlin Clark is being snubbed by the WNBA.”

The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, I was recommended more. That made sense. But then stories from, of all places, Fox News started appearing in my feed.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about the WNBA.

Headline after headline pitted Clark, the league’s white, straight-coded star, against other players, almost entirely Black and queer women.

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Caitlin Clark. Three headlines are pulled out: “Caitlin Clark fans unload on WNBA, Thomas after violent sequence leaves Fever star battered,” “WNBA star who hurt Caitlin Clark’s eye calls for league to take action against Trump administration policies”, and “Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese a jacka– for jealousy of Caitlin Clark in response to ESPN analyst.”

Fox News also singled out specific players, framing Angel Reese as “entitled” and “laughably bad,” despite Reese being named the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year and reaching the Finals in her third year (notably, before Clark).

Background graphic shows roughly 40 examples of Fox News’ online headlines about Angel Reese. Four headlines are pulled out: “Angel Reese embarrasses herself with cringe video, needs to get a grip: WATCH”, “Why does Angel Reese get a pass for acting like an entitled brat over her dumb Caitlin Clark comment?”, “Don’t be fooled, Angel Reese was laughably bad in another blowout loss”, and “Angel Reese dangerously peddles racist conspiracy theory after WNBA coach calls her two words.”

When it comes to sports, there are, at least seemingly, facts. This team won, and this team lost. This player scored a lot of points. You would expect a lot of similar coverage. But this was different. On their website, Fox News even elevated the WNBA right alongside… literal war.

A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026.

To measure just how deep this obsession ran, I turned to data.

I analyzed over 30,000 WNBA-related articles from 2019 to 2026 across Fox News (and its sports arm OutKick) against six peer outlets: the Associated Press, CBS (Sports + News), ESPN (+Andscape), The New York Times (+The Athletic), USA Today, and the Washington Post.

To see what was happening on television, I also analyzed thousands of cable news chyrons — the banners running across the bottom of the screen — from Fox News, CNN, and MSNBC (now MS NOW) dating back to 2017. See more in the methods.

on the web

### Which players get an outsized share of Fox News’ attention?

Compared with

on television

### The words used in television chyrons

Cable news chyrons, September 2017–November 1, 2026, from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye.

Let’s look at online headlines first. The center line here represents an equal balance. If Fox News and other outlets devoted the exact same percentage of their WNBA coverage to Clark, she would sit right in the middle.

# Reverse Engineering and Modifying Windows 8 apps

Hi folks,

In this article I’ll share the results of ad-hoc security vulnerabilities research I’ve done on windows 8 apps deployment. Specifically, we’ll discuss fundamental design flaws that allow to Reverse Engineer Win8 apps, modification of installed apps and the negative implications on Intellectual Property rights protection, Licensing models and overall PC security. Finally we’ll discuss some creative ideas on how to mitigate these security issues.

### Meet the mother-load: C:\Program Files\Applications

All Windows 8 applications in the developer preview are installed under the clandestine C:\Program Files\Applications location. I will hazard a guess and say that once the Windows App Store goes online it will install all apps under that folder. Currently the folder is an invisible one and cannot be accessed from Windows Explorer user interface on a new Win8 developer preview install.

Here’s an example of some of the 29 apps Win8 apps installed on the Win8 developer preview:

And here’s the hidden folder backing it up:

### Gaining Access to C:\Program Files\Applications

In essence you’ll need to navigate to that folder, hit “Security Tab” and set yourself up as the owner. Let me walk you through that process step-by-step.

1. Type in “C:\Program Files\Applications” in the Windows Explorer address bar and hit enter.

2. Observe in shock and dismay the system dialogue saying you don’t own a folder on your own machine. Hit “Continue”.

3. After hitting “Continue”, you’ll be confronted by the following dialogue:

Do not hit “close”, instead click the “security tab” link.

4. In the following system dialogue click “advanced”.

5. Click the “change” link in the owner security field.

6. Add in your live ID or windows 8 user name to the “select user or group” system dialogue.

7. Click “OK”, Click “OK”, Click “Ok”.

8. Type in “C:\Program Files\Applications” in the Windows Explorer address bar and hit enter. You now have access to the Applications folder.

### What type of apps ship with Windows 8?

Looking at this folder it’s fairly easy to determine what type of apps ship with Windows 8 developer preview.

### What’s in C:\Program Files\Applications?

For HTML apps the folder contains all of their source code and it can modified.

For C# apps the folder contains the XAML source code and a compiled reverse-engineerable and modifiable version of the C# code.

For C++ directX apps the folder contains compiled binaries. Honestly, C++ isn’t my specialty so I’ll avoid discussing it at any great length.

### Reverse Engineering HTML & Javscript & CSS Win8 apps

There’s a fundamental design flaw in the concept of HTML apps. HTML, Javascript and CSS are all interpreted languages, and not compiled languages. Meaning you have to ship the source code for your app instead of shipping compiled binaries. That puts the Intellectual Property of anyone choosing to write any HTML & JS & CSS only app for any platform under risk.

For example, here’s the HTML source code for the Tweet@rama Win8 app code:

And here’s the tweet@rama Javascript code that does the actual posting to Twitter:

### Modifying HTML & Javscript & CSS Win8 apps

Part of the problem with interpreted languages is that they don’t compile until the very instance they are executed. Which allows evil-doers to edit the code prior to execution.

For example, here’s a print screen of the tweet@rama default app;

Let’s modify the HTML, Javascript and CSS for this application: (for the sake of brevity we’ll only walkthrough a simple HTML change)

Notice that we’ve changed both the design and behaviour of the app by modifying the source code. The new design has a different title, and the new behaviour is using the picture of the logged in user as the background. We have the power to completely change both the visual design and the executing source code of HTML & CSS & JS win8 apps.

Viele Männer sprechen erst dann über seelische Belastungen, wenn der Druck kaum noch auszuhalten ist. Ihre psychischen Krisen sind deshalb oft schwer zu erkennen. Schon Jungs und junge Männer erleben insbesondere durch Social Media Leistungs- und Optimierungsdruck, der nicht selten in Ängsten, Überforderung und Einsamkeit endet. Der ARD GESUND Themenschwerpunkt "Mann, wie geht’s dir?" beleuchtet, warum Männer so selten Hilfe suchen und was sich ändern muss, damit sie früher Unterstützung bekommen.

### Risiko psychische Erkrankungen: Wichtige Diagnosen im Überblick

Wie sich psychische Erkrankungen bei Männern zeigen und was sie von Frauen unterscheidet.

## Serien & Podcast

### LIGHTWEIGHTS: Neue Dramedy-Serie

Zwischen Fitness, Leistungsdruck und ADHS-Diagnose: Die Serie begleitet die jungen Männer Sam, Linus und Malik.

8 Min

### Unsichtbar erschöpft: Hochfunktionale Depression

Hinter einer starken Fassade bleiben Warnsignale oft unbemerkt. Warum Männer schweigen und welche Wege aus der Depression führen.

87 Min

### Wie geht's, Johnny?

Der Comedian und Podcaster (Wissen mit Johnny) spricht mit Robin Gosens über ADHS, Panikattacken und Erwartungsdruck.

## Krankheiten & Behandlung

### ADHS bei Erwachsenen: Symptome, Diagnostik und Therapie

Auch im Erwachsenenalter können ADHS-Symptome zu Schwierigkeiten im Alltag führen. Welche sind das? Und was hilft?

### Angststörung: Symptome, Behandlung und Ursachen

Angststörungen können den Alltag stark einschränken. Welche Symptome typisch sind und was Betroffenen hilft.

### Depressionen: Symptome erkennen und Ursachen behandeln

Depressionen können unterschiedliche Ursachen haben. Nicht immer sind die Symptome eindeutig. Die Behandlung sollte möglichst früh beginnen.

### Dysmorphophobie: Was hilft bei gestörter Körperwahrnehmung?

Bei einer körperdysmorphen Störung leiden Menschen an Makel am eigenen Körper, die es eigentlich nicht gibt. Was hilft?

### Ketamintherapie: Droge Ketamin gegen schwere Depressionen

Ketamin, ein Narkosemedikament, verursacht Rauschzustände, die Depressionen lindern. Auch LSD und Psilocybin werden erforscht.

### Burnout - Symptome, Phasen und Behandlung

Starke Erschöpfung, geringes Selbstwertgefühl und Antriebslosigkeit sind Symptome von Burnout. Welche Behandlung hilft?

### Narzissmus: Verdeckt oder grandios - wann wird er krankhaft?

Narzissmus ist eine psychische Tendenz, die krankhaft sein kann. Welche Symptome kennzeichnen sie? Welche Formen gibt es?

### Dissoziative Identitätsstörung: Symptome und Behandlung

Traumata können eine dissoziative Identitätsstörung auslösen. Dabei wechseln sich mehrere Identitäten in einer Person ab.

### Mental Load: Wenn die Familie zur Belastung wird

Mental Load bezeichnet Überlastung durch die Organisation von Alltagsaufgaben. Sie entsteht oft durch Care-Arbeit.

### Schizophrenie - Symptome, Ursachen und Behandlung

Schizophrenie ist eine psychische Erkrankung. Typische Symptome sind Halluzinationen und Wahnvorstellungen. Was hilft?

### Skin-Picking: Wenn Hautkratzen zur Zwangsstörung wird

Bei der Skin-Picking-Disorder kratzen oder drücken die Betroffenen immer wieder an ihrer Haut und verletzen sie damit.

### Zwangsstörung: Symptome, Ursachen und Behandlung

Zwangsstörungen können den Alltag stark bestimmen. Welche Symptome typisch sind und welche Behandlung hilft.

## Entspannungs-Techniken

### Stress abbauen: Tipps zur Entspannung im Alltag

Achtsamkeitstraining, Yoga oder Meditieren: Mentale Techniken können helfen, Stress und Anspannung zu reduzieren.

### Wandern: Das macht Bewegung in der Natur mit der Psyche

Raus aus dem Alltag, rein in die Natur: Wandern kann Stress reduzieren, die Stimmung verbessern und Ängste lindern.

### Meditation: Entspannungstechniken helfen Körper und Psyche

Meditation kann Stress reduzieren, das Immunsystem stärken und wirkt positiv auf Depression. Doch es gibt Nebenwirkungen.

# Archaeologists Just Dug Up an Unused, Completely Pristine 6,000-Year-Old Axe Head - Nautilus

## Archaeologists Just Dug Up an Unused, Completely Pristine 6,000-Year-Old Axe Head

A precious object, not a weapon of war

7:00 AM CST on November 26, 2026

Archaeologists have been digging near the Terme di Sorano spa in southern Tuscany since independent archaeologist Stefano Giuntoli noticed a cavity at one of the thermal pools there back in 2024. The subsequent ruins they uncovered have been dated to around 4495–4335 BCE (the Neolithic), and sit on top of an ancient thermal spring. But since the work began, only a few actual objects have been recovered, indicating this was a specialized site, rather than a village or camp where a lot of human activity was happening.

The latest find—a seemingly untouched axe head carved out of greenstone, thought to date back around 6,000 years—further backs up that theory. As the axe head was never used, it’s believed that its presence is symbolic—perhaps used as a part of some kind of religious or spiritual ceremony rather than as a weapon.

Researchers have determined that the axe head is made out of eclogite, a rock formed at great depths and intense pressures. The early European farmers who lived here during the Neolithic may have obtained the carefully crafted piece through trades and exchanges, and ultimately left it as some kind of gift.

If so, it would be considered a votive offering, which is the act of placing objects in a place for sacred reasons, without any intention of getting them back. It’s possible that the thermal spring was seen as a boundary between worlds.

“The (Terme di Sorano) site is gradually becoming more unique and significant,” Jacopo Francesco Tulipano, one of the team of archaeologists still working at the site, said in a statement (via Google Translate). “The continuation of the work will allow us to gather new data and, once the excavation work is completed, to plan the enhancement of the area.”

items.body:
## when motion became a property of space

Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, an international network of artists began to explore the possibilities of [kinetic art](https://www.designboom.com/tag/kinetic-installations/) at the scale of architecture. Motors and electrical circuits found their way into museum galleries, where entire interiors could be animated with moving structures and artificial light. In some cases, the machinery responded to the viewer’s presence.

An early precedent for these experiments came from the Bauhaus. In 1930, Hungarian artist **László Moholy-Nagy** introduced his Light Prop for an Electric Stage, also known as the Light-Space Modulator, at an exhibition in Paris. As the machine’s metal components rotated, light passed through perforated surfaces and bounced off reflective elements. Its movements generated a second composition across the surrounding walls. Here was a sculpture whose physical dimensions accounted for only a fraction of the space it occupied.

László Moholy-Nagy, Light Prop for an Electric Stage (Light-Space Modulator) | video courtesy [SFMOMA](https://www.sfmoma.org/watch/laszlo-moholy-nagys-shadow-play/)

## from cybernetic sculptures to dynamic labyrinths

In 1961, a 52-meter steel tower by Franco-Hungarian artist **Nicolas Schöffer** rose beside the Palais des Congrès in Liège, Belgium. An arrangement of rotating reflective panels occupied its open framework, while an electronic control system coordinated its movements with light and sound. Schöffer also developed an animated light wall for the neighboring building. After dark, the project extended across the riverfront as reflections appeared on the surface of the Meuse.

Schöffer had been studying cybernetics, a field concerned with systems of communication and feedback. His earlier robotic sculpture, CYSP 1 (1956), incorporated sensors through which it could respond to changes in its surroundings. With the Liège project, the artist could begin to imagine how these relationships between machines and their environments might operate at an urban scale.

Nicolas Schöffer, CYSP 1 (1956) | image © Paris, Archives Nicolas Schöffer, courtesy Fonds de dotation Nicolas Schöffer, © ADAGP, Paris, 2022

## the interior as an instrument of movement

At the third Paris Biennale in 1963, the **Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV)** constructed a labyrinth of its own. The collective, whose members included Julio Le Parc and François Morellet, assembled a series of experiments with light and physical movement. Visitors encountered works that required their participation. GRAV would eventually take these experiments beyond the museum and onto the streets of Paris in 1966.

For Documenta III in Kassel in 1964, the German artists Heinz Mack, Otto Piene, and Günther Uecker of the **ZERO group**collaborated on**Light Room (Homage to Fontana)**. In the darkened gallery, seven kinetic sculptures and a projected image formed a single installation. Electric motors and timers governed the activity of its individual components. As reflective surfaces turned and the distribution of light changed, the room took on a rhythm of its own.

The work built upon experiments that Piene had begun in the late 1950s with his **Lichtballett** **(Light Ballets)**. The artist initially manipulated light sources by hand, before developing motorized devices that could perform their own sequences. For ZERO, the ephemeral qualities of light offered a way to work at an architectural scale without the construction of a permanent structure.

1963 Paris Biennale | video courtesy [OAM](https://oam.io/expositions/3e-biennale-de-paris)

Otto Piene, Lichtballett, 1961 | image © The Guggenheim Museums and Foundation

## gianni colombo destabilizes the geometry of a room

What might be one of the most compelling environments of the period emerged from the Italian artist **Gianni Colombo** ‘s research into spatial perception. A co-founder of Milan’s Gruppo T in 1959, Colombo had developed a series of kinetic works before turning his attention to installations large enough to accommodate the human body.

items.title: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging
items.subtitle: Researchers have uncovered a kidney protein that may hold an important key to vascular aging and longevity.
items.feedText: The protein helps prevent excess phosphate from accumulating in the blood and gradually turning flexible blood vessels rigid. In animal models, a deficiency accelerated blood vessel aging and significantly shortened lifespan, while reducing dietary phosphate helped lessen the damage.

items.body:
# A free multi-CDN, jsDelivr style - James Stone

## A free multi-CDN, jsDelivr style

28 Nov 26 post 1674 words #webdev #cdn #dns jsDelivr does something I have always found neat: it does not use one CDN, it uses several, and for every user it picks whichever one is fastest for them.fastest for them right now.right now, based on RUM. I wanted to see how close I could get to that on free tiers only. Plus the vanity of it is kinda nice. How many people can say their site is served from ~660340+ Cloudflare, 210+ Gcore and 114 Fastly340+ Cloudflare, 210+ Gcore and 114 Fastly, as at Nov 2026 data centers globally.

The experiment lives at cdn.jamesst.one, which now serves a copy of this site, and you can watch where it is routing at rum.jamesst.one.

### How a normal CDN works

A plain server has one IP address in one place, so every visitor’s packets travel all the way to it. A CDN instead announces the same IP address from hundreds of locations,from hundreds of locations at once (this is called anycast: one address, many machines, and the network decides which one you reach), and internet routing (BGP) delivers each visitor to the nearest one. That location serves a cached copy, and only goes back to the origin on a cache miss. For example, 151.101.1.242, one of Fastly’s addresses this site uses, answers in 0.6 to 2 ms from Globalping probes in Copenhagen, Singapore and Melbourne alike. No single machine can be that close to all three.

The above diagram is actually a simplification, because before that, a client first has to look up the IP address to connect to, i.e. DNS. A multi-CDN hooks into the DNS reply and picks which CDN is best, then that CDN’s anycast picks which specific data center based on network routing rules.

### How it fits together

The CDN is chosen in DNS. When your resolver asks for cdn.jamesst.one, the answer is a CNAME to one of three CDNs, and which one depends on where you are. Or, more accurately, the network you are on.

- DNS:Gcore Managed DNS. Its free plan supports “dynamic” records: a set of answers with metadata (countries, continents, networks) and pickers that choose one per query.
- The CDNs: Fastly, Gcore CDN and Cloudflare Pages. All three pull from the same origin and add the same response headers, plus a Server-Timing: cdn;desc="fastly" style header so every measurement knows who served it.
- rumd:rumd, the RUM daemon, as in Real User Monitoring: a small Go service that collects measurements, scores each CDN per country, continent and network, and recommends a routing policy.
- dnsctl: applies that recommendation to Gcore, but only once it has been stable for a few checks and a minimum interval has passed, so DNS does not flap.
### The free tier gotchas

ThingWhat I hitCloudflareThe free plan only proxies a domain if Cloudflare hosts its DNS. Cloudflare for SaaS (custom hostnames) works with outside DNS, but needs a root domain zone in your account, and I wanted DNS to stay on Gcore. Cloudflare Pages saved the day: a Pages project accepts a subdomain on someone else’s DNS as a custom domain. A tiny Worker in the project proxies to the origin and adds the headers.Gcore DNSOne dynamic record set, at most three records, minimum TTL 120s. So at most three CDNs can be live at once. (I checked: a fourth record is refused.)CertificatesEvery CDN has to prove it controls cdn.jamesst.one. Fastly uses a DNS challenge, but Gcore and Cloudflare Pages validate over HTTP, which only works while DNS sends the validator to them. The first certificate meant pointing DNS at Pages for a few seconds. Renewals are a problem I have not fully solved.

### Measuring without JavaScript

The first version used a small script on the page that read Resource Timing entries and beaconed them home. Which works but I would rather not put JS on pages for this. jsDelivr itself gets its RUM data from elsewhere: I think it used Cedexis, then PerfOps, rather than running a script of its own.

items.body:
Everyone asks themselves the same thing: what’s in it for me?

David Ogilvy spent his whole career answering that question. People call him the father of advertising, and for good reason. He wrote iconic campaigns for Rolls-Royce, Dove, and Hathaway shirts, and his book, Ogilvy on Advertising, is still in print forty years later.

Yet at 38, he was an unemployed college dropout.

He didn’t learn persuasion in a classroom or even a boardroom. He learned it on doorsteps in Scotland, selling stoves.

In this episode of Outliers, I break down seven timeless lessons from Ogilvy that you can use in your next email, sales pitch, presentation, or anytime you’re trying to convince someone. You’ll learn how to:

- Put a clear, unique benefit in your opening line
- Write to one person in plain English—without jargon or fluff
- Replace empty adjectives with specific facts that build trust
- Create curiosity that pulls people into your message
- Repeat what works and edit your drafts until they land

The true test of persuasion isn’t whether people admire your words. It’s what they do after reading them.

Picture Gallery with Views of Modern Rome by Giovanni Paolo Panini, via [WikiArt](https://www.wikiart.org/en/giovanni-paolo-panini/picture-gallery-with-views-of-modern-rome-1758).

Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure and industrial technology. This week we look at BAAJA, rayon for missiles, US gas consumption, Cyberarmageddon, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

No essay this week, but I’m working on a long follow up to my [technological search essay](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/technology-as-a-search-problem) that should be out next week.

## Housing and Cities

A neat dataset showing the relationship between excess deaths and temperature in cities around the world. You can really see the sensitivity to high temperatures in places without AC. [[Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/part-one-how-many-people-die-from-extreme-temperatures-and-how-could-this-change-in-the-future)]

The Senate passes the permitting reform bill BAAJA. [[NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/climate/senate-passes-baaja-permitting-bill-energy.html)] And Kalshi now gives BAAJA a 75% chance of becoming law. [[Kalshi](https://kalshi.com/markets/kxpermitbill/american-affordability-and-jobs-act/kxpermitbill-26sep)] And New Mexican Senator Martin Heinrich is in the Economist arguing for BAAJA. “ The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment. Those are necessary. But it does make these reviews a standardised part of a predictable process.” [[The Economist](https://www.economist.com/by-invitation/2026/11/15/a-plan-to-end-americas-most-expensive-bottleneck?giftId=ZDFhYjYzMTYtM2UxZi00Njg0LTk4NzEtMWM4NzNlZDk3OTdl)]

New type of nimbyism just dropped: people opposed to delivery drones flying over their backyard. [[WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/amazon-delivery-drones-4807e976?st=wrqyyy)]

How Dubrovnik, the Croatian city where King’s Landing scenes were shot in Game of Thrones, is coping with huge masses of tourists and (checks notes) Montenegrin drug cartels. [[The Times](https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/article/how-to-save-a-city-from-mass-tourism-when-the-mob-wants-you-dead-0g7d626m2)]

## Manufacturing

From the annals of manufacturing bottlenecks: producing more Patriot missiles requires, among other things, a specialized rayon fabric called Raycarb, processed by a single US company who sources it from a tiny number of companies (apparently just two), who are unable or unwilling to ramp up capacity as fast as the US would like. “ Only one rayon product of this kind is approved for use in the most advanced Patriot missiles, and it comes from the Kansas factory of a single supplier, Park Aerospace. With Patriot stockpiles shrinking, the Pentagon official pushed Park for more rayon to help ramp up missile production. It soon became clear that the company’s hands were tied. The problem lay not in Kansas but thousands of miles across the Atlantic near the vineyards of Bordeaux in France. That’s where Park’s supplier, ArianeGroup—a maker of space rockets and ballistic missiles—produces the carbonized rayon fabric, which it then ships to Park for further processing. ArianeGroup had been clear that supply was limited. ” [[WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/patriot-missile-rayon-problem-3f39dc98)]

Manufacturing automation startup Hadrian is buying Kutztown Foundry and Machine, a company that makes castings for, among other things, nuclear submarines. [[Manufacturing Dive](https://www.manufacturingdive.com/news/hadrian-acquiring-kutztown-foundry-machine-f6-upgrade-expand-pennsylvania/874947/)]

…

items.subtitle: A doctor speaks with her patient in the waiting room.

items.body:
To just toss a hot take into the permitting reform discourse, one thing that I think we see in these debates is that there is way too much non-park federally owned land in the American West, and that creates some very confusing exchanges about activities happening on “public lands.” It’s good to have parks. And obviously there’s lots of otherwise useful infrastructure that you wouldn’t want to put in a park. But if you look at the [federal land portfolio](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R42346.html?), it’s 12.5 percent run by the National Park Service and then 14 percent run by the Fish and Wildlife Service. A majority of the land, though, is run by either the U.S. Forest Service or else the Bureau of Land Management, and that land is *designed* for economic exploitation — logging, mining, ranching, and so forth — in a way that just somewhat arbitrarily excludes uses like housing development.

I think we should have more real parks and more real wildlife preservation and then more privately owned land that’s put to its highest and best use by market forces. A lot of what passes for “public land” preservation is in practice a kind of subsidy-masquerading-as-conservation to favored industries involved in natural resource extraction.

**Peter: I’m just retired from the tech industry, and need something to do after I finish Slow Boring in the morning. You’ve mentioned in the past that you thought there was not enough analytical work on policy related questions. There have also been examples of someone with a computer providing valuable data to the world, for example during Covid. So, what’s your list of topics that you wish someone would get to the bottom of?**

To pick just one example, because it’s a big topic and it’s been on my mind recently, the whole policy community has a very poor grasp of what exactly is going on with health care costs.

[↗ slowboring.com](https://www.slowboring.com/p/we-need-to-understand-health-care)

Previous

items.body:
Contrasting volumes of smooth plaster and rough local Morelo stone define this coastal home in Brazil, designed by local architecture practice Ambidestro.

Named Casa Los Cobos, the home is located in Xangri-Lá on Brazil's southern coast, and was designed to make the most of panoramic views out over the sea from the rear of the site.

Drawings and exterior photographs

Previous

Next

Drawings and exterior photographs

Close

Ground floor plan

First floor plan

Set back from the road, a series of routes both through and around the home "reveal the landscape gradually," including a path beneath a timber canopy and via a paved veranda screened by lush plants.

"The main opportunity was the merging of two adjoining lots into a single site that extends to the rear, where the landscape opens onto the water," Ambidestro co-founder João Pedro Crescente told Dezeen.

The ground floor of Casa Los Cobos has been given over almost entirely to a single large living, dining and kitchen space, wrapped by service spaces and bathrooms.

Full-height sliding glass doors allow this space to be opened out onto a large sheltered terrace alongside a swimming pool, with a lawn that slopes down to a nearby waterway.

"The ground floor is free of partitions: living, dining and the entertaining kitchen are integrated and turned toward the greenery, accommodating everything from a weeknight dinner to a Saturday party," Crescente told Dezeen.

"Between the living room and the water lie, in sequence, the veranda, the garden and the pool, which wraps around the house. The eye passes through these layers before reaching the backdrop," he added.

Both the exterior and interior have been given contrasting finishes of rough Morelo stone and white plaster and paint, with the rear terrace framed by white-painted masonry.

Interior photographs

Previous

Next

Interior photographs

Close

This is complemented internally with bespoke carpentry in pale oak, including a floating timber bar supported by a concrete column that defines one edge of the living space.

"The intention was to use natural, local materials in light, warm tones repeated inside and out, making the transition between spaces almost imperceptible," said Crescente.

"Moledo stone clads the facades and changes in appearance from morning to late afternoon. Other natural stones continue onto the floors and wet areas," he added.

A skylit staircase leads up to the more compartmentalised first floor of the home, which contains six en-suite bedrooms, two of which open onto a balcony overlooking the sea.

To provide both shading and privacy from the road, sliding timber shutters can be pulled down over the full-height bedroom windows.

Read:

Studio Arthur Casas affixes dramatic cantilever to Brazilian house

Other homes in Brazil recently featured on Dezeen include a home in São Paolo by Studio Arthur Casas featuring dramatic overhangs and cantilevers, and a low-lying dwelling by Sabella Arquitetura that is topped by a gridded timber roof.

items.title: Geldpolitik: Pablo Hernández de Cos wird neuer Chef der Europäischen Zentralbank
items.subtitle: Der Spanier wechselt von der Bank für Internationalen Zahlungsausgleich an die EZB-Spitze.
items.feedText: Pablo Hernandez de Cos: Der Spanier rückt Anfang nächsten Jahres an die Spitze der EZB. Foto: IMAGO/El Mundo Frankfurt, Brüssel. Pablo Hernández de Cos wird neuer Präsident der Europäischen Zentralbank ( EZB ). Der Spanier beerbt ab Februar Christine Lagarde an der Spitze der Euro-Notenbank. Darauf haben sich die Staats- und Regierungschefs der 27 EU-Länder auf dem Sondergipfel in Brüssel nach Handelsblatt-Informationen aus Diplomatenkreisen geeinigt. Damit verbunden sind weitere wichtige Personalentscheidungen für die Geldpolitik im Euro-Raum.
items.body:
# EZB: Pablo Hernández de Cos wird neuer Chef der Notenbank

Pablo Hernandez de Cos: Der Spanier rückt Anfang nächsten Jahres an die Spitze der EZB. Foto: IMAGO/El Mundo Frankfurt, Brüssel. Pablo Hernández de Cos wird neuer Präsident der Europäischen Zentralbank ( EZB ). Der Spanier beerbt ab Februar Christine Lagarde an der Spitze der Euro-Notenbank. Darauf haben sich die Staats- und Regierungschefs der 27 EU-Länder auf dem Sondergipfel in Brüssel nach Handelsblatt-Informationen aus Diplomatenkreisen geeinigt. Damit verbunden sind weitere wichtige Personalentscheidungen für die Geldpolitik im Euro-Raum.

Hernández de Cos ist gemäß den Richtlinien acht Jahre im Amt. Er wechselt von der Spitze der Bank für Internationalen Zahlungsausgleich (BIZ), gewissermaßen der übergreifenden Organisation der Zentralbanken weltweit, zurück zur EZB. Von 2018 bis 2024 war er als spanischer Zentralbankchef bereits Teil des EZB-Rats, der über die Geldpolitik im Euro-Raum entscheidet.

Der Deutsche Markus Brunnermeier soll ab Mai als neuer Chefvolkswirt ins sechsköpfige EZB-Direktorium einziehen und auf den scheidenden Philip Lane folgen. Das Amt gilt als das zweitmächtigste in der EZB. Brunnermeier, der einen exzellenten Ruf genießt und zuletzt an der US-Eliteuniversität Princeton gelehrt hat , wird in dieser Funktion auf Basis der konjunkturellen Lage die Zinssitzungen vorbereiten.

Die Französin Laurence Boone übernimmt das Ressort Finanzmärkte von Isabel Schnabel, die ab Januar zum Internationalen Währungsfonds ( IWF ) wechselt. Boone war einst Chefvolkswirtin der OECD und zuletzt bei der Bank Santander beschäftigt. Als Märkte-Vorstandin skizziert sie in jeder Ratssitzung die jüngsten Entwicklungen an den Finanzmärkten und weist auf potenzielle Risiken hin.

Die Neubesetzungen sind Teil eines umfassenden Personalpakets, das die Schwergewichte des Euro-Raums hinter verschlossenen Türen verhandelt haben. Maßgeblichen Einfluss hat neben der Historie an der EZB-Spitze unter anderem die Arithmetik zwischen Nord- und Südeuropäern im EZB-Direktorium.

Als Gegenkandidaten zu de Cos hatten die Niederlande ihren ehemaligen Notenbankchef Klaas Knot nominiert. In den vergangenen Tagen hatte sich aber bereits abgezeichnet, dass die Wahl auf de Cos fällt. Er hatte unter anderem die Unterstützung aus Deutschland und Frankreich.

Markus Brunnermeier: Er wechselt von der US-Eliteuni Princeton zur EZB. Foto: picture alliance/dpa Nun folgt der formelle Ernennungsprozess. So müssen fortan das Europäische Parlament und der EZB-Rat angehört werden. Wenn ihre Stellungnahmen angenommen sind, wird die Führung der Notenbank durch die Staats- und Regierungschefs offiziell ernannt. Dem Vernehmen nach könnte dies noch bis Weihnachten geschehen.

Durch Lagardes angekündigten Rücktritt zum 7. Februar waren die Euro-Staaten unter Handlungsdruck geraten. Ursprünglich lief ihre Amtszeit noch bis Ende Oktober. Um sich nach eigenen Angaben jedoch wieder „frei äußern“ zu können , hatte sich die Französin aber entschieden, vorzeitig abzutreten – kurz vor der Präsidentschaftswahl in ihrem Heimatland im nächsten April.

items.title: Bundesparteitag - BSW-Co-Vorsitzender De Masi schließt Koalitionen mit AfD aus
items.subtitle: Vor dem Bundesparteitag der BSW in Dresden hat deren Ko-Vorsitzender De Masi die Unterstützung einer AfD-geführten Regierung ausgeschlossen.
items.feedText: Fabio de Masi, BSW (Jens Kalaene / dpa / Jens Kalaene)Zwar gebe es dort einige gemeinsam beschlossene Anträge, doch handele es sich um eine nur geringe Zahl, so de Masi weiter. Er warf Linken und Grünen vor, in dem Bundesland nicht auf Angebote der Zusammenarbeit mit seiner Partei eingegangen zu sein. Auch die Ko-Vorsitzende Mohamed Ali lehnte Koalitionen mit der AfD ab. Es gebe große Unterschiede zwischen beiden Parteien, sagte sie im ZDF. Wenn aber ein Antrag gut sei, dann werde man ihm zustimmen - egal von wem er komme.Der bisherige Leitantrag der BSW für den Parteitag untersagt Koalitionen oder Tolerierungen einer AfD-Regierung, ermöglicht aber schriftliche Vereinbarungen über inhaltliche Zusammenarbeit mit der unter anderem in Sachsen-Anhalt als gesichert rechtsextrem eingestuften Partei. Die Spitzenkandidaten des BSW in Sachsen-Anhalt, Schulze und Wittig, wollen eine sachbezogene Zusammenarbeit mit der AfD.
items.body:
# Bundesparteitag - BSW-Co-Vorsitzender De Masi schließt Koalitionen mit AfD aus

Fabio de Masi, BSW (Jens Kalaene / dpa / Jens Kalaene)Zwar gebe es dort einige gemeinsam beschlossene Anträge, doch handele es sich um eine nur geringe Zahl, so de Masi weiter. Er warf Linken und Grünen vor, in dem Bundesland nicht auf Angebote der Zusammenarbeit mit seiner Partei eingegangen zu sein.

### Auch Ko-Vorsitzende Mohamed Ali gegen Koalitionen

Auch die Ko-Vorsitzende Mohamed Ali lehnte Koalitionen mit der AfD ab. Es gebe große Unterschiede zwischen beiden Parteien, sagte sie im ZDF. Wenn aber ein Antrag gut sei, dann werde man ihm zustimmen - egal von wem er komme.Der bisherige Leitantrag der BSW für den Parteitag untersagt Koalitionen oder Tolerierungen einer AfD-Regierung, ermöglicht aber schriftliche Vereinbarungen über inhaltliche Zusammenarbeit mit der unter anderem in Sachsen-Anhalt als gesichert rechtsextrem eingestuften Partei.

### Innerparteiliche Diskussion über Haltung zur AfD

Die Spitzenkandidaten des BSW in Sachsen-Anhalt, Schulze und Wittig, wollen eine sachbezogene Zusammenarbeit mit der AfD. Für diesen sogenannten "Magdeburger Weg" sprechen sich auch andere führende BSW-Politiker aus - vor allem aus den ostdeutschen Bundesländern. BSW-Gründerin Sahra Wagenknecht unterstützt eine Annäherung an die AfD ausdrücklich: Der "Magdeburger Weg" biete für die Partei "große Chancen", heißt es in einem Positionspapier der BSW-Grundwertekommission, der Wagenknecht vorsteht. Eine Koalition mit der AfD oder die Tolerierung einer AfD-Minderheitsregierung wird aber abgelehnt.

### "Keine Tolerierung einer AfD-Regierung"

Die Annäherung zur AfD sorgt allerdings parteiintern für Widerstand. Die BSW-Gründungsmitglieder Dagdelen, Ernst, Leye und Rabie schrieben in einem Gastbeitrag für die "Zeit", zum Gründungskonsens des BSW habe "die klare politische Abgrenzung zur AfD" gehört - dieser werde jetzt infrage gestellt. "So richtig es war, die Brandmauer abzulehnen, die ausschließlich der AfD genutzt hat, so falsch ist es, sich mit der AfD gemein zu machen."Der "Magdeburger Weg" drohe "zu einer politischen Kooperation mit der AfD zu werden", ohne je im Bundesvorstand beschlossen worden zu sein, kritisieren die BSW-Politiker. "Dies würde das BSW nachhaltig kompromittieren und auf Dauer politisch überflüssig machen." Sie fordern stattdessen: "Keinerlei Tolerierung einer AfD-Regierung. Keine Kooperationsvereinbarungen. Keine Enthaltung bei alleiniger AfD-Kandidatur für das Amt des Ministerpräsidenten."

### BSW will sich bei Ministerpräsidentenwahl in Sachsen-Anhalt enthalten

In Sachsen-Anhalt findet am 8. Dezember die Wahl des AfD-Politikers Siegmund zum Ministerpräsidenten an. Dafür ist die AfD - zumindest im ersten und zweiten Wahlgang - auf Stimmen aus anderen Parteien angewiesen. Das BSW kündigte an, sich enthalten zu wollen. Ob die fünf Abgeordneten sich daran halten, wird aber schwer nachzuprüfen sein, denn die Wahl ist geheim.Diese Nachricht wurde am 27.11.2026 im Programm Deutschlandfunk gesendet.

items.body:
I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.

“I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie, the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade.

The spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for.

Carroll Dunham in his home studio in Cornwall, Connecticut.

Photo Laurie Simmons

Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses in varying states of specificity, usually attached to the bodies or the faces of humanoids engaged in sex or violence. This scenery belongs to a tradition of ridiculous bodily extremes, from Greek vases to Thomas Rowlandson to Gustave Courbet to Nicole Eisenman. His style, meanwhile, belongs to the black outlines and dropped-in colors of cartoons. That graphic clarity seems to ask us to read his bodily subjects loud and clear, without any of the technical seduction of peers like Lisa Yuskavage or John Currin.

Although his loud and lusty scenarios committed no real transgression (Peter Saul took care of that in the ’60s, then Robert Mapplethorpe in the ’80s), what may genuinely surprise the uninitiated is the academic remove that characterizes the writing about Dunham. His work is discussed—and discussed primarily by those born before 1975—almost exclusively in the specialist language of form or space or paint application, with little reference to the subject matter. It seems that the writers in Camp 1 understand the shock factor that attends men dildoing their rectums with pistols, or angrily ejaculating on each other from enormous penis-noses, as ammunition against the claim that subject should dictate one’s opinion of a painting. As if to deny the charge of prudery, some of them describe moments of rapture. On a Dunham painting made between 2006 and 2012, of a giant woman spreading her anus and vagina above a landscape like a parade float, the artist Paul Chan wrote of feeling transported: “When I entered the room where it hung [at the Whitney], I gasped. The painting was at once exuberant, provocative, and entrancing. It literally took my breath. I quickly glanced at the other people in the room. Was anyone else having an asthma attack looking at this?”

Representing Camp 2 are John Yau (The Brooklyn Rail, 2007: “Saul is an iconoclast and Dunham is a wannabe.”) and a young man in a basketball jersey I met at the Chicago show. This man was examining a pencil scribble from 2020 of a fist clasping an erection, the balls parted and meatus shaped like a teardrop. I asked him what he thought, and he said, “I feel like I’m being pranked.”

# Sallust's Theorem - Sketchplanations

SubscribeGet the book!Big Ideas Little PicturesPresenting something?Explore the Explainer KitPrefer to listen?Try the podcast🎉 Help keep Sketchplanations ad-free🎉 Keep this ad-free🎉 Help keep Sketchplanations ad-freeby supporting me

## Sallust's Theorem

- Download
- Prints
👇 Get new sketches each week

The surprising benefit of a common enemy

Sallust’s Theorem is that fear of an external enemy promotes internal social unity.

Perhaps more pertinent is the other side of Sallust’s Theorem: the absence or removal of an external enemy leads to internal moral decay and conflict.

Sallust, or more fully Gaius Sallustius Crispus, was a Roman historian and politician around the time of Julius Caesar. Remarkably, several of his works have remained intact to be read over 2000 years later.

Sallust describes unity in the face of common enemies and decline in their absence at several points in the history of Rome’s Republic. His strongest example is the fear of Carthage.

Here’s Sallust in his work The War with Jugurtha, chapter 41 (Latin terms included):

“…before the destruction of Carthage the people and senate of Rome together governed the republic peacefully and with moderation. There was no strife among the citizens either for glory or for power; fear of the enemy (metus hostilis) preserved the good morals of the state.

But when the minds of the people were relieved of that dread (formido), wantonness and arrogance naturally arose, vices which are fostered by prosperity. Thus the peace for which they had longed in time of adversity, after they had gained it proved to be more cruel and bitter than adversity itself.

For the nobles began to abuse their position (dignitas) and the people their liberty (libertas), and every man for himself robbed, pillaged and plundered. Thus the community was split into two parties, and between those the state (res publica) was torn to pieces.” (quoted from Neal Wood, see below)

Sallust sees Rome’s rise and decline as a psychological progression from liberty through glory and ambition to avarice (greed).

You may remember Carthage from the Colosseum scene in the film Gladiator, where Maximus is forced to represent the Carthaginians in Rome’s great victory at the “Battle of Carthage.” It doesn’t go to plan.

Tim Marshall introduced me to Sallust’s Theorem in his fascinating and relevant book Prisoners of Geography. He summarises Sallust’s idea in terms of alliances: “alliances are only strong with the fear of a common enemy.”

In some ways, Sallust’s Theorem is about the danger of getting what we want. We may resent a demanding boss, a fierce local rival, a struggle to build ourselves up from nothing, or a powerful business competitor, yet find that they gave us purpose and brought out the best in us as a group. We can miss them when they’re gone.

I believe the term Sallust’s Theorem was introduced by Neal Wood in Wood, N. (1995). Sallust’s Theorem: A Comment on “Fear” in Western Political Thought. History of Political Thought, 16(2), 174–189.
