items.body:
Cover Image by [Gustavo Fring](https://www.pexels.com/@2206740/) from Pexels

*By Althea Need Kaminske*

Perhaps one of the more obvious pieces of advice that I give medical students about learning is to remember that our brains are in our bodies. Yes, I know that these are very smart, high achieving students who know quite a bit about anatomy and biology. But I also know that in an educational system and society that focuses so much on productivity, it can be easy to compartmentalize our lives. To become so focused on maximizing spaced retrieval practice (yay!) that we forget to prioritize sleep, nutrition, and exercise (boo!). In high-stress and fast-paced environments it can be difficult to remember that we are, ultimately, animals. Creatures that need sleep, a healthy diet, and daily walks.

A recent meta-meta-analysis by Singh et al. (2025) examined the effectiveness of exercise for improving cognition (1). The analysis included 133 meta-analysis, which themselves comprised a total of 2,724 randomized control trials. I’ll break down the results, but the overall finding was pretty notable: **exercise, even light intensity, benefits general cognition, memory, and executive function across all populations.**

The meta-meta-analysis classified outcomes into three categories: general cognition, memory, and executive function. General cognition was measured by scales like the Mini-Mental State Examination, Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale - Cognitive Subscale which are used in medical settings to assess overall cognitive functioning. Memory was measured by instruments like the Wechsler Memory Scale and Verbal Learning Test which measure short-term memory and episodic memory. Executive function was measured by tools like the Digit-Span Test, Digit Span-Backwards, Digit-Span Forwards, and Trail Making Test Part A and B which measure visual and verbal working memory and attention.

## General Cognition and Exercise

There was a significant effect of exercise for improving general cognition. This effect was found across all age groups. The effect varied as a function of exercise type, with a moderate-to-large effect for exergames, and a small-to-moderate effect for aerobic, dance, mind-body, mixed mode, resistance exercise, and other. The effect of exercise on general cognition did not vary as a function of exercise intensity, however interventions that lasted for 1-3 months had the greatest effect on general cognition compared to interventions lasting 4-6 months or greater than 6 months. Finally, the beneficial effects of exercise on general cognition did not vary as a function of session frequency, session duration, or weekly duration.

## Memory and Exercise

There was a significant effect of exercise on memory. This effect was stronger in children/adolescents than in older adults (though benefits were still present in older adults). The effect also varied as a function of exercise type, with large effects for exergames, small-to-medium effects for aerobic, dance, mind-body, mixed mode, and resistance exercise. The effect of exercise on memory did not vary as a function of exercise intensity or intervention length. Further, the beneficial effect of exercise on memory did not vary as a function of session frequency or duration (there was an insufficient number of studies to draw conclusions about weekly duration).

## Executive Function and Memory

There was a significant effect of exercise on executive function. This effect was stronger in children/adolescents than in older adults (though benefits were still present in older adults). The effect also varied as a function of exercise type with exercises categorized as “other” as having a greater effect compared to aerobic, dance, exergames, mind-body, mixed mode and resistance exercise. The effect of exercise on executive function did not vary as a function of exercise intensity or intervention length. Further the beneficial effects of exercise on executive function did not vary as a function of session frequency, session duration, or weekly duration.

## Why does exercise benefit cognition?

items.body:
Mit Pauken, Trompeten und „Jauchzet, frohlocket“ beginnt am Sonnabend, 12. Dezember, um 19.30 Uhr das Weihnachtsoratorium von Johann Sebastian Bach in der Martin-Luther-Kirche. Unter der Leitung von Elke Voigt erklingen die ersten drei Kantaten des Werkes.

Dresdner Bachchor unter der leitung von Elke Voigt – Foto: Kirchgemeinde

Traditionell erklingen die ersten drei Kantaten in der Martin-Luther-Kirche am Sonnabend vor dem dritten Advent. Der Dresdner Bachchor, ein eigens zusammengestellter Jugendchor und die Sinfonietta Dresden gestalten den Konzertabend. Als Solistinnen und Solisten wirken Heidi Maria Taubert (Sopran), Ewa Zeuner (Alt), Jonas Finger (Tenor) und Cornelius Uhle (Bass) mit.

An ausgewählten Stellen kann das Publikum in die Choräle einstimmen.

## Fast 300 Jahre Weihnachtsmusik

Johann Sebastian Bach komponierte sein Weihnachtsoratorium 1734 als Leipziger Thomaskantor. Anders als heute üblich, erklangen die sechs Kantaten damals nicht an einem Abend, sondern an sechs verschiedenen Festtagen zwischen Weihnachten und dem Dreikönigstag.

Die ersten drei Kantaten schrieb Bach für die damals noch üblichen drei Weihnachtsfeiertage. In Rezitativen, Arien, Chören und Chorälen erzählen sie von der Geburt Jesu, der Verkündigung durch die Engel und der Anbetung durch die Hirten.

Für das Weihnachtsoratorium griff Bach auch auf eigene weltliche Kompositionen zurück. So stammt die Musik des berühmten Eingangschors „Jauchzet, frohlocket“ aus einer Geburtstagskantate für die sächsische Kurfürstin und polnische Königin Maria Josepha. Ursprünglich sang der Chor dazu „Tönet, ihr Pauken! Erschallet, Trompeten!“.

Das Konzert findet in der Martin-Luther-Kirche statt. Foto: Archiv, Anton Launer

Heute gehört das Weihnachtsoratorium zu den bekanntesten Werken Bachs und vielerorts fest zum musikalischen Programm der Adventszeit.

## Weihnachtsoratorium in der Martin-Luther-Kirche

- Sonnabend, 12. Dezember 2026, 19.30 Uhr
- Martin-Luther-Kirche, Martin-Luther-Platz
- Johann Sebastian Bach: Weihnachtsoratorium, Kantaten I bis III
- Eintritt: 26 oder 22 Euro, ermäßigt 16 oder 14 Euro. Für Kinder und Jugendliche unter 18 Jahren ist der Eintritt frei.
- Kartenvorverkauf im Gemeindebüro am Martin-Luther-Platz 5 zu den Öffnungszeiten und [online bei Reservix](https://kirchspiel-dresden-neustadt.reservix.de/p/reservix/event/2560160).

items.body:
## Town Comes Together To Guide Child’s Medevac Plane After Runway Lights Broke

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/igiugig-alaska-runway-medevac-plane/)

The remote village of Igiugig, Alaska, has given the world a masterclass in solidarity. Even more impressive, they did so despite only having a population of about 70 people. When a medical evacuation team couldn’t land at the local airport to help a child because the runway lights were broken, the city showed up, lining up their cars to guide the plane with their headlights.

It all started when Ida Nelson, head tribal clerk based in this small southwest Alaska village, heard a loud noise after 11:30 PM on August 28, 2020. “When they first flew over, I was like ’oh my gosh,’ that sounds like a weird vehicle. I’ve never heard that truck before. And it wasn’t a truck, it was an airplane,” Nelson told [KTOO](https://www.ktoo.org/2020/08/29/the-runway-lights-broke-but-igiugig-guided-in-a-childs-medevac-plane-with-headlights/). “Anytime there’s any type of planes flying after dark, you always assume it’s going to be something urgent and an emergency.”

And it was an emergency: a LifeMed Alaska crew was trying to land. When Nelson, who lives close to the airport, looked outside, she realized the runway lights weren't working. Worried, she got in her truck, where she met a local pilot who had also noticed the issue. While pilots can usually turn runway lights from their aircraft, that didn’t work this time. Nelson and the pilot also tried turning on the lights manually from the ground to no avail.

Concerned, Nelson offered to light up one end of the runway with her truck, but they still needed more help. And so, Nelson’s neighbor rallied the community, making 32 phone calls. Meanwhile, the pilot hopped into his own plane and contacted the LifeMed crew. “I was feeling nervous, anxious because this is late at night and this is someone’s child,” Nelson told[CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/2020/09/01/us/alaska-village-medical-evacuation-trnd). “The only thing I could think of was how quickly I could get other people here to help because what if that was my baby’s plane?”

Within 20 minutes, 20 people had shown up in their vehicles, many in their pajamas, ready to follow the plane crew’s instructions. The townspeople staggered their cars and 4-wheelers along the runway so the pilot could see end to end. The people remained in place as the plane landed, boarded the patient, and departed safely for Anchorage, where the young patient made it to the hospital in stable condition.

While the LifeMed Alaska crew are no strangers to harsh Alaskan conditions, they were impressed by the community’s efforts to help one of their own. The team took one photo of the Igiugig runway lit up by its residents as they took off, and shared it on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CEmfI8aBGng/) with the message, “It’s amazing what a community can accomplish with a little ingenuity and a lot of determination!”

items.title: Wenn Wissenschaftskommunikation zur Sicherheitsfrage wird
items.subtitle: Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt.
items.feedText: Elisabeth Waczek vom Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF) erklärt, wie Wissenschaftskommunikation zu einer differenzierten Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung beitragen kann. Elisabeth Waczek ist studierte Philosophin und Referentin für Wissenstransfer am PRIF – Leibniz-Institut für Friedens- und Konfliktforschung. Einer ihrer Schwerpunkte liegt in der Wissenschaftskommunikation des Clusters Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR), an der Schnittstelle von Technologie un…
items.body:
Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt. Elisabeth Waczek vom Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF) erklärt, wie Wissenschaftskommunikation zu einer differenzierten Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung beitragen kann.

**Elisabeth Waczek** ist studierte Philosophin und Referentin für Wissenstransfer am PRIF – Leibniz-Institut für Friedens- und Konfliktforschung. Einer ihrer Schwerpunkte liegt in der Wissenschaftskommunikation des [Clusters Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)](https://www.prif.org/forschung/cntr), an der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit.

**Seit dem russischen Angriff auf die Ukraine wird deutlich intensiver über Sicherheit und militärische Technologien diskutiert. Spüren Sie seit der Gründung Ihres Forschungsclusters 2023 ein wachsendes Interesse an Ihrer Arbeit?**

Wir spüren definitiv ein wachsendes Interesse.

Unser Fokus liegt auf Rüstungskontrolle im weiteren Sinne. Wir beschäftigen uns mit der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit. Zu Beginn habe ich es als eine deutlich größere Herausforderung wahrgenommen, die Relevanz dessen zu erklären. Mittlerweile merke ich: Das haben viele Leute auf dem Schirm. Diese Themen sind stark ins Bewusstsein gerückt. Viele Leute in Europa haben nun das Gefühl, wir müssen uns wieder stärker mit dem Thema Sicherheit auseinandersetzen.

**Ihr Forschungscluster beschäftigt sich mit Technologien, die bestehende Machtverhältnisse verändern könnten. Woran erkennen Sie, dass eine technologische Entwicklung über die Fachcommunity hinaus sicherheitspolitisch relevant wird?**

Unsere Mitarbeitenden aus den Sozialwissenschaften und aus den Natur- und Technikwissenschaften kommen gemeinsam zu einer Einschätzung: Ist das eine Entwicklung, die disruptives Potenzial hat?

Konkret bedeutet das zum Beispiel: Lassen sich neue Technologien oder Forschungsergebnisse missbrauchen, um Waffen herzustellen? Welche Akteur*innen könnten Zugang bekommen, die ihn zuvor nicht hatten? Reicht bestehende Regulierung noch aus, um schädliche – vielleicht auch unbeabsichtigte – Folgen zu minimieren? Gefährlich wird es zum Beispiel, wenn Technologie die Dynamiken so stark beschleunigt, dass deeskalierende Instrumente wie die Rüstungskontrolle nicht mehr Schritt halten können, oder wenn sich nicht mehr feststellen lässt, woher eine Bedrohung kommt.

Interessanterweise kommen unsere Wissenschaftler*innen auch immer wieder zu der Einschätzung, dass dieses disruptive Potenzial gar nicht so dramatisch ist. Oft geht dem viel Hype voraus und besonders reißerische, aber vielleicht eher unwahrscheinliche Szenarien bekommen viel Aufmerksamkeit. Beim Thema KI zum Beispiel. Da ist es Aufgabe der Wissenschaft, erst einmal einen nüchterneren Blick einzunehmen und zu schauen: Wie gefährlich ist das denn wirklich? Welche Anwendungen haben das größte Potenzial negativer Auswirkungen und wo liegen womöglich auch Chancen? Am Ende kommt oft so etwas dabei raus wie: Ja, man muss das Thema ernst nehmen, aber man sollte nicht in Panik verfallen.

**Wenn Sie sich etwas für die gesellschaftliche Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung wünschen könnten: Was sollte die Öffentlichkeit aus Ihrer Sicht besser verstehen, um einen informierten Umgang mit diesen Themen zu ermöglichen?**

### Cluster Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)

Das CNTR am PRIF untersucht, wie neue Technologien und wissenschaftliche Entwicklungen die internationale Sicherheit beeinflussen. Forschende aus verschiedenen Disziplinen analysieren mögliche Risiken und Chancen technologischer Innovationen und entwickeln Empfehlungen, um die internationale Rüstungskontrolle zu stärken.

Ein Beispiel: Ich war auf einer Tagung, bei der die Sprache auf das Thema Dual-Use-Forschung kam. Das sind Forschung oder Technologien, die legitime zivile Anwendungen haben, aber auch in militärischer Weise gebraucht oder in illegitimer Weise missbraucht werden können.

items.title: How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)
items.subtitle: “Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food…
items.feedText: “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a letter of objection from one Rosalie Levine of L…
items.body:
“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” [writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne](https://www.nytimes.com/1976/11/22/archives/westchester-weekly-what-taste-means-to-one-man-in-the-kitchen.html?eafs_enabled=false). “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a [letter of objection](https://www.nytimes.com/1977/01/12/archives/westchester-weekly-letters.html) from one Rosalie Levine of Lakewood, California.

“I live alone, I must control my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV dinner’s price “cannot possibly be bettered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready dinner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to prepare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up afterward.” While none of these advantages were accidental, the oft-told story of the concept’s emergence begins with a corporate crisis.

“In 1953, someone at Swanson colossally miscalculated the level of the American appetite for Thanksgiving turkey, leaving the company with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” [as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/tray-bon-96872641/). “Inspired by the trays of pre-prepared food served on airlines,” Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas set the machinery in motion to package the unwanted meat with gravy and sides like cornbread and sweet potatoes, ready for stocking in America’s frozen-food aisles.

The following year, Swanson sold ten million such “TV dinners,” a name attributed to both the shape of the boxes and the form of entertainment families tended to enjoy while eating the meals within. “In 1950, only 9 percent of U.S. households had television sets — but by 1955, the number had risen to more than 64 percent, and by 1960, to more than 87 percent,” writes Kovie Biakolo in [a more recent Smithsonian piece](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/brief-history-tv-dinner-180976039/). (Among the Smithsonian Institution’s holdings, incidentally, is [an original Swanson TV dinner tray](https://www.si.edu/object/swanson-tv-dinner-tray%3Anmah_741033).) Another breakthrough came with the introduction of microwave-safe trays, bringing total preparation time under ten minutes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Americans rekindled their love affair with frozen meals, “spending nearly 50 percent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

Where holiday and commercial lore intersect, the details tend to get complicated. Swanson’s TV dinner did have its precedents: the core technology for quick-freezing packaged foods was invented over a century ago by entrepreneur Clarence Birdseye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remembers as “little cryogenic miracles”), and in the late 1940s, different companies planned or attempted to bring frozen meals to market under brands like Strato-Plates, FridgiDinners, and One-Eyed Eskimo. None of those names tapped into the technology transforming not just American mass culture, but also the American way of life. In the fifties, associations with television (and, indeed, with air travel) carried a kind of sophistication they certainly don’t have today. Perhaps Craig Claiborne would be pleased that Americans never quite accepted microwaved TV dinners as a substitute for the Thanksgiving meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is another matter entirely.

items.body:
### “Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment.”

“The encounter between two differences is an event,” French philosopher Alain Badiou wrote in his tremendous treatise on [why we fall and how we stay in love](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/26/alain-badiou-in-praise-of-love/). “On the basis of this event, love can start and flourish. It is the first, absolutely essential point.”

And yet at the heart of this essential event is often something beyond the two — something often improbable, almost always inessential in itself, which somehow magnetizes the two differences into a unit of belonging.

The power of that mysterious and magical something is what the poet and essayist **Donald Hall** (September 20, 1928–June 23, 2018) explores in a gorgeous essay titled “The Third Thing,” which appeared on the pages of [Poetry](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine) — the world’s most enduring and visionary poetry magazine — in the autumn of 2004.

Donald Hall and Jane Kenyon

Reflecting on his life with the love of his life — the poet Jane Kenyon, herself the keeper and giver of [uncommonly clarifying wisdom on writing and life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/15/jane-kenyon-advice-on-writing/) — Hall considers the secret to the kind of lasting love that blooms between the mundane and the magical. An epoch after Virginia Woolf exulted in [“the bead of sensation”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/11/virginia-woolf-on-relationships-marriage/) that punctuates the dailiness of any durational love to make it last, Hall writes:

> Jane Kenyon and I were married for twenty-three years. For two decades we inhabited the double solitude of my family farmhouse in New Hampshire, writing poems, loving the countryside. She was forty-seven when she died. If anyone had asked us, “Which year was the best, of your lives together?” we could have agreed on an answer: “the one we remember least.” There were sorrowful years — the death of her father, my cancers, her depressions — and there were also years of adventure: a trip to China and Japan, two trips to India; years when my children married; years when the grandchildren were born; years of triumph as Jane began her public life in poetry: her first book, her first poem in the New Yorker. The best moment of our lives was one quiet repeated day of work in our house. Not everyone understood. Visitors, especially from New York, would spend a weekend with us and say as they left: “It’s really pretty here” (“in Vermont,” many added) “with your house, the pond, the hills, but … but … but … what do you do? ”
> What we did: we got up early in the morning. I brought Jane coffee in bed. She walked the dog as I started writing, then climbed the stairs to work at her own desk on her own poems. We had lunch. We lay down together. We rose and worked at secondary things. I read aloud to Jane; we played scoreless ping-pong; we read the mail; we worked again. We ate supper, talked, read books sitting across from each other in the living room, and went to sleep. If we were lucky the phone didn’t ring all day… Three hundred and thirty days a year we inhabited this old house and the same day’s adventurous routine.
> What we did: love.

Art from [The Missing Piece Meets the Big O](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/02/12/the-missing-piece-meets-the-big-o-shel-silverstein/) — Shel Silverstein’s allegory of the secret to lasting love

But the substance of this daily love, Hall argues, is not the stuff of romantic tropes. Echoing *Little Prince* author Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s [beautiful insistence](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/01/01/what-is-love/) that “love does not consist of gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction,” Hall writes:

items.title: Mindful Eating
items.subtitle: This food reveals your connection with the Earth.
items.feedText: With mindfulness we can see that many elements—the rain, sunshine, earth, and the labor of the farmers, drivers, food sellers, and cook—have all come together to form each wonderful meal. When we eat in mindfulness, we can see that the entire universe is supporting our existence. Having the opportunity to sit and enjoy a wonderful meal is something precious, something not everyone has. Many people in the world are hungry. items.body:
Mindful eating is an important part of our meditation practice—from chopping vegetables to eating with awareness to cleaning up. With [mindfulness](http://google.com/url?q=https://tricycle.org/buddhism-misunderstandings/%23mindfulness-primary-practice&sa=D&source=editors&ust=1794344459664192&usg=AOvVaw3noZmbxwjn3sqon9r8wjed) we can see that many elements—the rain, sunshine, earth, and the labor of the farmers, drivers, food sellers, and cook—have all come together to form each wonderful meal. When we eat in mindfulness, we can see that the entire universe is supporting our existence.

Having the opportunity to sit and enjoy a wonderful meal is something precious, something not everyone has. Many people in the world are hungry. When I hold a bowl of rice or a piece of bread, I know that I am fortunate, and I feel [compassion](https://tricycle.org/tag/compassion-karuna/) for all those who have no food to eat or who are without friends or family. We can be aware of this right at our dinner table. Mindful eating can cultivate seeds of compassion and understanding. Those seeds can sprout and grow inside us and give us the determination to do something to help hungry and lonely people to be nourished.

The kitchen should be a place of meditation. You might want to create a kitchen altar to remind yourself to practice mindfulness while cooking. It can be just a small shelf with enough room for an incense holder, a small flower vase, a beautiful stone, a small picture of an ancestor or a spiritual teacher, or a statue of the Buddha or a [bodhisattva](https://tricycle.org/glossary/bodhisattva/)—whatever is most meaningful to you. When you come into the kitchen, you can begin your work by offering incense and practicing mindful breathing.

While cooking, allow enough time so you don’t feel rushed. Be aware that you, and the people you’re cooking for, depend on this food. This awareness will help you to cook healthy food that’s infused with your love and mindfulness.

When the food is on the table and everyone is seated, practice at least three mindful breaths before beginning to eat. You can say:

*Breathing in, I calm my body.* *Breathing out, I smile.*

If you’re eating alone, promise yourself just to eat and to be with the food, and not to read or listen to the radio or watch a screen during the meal. If you’re eating with others, take the time to really look at each of them and smile. Sitting at the table with other people is a chance to offer an authentic smile of friendship and understanding. It’s very easy, but not many people do it. To me, the most important part of the practice is to look at each person and smile. If people eating together cannot smile at each other, then something isn’t right.

After breathing and smiling, look down at the food in a way that allows it to become real. This food reveals your connection with the Earth. Each bite contains the life of the sun and the Earth. The extent to which your food reveals itself depends on you. You can see and taste the whole universe in a piece of bread!

Contemplating your food for a few seconds before eating, and eating in mindfulness, can bring you much happiness. You can say:

*In this food* *I see clearly the presence* *of the entire universe* *supporting my existence.*

When you’ve finished eating, take a few moments to notice that your bowl or plate is now empty and your hunger is satisfied. You can take a moment to be grateful that you have had this nourishing food to eat, supporting you on the path of love and understanding, by saying:

*The plate is empty.* *My hunger is satisfied.* *I vow to live* *for the benefit of all beings.*

When you’re cleaning the kitchen or [washing dishes](https://tricycle.org/magazine/wash-your-bowl/), do it as if you were washing a baby, and you can feel joy and peace radiate within and around you. You can say to yourself:

*Washing the dishes* *is like bathing a baby.* *The profane is the sacred.* *Everyday mind is enlightened mind.*

…

items.body:
**Born Erased** brings together two sides of Bulgarian musician Angel Simitchiev’s musical practice: the dark ambient experimentation of his former solo project Mytrip and the harsher sounds of Dayin, which he once described as “Harsh drones and regret. But it’s a relief.” His third outing as Born Erased, *What You Destroy, I Love*, revisits the concrete angst of his 2023 debut, *I Am the End of the World*, with a heavier emphasis on guitars and live percussion. There’s even a touch of colour, at least in Silvana Ilieva’s artwork, which resembles molten lava flowing beneath the earth’s surface.

Simitchiev, however, offers no soothing remedy for the world’s ailments. Written in response to the seemingly endless cycle of wars, human suffering and environmental destruction, the album is an expression of anger at humanity’s willingness to sacrifice life and the natural world in pursuit of power and profit. The opening “Knife Hands” establishes the mood with crushing drones that ebb and flow beneath skies already blackened by an unrelenting darkness, like ink rapidly spreading across watercolour paper. “Sea of Skin” begins with a low rumble from the earth’s core before erupting into post-rock territory, propelled by drums and distorted guitars.

As Simitchiev explains in the accompanying interview, the compositions began as ambient pieces, with drummer Nedislav Miladinov invited to respond freely to their atmosphere. Only afterwards did Simitchiev write the guitar and bass parts around the recorded drums. This approach accounts for some of the music’s unpredictable momentum, as the pieces expand and contract under their own considerable weight.

On “Diamond Silence”, the magmatic force reaches the surface, accompanied by the ghostly vocals of Romain Barbot of Saåad, whose fragile presence offers a rare moment of intimacy. “Like Wraiths” takes us across scorched earth, while “The Last Embrace” moves through coruscating textures, with Siavash Amini contributing additional layers of noise and disquiet.

“Unbelonging” retreats into more familiar dark ambient territory, its steady drumming offering a deceptive sense of reassurance as sweeping, glacial drones clear the horizon of any remaining sonic debris. The piece eventually erupts into a volcanic torrent of distortion, dispelling any illusion of safety. It’s this false familiarity that makes the album so unsettling: just when the music seems to offer some respite, the ground gives way again.

The closing “A Future Without the Body” abandons all hope of salvation. Its thrusting, strident passages seem intent on stripping away the last remnants of humanity before gradually dissipating into thin air. The silence left in their wake is all the more powerful.

*What You Destroy, I Love* offers little prospect of redemption. Simitchiev’s anger is directed not at the natural world but at humanity’s determination to destroy it, along with itself. If there is any hope remaining, it lies in the possibility that the planet might eventually reclaim what we have so recklessly squandered.

Born Erased live by Niya Kirkova

To uncover the different layers of the production process I have reached out directly to [Angel Simitchiev](https://linktr.ee/angelxsimitchiev).

**What You Destroy, I Love sounds considerably heavier than [Birds Drink My Blood](https://bornerased.bandcamp.com/album/birds-drink-my-blood), with elements of shoegaze and post-rock. In some ways, it feels closer to your debut, [I Am the End of the World](https://bornerased.bandcamp.com/album/i-am-the-end-of-the-world), which drew on your background in hardcore punk. Was this a conscious return to that sound? And how much did Nedislav Miladinov’s drumming influence the direction of the album?**

…

items.body:
The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the [Vancouver Art Gallery](https://www.vanartgallery.bc.ca/art-of-wellbeing/), and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend [PaRx](https://www.parkprescriptions.ca/), Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access.

Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

*Credit: Vancouver Art Gallery*

## An artful approach to treatment

The process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

After the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

This is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

items.feedText: # The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark Peter Kirn - November 25, 2026 Add comment In northern Europe, it’s that time of year that disappears under a thick blanket of cloud, and the hours of daylight seem to melt away into cinder gray. That calls for some cozy comforts. And look at this: some new acoustic instrument engineering, and a tiny acoustic piano. This is not a toy piano — which is a lovely instrument, just in fact, I’d argue not a piano at all. Toy pianos, with metal (or sometimes glass or xylphone) bars, are essentially their own class of percussion instrument that happens to have a piano-style keyboard manual. No, this is a wonderfully scaled-down acoustic piano, as in, honey I shrunk the spinet.
items.body: # The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark - CDM Create Digital Music MusicMusic techTech ## The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark Peter Kirn - November 25, 2026 Add comment In northern Europe, it’s that time of year that disappears under a thick blanket of cloud, and the hours of daylight seem to melt away into cinder gray. That calls for some cozy comforts. And look at this: some new acoustic instrument engineering, and a tiny acoustic piano. This is not a toy piano — which is a lovely instrument, just in fact, I’d argue not a piano at all. Toy pianos, with metal (or sometimes glass or xylphone) bars, are essentially their own class of percussion instrument that happens to have a piano-style keyboard manual. No, this is a wonderfully scaled-down acoustic piano, as in, honey I shrunk the spinet. (To this day, my favorite instrument of all time was the childhood Everett spinet, a friendly US-built model. Helsinki-based pianist Antti Kujanpää recorded this beautiful demo, which has every right to go a bit viral at this moment on Earth. (He didn’t even do a thumbnail looking surprised pointing at anything! See?) They really did manage to make it small. The Danish-built Keybird L1, supporting by a crowdfunding campaign of all things, is only 39 kg, 70x115x55 cm, but still has four octaves and you can play it with even-softer felt engaged, and it comes with a tuning key. It’s clearly a piano you would have a very different relationship with than the 19th century monster we’ve inherited. It’s a piano you can tune. It’s a piano you can carry around. I’m intrigued by the phrase “one of the smallest acoustic pianos on the market.” It’s the smallest I’ve seen. Optional add-ons give it MIDI capabilities and Helpinstill pickups, plus the usual accoutrements like a tuning kit and road case. Some outlets picked this up earlier this year, but the appearance of this video indicates that they are now starting to ship, as promised, this quarter. Antti’ has this lovely solo album, too. Listen, let me tell you, I like music. Sometimes I like it to sound like a swarm of alien bees set to tear out your eardrums, and sometimes I like it to sound like this. Afterimage by Antti Kujanpää That being said, I do hope there’s some angular, dissonant music composed for it, too! I imagine that could be fragile and strange, like a snowflake on a moon of Jupiter. Uh, if anyone has one and wants a composer, I volunteer. If you want one yourself, it’s €3.750,00 incl. VAT — but expect some time to get one. Over ten years ago, I wrote an extended feature on another new acoustic piano — the Una Corda, now positively enormous at 100 kg. > Acoustic Revelation: Inside the Una Corda, the 100kg, 21st Century Piano Built for Nils Frahm But here as now, even as someone who’s spent long hours at the desk of a Steinway grand, I am absolutely overjoyed to see the tyranny of the Steinway Model D-274 finally seeing some resistance. (Even competing models from Yamaha and others are closely related in design.) We’ll always have the Model D. It’s long past time to have something else, too. items.body:
# Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

Back to Articles

## Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

TeamArticlePublished November 26, 2026 Upvote 25

angtangtggml-orgSimon Pagezypagezyhfggml-orgAbdennacer Badaouibadaouiggml-org

The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

### Quick start

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

- In the Overview tab, compare quantizations for one hardware, model, and build. The two charts show PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens), both starting at context depth zero.
- In the Build history tab, track PP512 and TG128 across all recorded builds for the selected hardware, model, and quantization.
- In the Contextscaling tab, see how token-generation throughput changes as the existing context grows, for the selected build, hardware, model, and quantization.
### What the numbers mean

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:

TestWorkloadWhat it helps you assessPP512Process 512 input tokensHow quickly the model processes a promptTG128Generate 128 tokensHow quickly the model produces output

Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

### How we run the benchmarks

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

### Inspect and reuse the results

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

### Join the conversation

Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

items.body:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

items.body:
# Was ist Intelligenz? Menschliches Denken, künstliche Intelligenz - Spektrum der Wissenschaft

## Was ist Intelligenz? Menschliches Denken, künstliche Intelligenz

Im Stadtpark drückt eine Krähe mit ihrem Schnabel auf den Knopf eines Wasserspenders. Ein dünner Strahl schießt hervor. Eine zweite Krähe tritt heran und trinkt. Dann wechseln die Tiere die Rollen. Währenddessen spazieren Menschen vorbei, ohne stehen zu bleiben. Auf sie wirkt die Szene wohl nicht ungewöhnlich. Die Krähen haben offenbar beobachtet, wie Menschen den Automaten bedienen. Doch was spiegelt das Verhalten der Vögel eigentlich wider? Die spontane Antwort lautet: Das ist selbstverständlich intelligentes Verhalten. Schwieriger wird es allerdings, zu erklären, was damit eigentlich gemeint ist. Denn der Begriff »Intelligenz« entzieht sich bis heute überraschend hartnäckig einer klaren Definition. Können Krähen abstrakt denken? Verstehen sie Ursache und Wirkung? Oder wiederholen sie lediglich ein bewährtes Verhalten? Und wäre auch das schon intelligent? Die Szene lässt sich je nach wissenschaftlichem Hintergrund unterschiedlich deuten. Manche Fachleute definieren Intelligenz über die Fähigkeit zur Problemlösung. Andere interessieren sich für die dahinterliegenden neuronalen Prozesse. Wieder andere knüpfen Intelligenz an das Nutzen von Symbolen wie etwa Schrift oder Zahlen. Und seit Maschinen Schachweltmeister besiegen, Bilder erschaffen und Texte verfassen, stellt sich zudem die Frage, ob Intelligenz überhaupt ein biologisches Gehirn voraussetzt. Die folgenden vier Gespräche nähern sich dem Begriff aus jeweils unterschiedlichen Perspektiven – und suchen Antworten auf eine scheinbar einfache Frage: Was ist Intelligenz? Tierkognition: Intelligenz befähigt zur Lösung von Problemen Julia Fischer ist Professorin für Primatenkognition an der Georg-August-Universität Göttingen und leitet die Abteilung Kognitive Ethologie am Deutschen Primatenzentrum. Für sie hängt Intelligenz davon ab, welche Probleme ein Lebewesen in seinem ökologischen Kontext lösen muss.

items.body:
[Javier Hidalgo](https://jepson.richmond.edu/faculty/bios/jhidalgo/), a philosopher at the University of Richmond, has developed a classroom simulation game to teach about different ancient philosophies called “Ancient Philosophy as a Way of Life.”

Generously, Professor Hidalgo has created a [website](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/) to share the game with anyone who may wish to try it out in their own courses.

He writes:

> [Ancient Philosophy as a Way of Life](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/) is a free classroom role-playing game that introduces students to Hellenistic philosophy, plus a bit of Buddhist philosophy.
> The game is set around 150 BCE at the court of Menander, a king who ruled a Hellenistic kingdom that included part of the Indian subcontinent. Four delegations of philosophers (Stoics, Epicureans, Buddhists, and Skeptics) arrive at court, each claiming to offer the best way of life. Some students play the philosophers, while others play members of the court, each of whom faces a personal dilemma and must decide which philosophical school to join. The philosophers present their views, lead the court through a brief philosophical exercise, and offer advice on the court members’ dilemmas. At the end, the court members announce their allegiances and the king awards royal patronage.
> There is no predetermined winner: when I ran the game in two sections of my ethics course, different philosophical factions won. Students engaged in sustained debate about the merits of the different schools and also seemed to have fun with the game.
> The game takes two class sessions, one for preparation and one for play, although a third session might be useful for larger or more talkative classes. It works for classes of 7 to 30 students and assumes no background in philosophy. The goal of the game is for students to encounter these philosophies as live options rather than merely as historical doctrines. Students have to understand a view well enough to defend it against objections, apply it to concrete problems, and experiment with its practices.
> The game is inspired by [Reacting to the Past](https://reactingconsortium.org/) games (which I love!) but is shorter than a standard Reacting game and is designed to emphasize philosophical debate in particular. The [website](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/#materials) has everything an instructor needs to run the game: a student gamebook, an instructor’s manual, faction handouts, role sheets, dilemma cards, and ballots. All materials are free to download.

Check it out. Professor Hidalgo adds, “The game is still in development and I would welcome feedback from anyone who tries it.”

items.body:
Hi folks,

As you might have noticed my blog has undergone a metamorphosis and is now Windows 8 Metro style inspired. It’s also no longer in Silverlight.

What are the top 2 features of this blog?

One of the top two features I’m quite excited about is a home page with flipping tiles. If you haven’t seen it yet head on over to https://justinangel.net/ and have a look.

Another feature I’m quite enamored with are the interactive sidebar charms:

What’s the complete featurelist?

Posting from Windows Live Writer

Tiles Home Page

Flipping animation

TwitPic Tiles

Twitter tile

Article Tile with Topsy Counter

Category Tiles

Sliding Charms Sidebar

Sliding animation

Social Networks Sharing

Interactive Search

Inline Feeds

Contact details

Metro Inspired UI pages

Home Page

Category List

Articles

Hierarchal article comments

Back office Management

RSS 2.0 and Atom 1.0 Feeds

User Friendly URLs

SEO: Site Map and Robots.txt

Google Analytics

Full Source code

What technologies were used?

ASP.Net MVC3 Razor View Engine: User interface front end.

ASP.Net Dynamic Data: The back office management portal.

HeadJS: Used to load Javascript files in parallel and add HTML5 cross-browser support with some poly-fills.

jQuery: Javascript minimum bar.

jQuery.Templates: Used to render hierarchical comments at the client side.

jQuery.Validate: Used to validate comments at the client side.

jQuery.QuickFlip: Used to create the flipping home page tiles.

jQuery.highlightText: Used to highlight text during searches.

SQL Server 2008:  Database.

Entity Framework: Database OR/M.

MSTest: Unit testing framework.

RhinoMocks: Unit Test mocking.

Unity: Inversion of control framework.

WCF Syndication Services: RSS 2.0 and Atom 1.0 feeds.

Starbucks: Supplier of caffeine.

What happened to your Silverlight blog?

I consider my online presence to be a playground I can use to experiment with. It’s all about trying new things and figuring out what works and what doesn’t. I consider my Silverlight blog to be a huge success, it worked for 2 years and with the exception of some minor justifiable UX complaints I really liked it.

You shouldn’t read anything into my personal technology choices. I rewrote this blog because I felt like it.

Feel free download the Silverlight Weblog @ http://silverlightweblog.codeplex.com/

Is MetroBlog open source?

Yes it is. The source code is open source under MS-PL and can be downloaded from codeplex @ http://MetroBlog.codeplex.com

Tell me more about your home page tiles…

The home page actually displays data from multiple data sources (Blog posts, Twitter, TwitPic and Topsy). And by using flipping tiles I’m able to convey more data in the same screen real-estate.

Over here you can see where the latest blog posts come from:

And the Twitter counter comes from http://topsy.com.

Next we’ve got the Category tiles for the home page:

Another data source is TwitPic showing the latest TwitPics on my account:

And finally there’s a tile with my latest tweet:

The combination of that rich data in a cohesive UX is something that I’m quite happy about.

Thank You!

I’d like to thank the beta testers who helped make this blog significantly better.

Chris Walsh (@ChrisWalshie)

Martin Rauscher (@Hades32)

Anoop Madhusudanan (@amazedsaint)

Aleksandr Sasha K. (@Arktronic)

Rodrigue Hajjar (@rodrigue_)

Matt Hidinger (@matthidinger)

@choudeshell

I’d also like to thank every single open source developer who contributed to the frameworks I’m using.

Comments? Thoughts? Feedback? Something sucks?

Sound off in the comments! Please, I really could use your feedback.

Sincerely,

-- Justin Angel

Tips for Brainstorming 100 Ideas an Hour

Bing Gordon is the former Chief Creative Officer of Electronic Arts, Amazon board member, and a partner at Kleiner Perkins.

He served on Amazon’s board for more than a decade, a seat he earned after giving Jeff Bezos five ideas. The first was Amazon Prime. Bing describes the week two directors told him they wanted to resign, and the fix he proposed: Bezos opens each meeting with what’s on his mind, and six-page memos replace slide decks.

He explains Bezos’s first rule for the board, “first, do no harm,” and the “institutional no” Bezos wanted the board to help Amazon avoid. He lays out the three behaviors Bezos looks for in people who are right a lot, why Bezos dropped one-on-ones, and how every Amazon candidate faces a seven-person interview loop built on the leadership principles.

Bing then turns to what games taught him. He explains why moving a game from an 80 to a 90 doubles sales, why Steven Spielberg recut films until nobody left their seat, and how expansion packs for The Sims shaped his pitch for Prime.

He shares the David Ogilvy lessons that never made the books, including that 90% of people who recall an ad remember the headline and only 25% remember the body copy.

**Available Now: [YouTube](https://youtu.be/EsNvJrkgAr4?si=9bYvgZBHNosigLKe) | [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/2D0zv8io3fTmXKK92a4cHk?si=3359859315f34cd2)**|**[Apple Podcasts](https://podcasts.apple.com/ca/podcast/learning-from-bezos-jobs-and-spielberg-bing-gordon/id990149481?i=1000803770770) | [X](https://x.com/shaneparrish/status/2125200843481711087?a=P9Pgv1GUv1mvTxjPAGk&s=20) | [Transcript](https://fs.blog/knowledge-project-podcast-transcripts/bing-gordon/)**

## Tiny Lessons

Some of my favorite ideas and lessons from this episode.

**Founders, Leadership, & Boards**

- “The board members who say, ‘You should do this, you should do this,’ are dangerous, especially if they’re confident and handsome.”
- “When your board says, ‘Let’s bring in experienced people for adult supervision,’ you have to get those people off your board because adult supervision usually means somebody who’s over the hill, has a great resume and is not willing to roll up their sleeves.”
- “The board’s number one job should be help the founder be a learning machine and see the future.”
- “Behind closed doors, we have a debate. As a manager and team, when we walk out the door, we never second guess each other in public.”
- “Don’t argue with tone of voice, but argue with data, put the problem out in the middle of the room, and then let’s come up with a point of view.”
- Push the ability to say yes as far down in the organization as possible, or layers of bureaucracy will create an institutional no that kills your speed.

**Decision-Making, Learning, and Culture**

- “People who are right a lot are constantly willing to change their mind.”
- “Most humans have trouble updating their decision process with new data.”
- “It’s very likely that the founders who tap out at about 500 people have voted not to keep learning.”
- “The values you espouse have no correlation to company success. What’s correlated is the values you espouse get built into the company daily fabric, and that’s what’s important.”
- “Always know more than anybody in the room about your client’s business.”
- Skeptical optimists win because they can hold a big, life-changing idea in one hand while clearly seeing how it might fail in the other.

**Creativity, Quality, and Product**

Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at a Brooklyn building collapse, BAAJA’s odds of passing, reusing old memory in new phones, a nationwide aircraft ground stop, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

## Housing and Cities

A 3 story building in New York partially collapsed into an adjacent construction site that was being excavated, killing 8 people and injuring 18. Good reminder that for as burdensome as various building regulations can sometimes be (particularly in New York, with its ubiquitous sidewalk sheds), they don’t exist for no reason. [[Construction Dive](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/project-fatal-brooklyn-collapse-stop-work-order/874545/)]

On the other hand, that doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t evaluate code requirements to see if the benefits they bring are worth the cost. An article in the Washington Post argues that many requirements to upgrade electrical panels for higher load devices are often unnecessary. “ Outdated industry practices and in some places outdated electrical codes are regularly resulting in the recommendation that people need to upgrade their electrical panels if they want to add appliances such as induction stoves, heat pumps and electric-vehicle chargers. The expense — at a median of $3,500, and triple or quadruple that in some settings — is deterring some energy-efficient upgrades and making the projects far more costly for those who proceed. But some researchers say panel upgrades are almost always unnecessary. One report this year found that 98 percent of homes with 100-ampere panels, the smallest common size, have room to add popular electronic devices. ” [[Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/09/people-are-paying-thousands-home-upgrade-thats-often-unnecessary/)]

The US now has over 1500 mass timber buildings, up from fewer than 100 a decade ago. [[The Real Deal](https://therealdeal.com/national/2026/11/11/mass-timber-gains-as-developers-look-beyond-steel-concrete/)]

The current probability of permitting reform bill BAAJA becoming law is little over 50% on Kalshi. [[Kalshi](https://kalshi.com/markets/kxpermitbill/american-affordability-and-jobs-act/kxpermitbill-26sep)]

A Houthi missile hit Saudi state oil company Aramco’s skyscraper in Riyadh. [[X](https://x.com/AMK_Mapping_/status/2119390132587598203)]

A new Nicholas Bagley paper on the cost of federal permitting, arguing that the real costs of things like NEPA is the huge amount of effort agencies put in to try and make things “litigation proof”. “ The evidence does suggest, however, that the bulk of the costs of the federal permitting regime stem from the defensive measures agencies and developers take to guard against the risk of a bad outcome in court. That insight allows for a rough evaluation of the likely effects of popular permitting reform ideas. Some—including popular ones like time limits and statutes of limitations—are unlikely to accomplish much. Only those reforms that change the incentives created by the risk of judicial review will meaningfully move the needle. ” [[Nicholas Bagley](https://nicholasbagley.com/assets/papers/costs-of-federal-permitting.pdf)]

A progress report from the Center for Land Economics, which advocates for land value taxes to make more efficient use of urban land. ” Three states passed laws enabling land value taxes in some form: Kentucky, Virginia and New York. In each of them we’re now helping cities work out how to put them into practice. Five more states and DC considered similar bills. This is the most legislative momentum the movement has seen in decades… ” [[Land Economics](https://blog.landeconomics.org/p/what-cle-did-in-year-two)]

[↗ construction-physics.com](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/reading-list-11142026)

items.title: The Hidden Spiegeltent in Chicago, Illinois
items.subtitle: These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair.

items.body:
Spiegeltents were made to travel. These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair. They went up fast and came down fast. The one on Randolph Street is not going anywhere. It was built indoors, on the 14th floor of a Loop building.

The building opened in 1926. Rapp & Rapp designed it, with the Oriental Theatre movie palace on the lower floors. The theater is now the James M. Nederlander Theatre. The whole building stands on the site of the Iroquois Theatre, where a fire in 1903 became one of the deadliest in American history.

High above the theater, the architects put a large hall for Masonic meetings. It sat empty for decades. Later it was turned into offices, and a dropped ceiling hid the room completely. When the building was converted into the Cambria Hotel, workers took that ceiling down and found the old hall again, steel bow trusses and all.

In 2019 the tent came over from Belgium in pieces, about 4,000 of them. Belgian tent builders put it together inside the hall, the traditional way, with no nails. It is about 72 feet across. From the hall, it looks like a small circus parked under factory trusses. Inside, there is carved wood, stained glass, velvet and mirrors everywhere. The mirrors are not just for looks. They let guests see around the posts that hold up the roof.

Since October 2026, the tent has been the home of Kermess by Circensia, which kept it right at the center of the room.

items.body:
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of [Cappadocia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia), a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In *[The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse](https://hemeria.com/en-us/products/the-untold-story-of-the-yilki-horses)*, photographer [Nur Tucker](https://nurtucker.com/) captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the [yilki breed](https://www.yilkiatlari.org.tr/en/history.html) that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb *yılmak*, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In *The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,* Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.

The book is available for purchase directly from [Hemeria](https://hemeria.com/en-us/products/the-untold-story-of-the-yilki-horses), and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/nurtuckerphotography/?hl=en).

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a [Colossal Member](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members) today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article [Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/11/the-untold-story-of-the-yilki-horse-nur-tucker-book/) appeared first on [Colossal](https://www.thisiscolossal.com).

items.body:
# Berlin - CDU-Politiker Winkel verteidigt Kompromissvorschlag zur Rente mit 63 - bisher kein Einlenken der SPD

Johannes Winkel verteidigt den Vorschlag, Geringverdienern die Frührente weiterhin abschlagsfrei zu ermöglichen. (Henning Kaiser / dpa / Henning Kaiser)Man müsse von Maximalpositionen Abstand nehmen, um zu einer Lösung zu kommen, sagte Winkel im Deutschlandfunk. Der stellvertretende Vorsitzende der Jungen Union, Reddig (CDU), nannte den Vorschlag im ZDF ein Kompromissangebot an die SPD. Die von der Regierung eingesetzte Rentenkommission habe gute Vorschläge gemacht, wie die Rente verbessert werden könne, sagte Reddig. "Dort haben wir beschlossen, dass wir die Rente mit 63 sogar abschaffen und ersetzen durch eine Regelung, die vor allem die Menschen trifft, die körperlich nicht mehr können", sagte Reddig. Dies stieß aber auf Widerstand sowohl in der SPD als auch in Teilen der Union, weshalb die Gesamtreform seit Monaten blockiert ist.Dem neuen Vorschlag zufolge sollen diejenigen weiterhin Anspruch auf die abschlagsfreie Rente haben, die 45 Versicherungsjahre vorweisen können und in ihrem Arbeitsleben weniger als 70 Prozent des Durchschnittseinkommens verdient haben. Langjährig Beschäftigte mit höherem Einkommen müssten hingegen höhere Abschläge hinnehmen, wenn sie vor Erreichen der regulären Altersgrenze in Rente gehen.Die Renten-Fachfrau der SPD-Bundestagsfraktion, Klose, nannte den Vorschlag nicht hinnehmbar. "Ich finde die Grenzen, die da gesetzt werden, viel zu niedrig", sagte sie. Die stellvertretende Fraktionsvorsitzende der SPD im Bundestag, Esdar, sagte im Deutschlandfunk , der Vorschlag würde "90 Prozent derjenigen schlechter stellen, die heute die Rente nach 45 Jahren abschlagsfrei bekommen". Sie begrüßte zumindest, dass die Union sich "kompromissbereit" zeige. Bundesarbeitsminister Schweitzer sagte gestern Abend in Berlin, er freue sich über die Vorschläge, zwar nicht inhaltlich, aber sie machten deutlich, dass auf allen Seiten Bewegung eingetreten sei, sagte der SPD-Politiker. Er habe ein großes Interesse daran, dass man schnell vorankomme.Diese Nachricht wurde am 27.11.2026 im Programm Deutschlandfunk gesendet.

items.body:
Imagine you’re in a seat in the theatre. The stage has a back and sides, but is open to the audience. And yet, the actors behave as though they can’t see the rows of people watching. It’s as if there’s a fourth wall.

The fourth wall is the imaginary barrier between the fictional world and the audience in TV, film, or theatre.

As the audience, you are in a privileged position of watching these private scenes play out in front of you.

Origin of the Fourth Wall

An early description of this invisible barrier as a wall comes from our pal Denis Diderot (also of The Diderot Effect) in his 1758 writing Discours de la poésie dramatique (translated):

"Whether you are writing or acting, give no more thought to the spectator than if he did not exist. Imagine a great wall at the edge of the stage separating you from the audience; act as though the curtain had never risen."

I love Denis’ comment about acting as though the curtain had never risen. I’m not an actor, but I would guess that being able to ignore that there’s an audience, or a camera, might help create a more realistic performance.

Breaking the Fourth Wall

Now, you might take issue with Diderot’s notion, especially if you’ve ever been to a pantomime. Many shows don’t treat the fourth wall as a wall. A pantomime is expected to engage the audience by acknowledging that there will be things the audience can see on stage that a character perhaps can’t—“It’s behind you!” Other times the audience are explicitly part of the show.

Some shows have characters turn and share private thoughts directly into the camera, or simply give a knowing glance. This is known as breaking the 4th wall. Phoebe Waller-Bridge did this all the time in Fleabag, making the viewers her confidants in the scene.

We recently enjoyed a family viewing of Monty Python and the Holy Grail, which does it rather spectacularly, merging the medieval and the modern.

Related Ideas to The Fourth Wall

Front Stage, Back Stage

Diagonal Billing

The Third Teacher

Information Radiator

The Diderot Effect

Mean-World Syndrome

Here’s Diderot’s passage in the original French:

"Soit donc que vous composiez, soit que vous jouiez, ne pensez non plus au spectateur que s’il n’existait pas. Imaginez sur le bord du théâtre un grand mur qui vous sépare du parterre ; jouez comme si la toile ne se levait pas."

items.body:
*Die Neustadt leuchtet wieder weihnachtlich. Seit Montag waren Torsten Wiesener und Elektriker Robert Ryssel im Viertel unterwegs, um die Weihnachtsbeleuchtung aufzuhängen. Seit Donnerstag ist alles fertig.*

Das Sternhänger-Duo im Einsatz auf der Sebnitzer Straße. Foto: Anton Launer

Routiniert greift sich Wiesener einen Stern und eine Kette, Ryssel zieht am Hebel und ab geht’s in Richtung Dachrinne. Kaum sind die beiden oben angekommen, haken sie die Kette ein. Dann schwenkt der Arm des kleinen Hubsteigers in die Mitte. Ryssel schließt die Kette an die Straßenbeleuchtung an und weiter geht’s zur anderen Straßenseite. Dann wieder runter, ein paar Meter weiter – und das Spiel beginnt von vorn.

Seit vielen Jahren installiert das eingespielte Duo für den Gewerbe- und Kulturverein Dresden Neustadt die Lichterketten und Sterne in den Straßen des Viertels. Die ersten Lichterketten hingen bereits Anfang der 1990er-Jahre. Damals gab es jedoch nur vereinzelt Ketten und auf der Alaunstraße eine Zeit lang einige Herrnhuter Sterne.

Weihnachtlich beleuchtete Louisenstraße – Foto: Anton Launer

In diesem Jahr sorgen 165 Lichterketten, 169 Sterne und acht Kandelaber für weihnachtliches Licht. Aneinandergereiht messen die Lichterketten mehr als zweieinhalb Kilometer. Auf der Görlitzer und der Rothenburger Straße verhindern die Oberleitungen der Straßenbahn das Aufhängen der Ketten. Dort verbreiten Kandelaber an den Hauswänden Weihnachtsglanz.

## Pläne für die Königsbrücker Straße

Schon 2011 begann der Verein, die Leuchtmittel auf stromsparende LED-Technik umzustellen. Die elektrische Leistung der gesamten Weihnachtsbeleuchtung beträgt heute nur rund 4,5 Kilowatt. Mit Zeitschaltuhren begrenzt der Verein zusätzlich die Leuchtdauer. Zwischen 1 und 6 Uhr bleibt die Beleuchtung ausgeschaltet, Freitag und Sonnabend erst ab 2.45 Uhr.

Mittlerweile leuchten in vielen Straßen der Äußeren Neustadt Lichterketten und Sterne. Wiesener hat schon die nächste Straße im Blick. „Wir wollen auch auf der Königsbrücker Weihnachtsbeleuchtung installieren“, sagt er. Der Verein stimmt die Pläne bereits mit der Stadtverwaltung ab. Die Lichter sollen aber erst nach Abschluss der Bauarbeiten installiert werden.

Das Projekt finanziert der Verein traditionell mit Beiträgen von Gewerbetreibenden, Hauseigentümer*innen und einigen Anwohner*innen. Seit 1992 engagiert sich der [Gewerbe- und Kulturverein](https://www.01099.info/) für die Neustadt.

Leuchtet auch weihnachtlich: Erika und Kurt haben extra eine Bresche in das Gestrüpp geschlagen. Foto: Christoph Springer

## Neustädter Kiez’lmarkt

Angelaufen ist auch die siebte Ausgabe des Neustädter Kiez’lmarktes. Die während der Corona-Pandemie entstandene Aktion der Neustädter Händler*innen hat sich inzwischen etabliert. In diesem Jahr beteiligen sich 17 Läden.

Wer in einem der teilnehmenden Geschäfte für mindestens 100 Euro (in ausgewählten Geschäften bereits ab 50 Euro) einkauft, bekommt eine Flasche Glühwein oder alkoholfreien Winterpunsch der Firma Gustav Müller geschenkt. [Weitere Infos](https://www.kiezlmarkt.de/).

items.title: How to Touch the Nothingness Behind Everything: Kahlil Gibran on the Seven Selves
items.subtitle: A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.
items.feedText: A self is a forest. A self is a ship. Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of l…
items.body:
A self [is a forest](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/09/pando/). A self [is a ship](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/08/plutarch-the-ship-of-theseus-ted-ed/). A self [is an illusion](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/), and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is [a sum of selves](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/04/10/parts/), contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

[Kahlil Gibran](https://themarginalian.org/tag/kahlil-gibran) (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about [the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/04/04/youth-and-age-kahlil-gibran/), takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic [The Madman](http://www.amazon.com/Madman-His-Parables-Poems/dp/0486419118/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/madman-his-parables-and-poems/oclc/242642&referer=brief_results) | [free ebook](http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5616)).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated [the Japanese concept of ma](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/07/ma/).)

Kahlil Gibran

> THE SEVEN SELVES
> by Kahlil Gibran
> In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
> selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:
> First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
> with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
> by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.
> Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
> given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
> and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
> his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
> existence.
> Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
> of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
> who would rebel against this madman.
> Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
> was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
> I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
> who would protest against serving this madman.
> Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
> the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
> rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
> I, not you, who would rebel.
> Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
> with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
> and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
> solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.
> Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
> man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
> fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
> lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
> in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
> life.

…
