items.body:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our [recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure](https://doi.org/10.1177/01650254261485170), an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

## 1. Compassion has to survive peer dynamics

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

At first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: Compassion unfolds within relationships.

During adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

When educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on [teaching empathy or kindness](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_educators_are_using_kindness_to_transform_schools). Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

## 2. Compassion involves social risk

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

The question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

items.body:
Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and actions, many people have asked me for my opinion on this event.

The good news for the curious among you is that I captured my thoughts in an op-ed for *The New York Times*, which they published Thursday, the same day that Anthropic went public. It was titled “[Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/opinion/anthropic-ipo-ai-regulation.html),” and it opens as follows:

“By the close of the stock market today, Anthropic will have become a central pillar of the American economy. This is deeply concerning to me, because it’s unclear how many of the retail and institutional investors handing over their money to Anthropic realize that they are, in some sense, funding a doomsday cult that also happens to build enterprise software.”

My use of “doomsday cult” isn’t facetious; it underscores a critical reality. As many have reported ([including myself](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/opinion/ai-silicon-valley.html)), the leaders of Anthropic have long believed that AI is destined to transform the human species, either delivering a utopia or killing us all. They see themselves, with their highly rational minds, trained on long hours during the 2000s debating these issues on blogs like *Less Wrong* and *Overcoming Bias*, as the select few who must rise up to guide humanity through this next evolution.

This may sound like hyperbole, but it’s not. [It’s exactly what they believe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jt508VjX2H8).

Some ask, “Why is this a problem? If any company is going to advance AI, shouldn’t it be one that cares about bad outcomes?”

As I elaborate in my op-ed, the situation is not so simple. Anthropic’s belief that transformational AI is imminent has made it reckless. Anthropic now releases models faster than they can build safeguards because they believe the fate of the human race depends on getting to superintelligent AI first. (Case in point: earlier this year, they announced they were relaxing rules that required them to slow down development if models became hard to control. Their reason? If they applied such rules “unilaterally,” other – presumably less righteous – parties might get ahead of them in the race.)

Indeed, Anthropic stated a key rationale for their IPO is to raise the money needed to accelerate investments in so-called “recursive self-improvement,” where AI systems upgrade themselves. This is, of course, a terrible idea, as it creates models that are even less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing, but sees no alternative if they’re to continue as humanity’s shepherd through this revolution.

It’s unclear to what degree they even care about profits or building a durable business. As I summarize in my op-ed:

“It’s a business plan that starts with a lot of red ink and then abruptly ends with superintelligence arriving and rendering money superfluous.”

To be clear: generative AI is an incredibly important technological revolution. It brings with it great promises and real risks. But the right way to navigate these innovations can’t possibly be to let a small number of people in Silicon Valley, who have been worshipping AI as a millenarian agent since well before LLMs entered the scene, gather as much money as possible to fund their self-proclaimed role as prophets who will lead the rest of us to their idiosyncratic vision of a better future.

#### In Other News

For more on the question of whether Amodei and company are right in their beliefs that we’re on a trajectory toward superintelligence, check out [my recent technical article](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-superintelligence-debate) for the *IEEE Spectrum*, which lays out an engineering case against the feasibility of AI superintelligence. (You should also consider signing up for the Spectrum’s always insightful [AI Alert newsletter](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-alert-signup).)

items.body:
## Beyond the human hand: designing with the living world

When **[the Design Museum, London](https://www.designboom.com/tag/design-museum-london/)** developed More than Human: Making With the Living World, it began with a deceptively simple proposition: what if design were not understood as solely by and for humans, but as something shaped in collaboration with animals, plants, and ecosystems?

Living environments are already shaped by countless organisms and relationships, each participating in the ecosystems of which humans are also a part. The **[exhibition](https://www.designboom.com/tag/exhibitions/)** asks how design might acknowledge these relationships, shifting away from an understanding of nature as a resource toward ways of craft that recognize other living beings as participants and collaborators. Ultimately, it invites us to develop more reciprocal and responsible relationships with the living world.

Following its presentation in Zurich, the exhibition now makes it way to Singapore. From November 28, 2026, to May 16, 2027, visitors can experience **[More than Human: Making With the Living World](https://www.marinabaysands.com/museum/exhibitions/more-than-human.html?utm_source=dboom&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=merkle_dm_asm_sg_awr_na_exhib-morethanhuman2026&utm_term=content-na&utm_content=adv-na-morethanhuman-nov26)** at ArtScience Museum.

Pollinator Pathmaker: Perceptual Field 7SzzLn6GnY97DSo7hCSLMf by Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg, installation view at the Design Museum, London

all images courtesy of ArtScience Museum

## The Asia debut of More than Human: Making With the Living World

Building on the original London presentation, the **[Singapore edition](https://www.marinabaysands.com/museum/exhibitions/more-than-human.html?utm_source=dboom&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=merkle_dm_asm_sg_awr_na_exhib-morethanhuman2026&utm_term=content-na&utm_content=adv-na-morethanhuman-nov26)** has been significantly expanded and co-curated by ArtScience Museum and the Design Museum, London, with support from the DesignSingapore Council.

Twenty-four works and installations by regional artists, including commissions, adaptations, and international loans, join the existing exhibition. This brings the total to more than 140 artworks, objects, and installations contributed by close to 55 artists, designers, architects, researchers, and communities, notably featuring the works of eight local Singaporean designers.

The additions bring perspectives from across Southeast Asia into the exhibition, exploring how design can be understood as part of living, interconnected systems rather than as something separate from the living world.

Pollinator Pathmaker: Perceptual Field 7SzzLn6GnY97DSo7hCSLMf by Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg, installation view at the Design Museum, London

## designing with other species

The exhibition includes basketry by Ye’kuana people from the Amazon region, whose practices reflect relationships between material gathering, cultural knowledge, and the forest.

There is also Aki Inomata’s How to carve a sculpture. Inomata placed wooden blocks in beaver enclosures and collected the forms left by their gnawing. Because beavers tend to chew around hard knots, the wood itself helps shape what emerges. She presents the beaver-gnawed originals alongside two versions enlarged to three times their size: one hand-carved by a sculptor, the other produced using computer-controlled milling (CNC). By placing all three side by side, Inomata asks who, or what, creates a sculpture: the beaver, the wood, the sculptor, the machine, the artist, or the relationships among them?

Kelp Council by Julia Lohmann, installation view at the Design Museum, London

Taking a more hands-on but equally reflective approach, MOTH’s The More-than-human Rights mural explores Rights of Nature frameworks, exploring a world where rivers and ecosystems are recognized as living entities with intrinsic rights. Masks available to visitors reveal texts hidden in the mural.

# A Jazz Walk Incoming — Roden Newsletter Archive

### RodenIssue #120November 22, 2026

## A Jazz Walk Incoming

### Twenty-one days of chasing jazz and Shōwa in Kyūshū

Roden Readers —

Fall! Finally! Jacket weather! Sweaters! Snow on Fuji! Oh, my!

What has been going on this past month? A whole lotta hermiting. I’ve been on a decidedly teenager-like (or Mishima-like, if you prefer; the man almost never rose before noon) schedule, which my body clock seems to love, working late into the night and passing out around two or three and then waking up around ten or eleven, pounding a big ol’ smoothie, and then working like mad from noon to six, breaking for a nice dinner with friends, and then diving back under until my futon calls. This is an ideal schedule for me. Because I am insane. I basically never shifted back from Europe time to Japan time in October. Also, a smoothie + slow, delicious dinner turns out to be a great eating schedule? I feel light and energetic. Am I an adult? I’m not sure. I do push-ups and walk 10,000 steps a day. Such is the glamorous life of being self-employed at forty-six years old while the world speedruns its own unique flavor of insanity in the background. Is the singularity here yet?

#### #SHŌWA! COLOSSUS!

My big announcement here is a new pop-up newsletter / “tour” starting in two days (on Wednesday the 25th). It’s called: SHŌWA㍼COLOSSUS.

Sign up here (as with all my pop-ups, you have to enthusiastically opt in):.

For twenty-one+ days I’ll be on the road visiting some of the last remaining classic jazz kissas of Kyūshū. As usual, I’ll be sending daily dispatches and more. As usual, I have no idea what we’ll discover. And as usual, I am forever grateful to my SPECIAL PROJECTS members who make projects like this possible. All funding and support for these tours (which are complicated, expensive, slightly crazy affairs) comes directly from memberships and book sales.

If you don’t mind sharing the Ridgeline link, or the Instagram post, please do. These tours are one of the few chances to grow my audience without having to be a full-time social media bobblehead. I appreciate it!

#### #Holiday Presents?

Thank you to everyone who has grabbed a notebook! They’re almost sold out. We have about fifty sets left. If I make some more, it won’t be until next year.

Things Become Other Things, the hardcover black-and-white Random House edition, is available for a paltry $18 shipped from the Evil™ Amazon® (and probably about $25 book-in-hand from your local bookshop, which you should go to, say hello to the people working there, smile at a few customers, smell the smells of literal tons of paper lined up on the walls; and if they don’t have a copy and you request one, a thousand baby kittens are instantly born into loving families).

Here’s what’s available in the fancy SPECIAL PROJECTS shop:

- Kissa by Kissa 6th ed., unsigned
- Things Become Other Things, fine art 2nd ed., signed
- OTHER THING, first ed., signed
- ⬤ — a made-in-Japan lay-flat notebook (I should have signed these)
Just a reminder, SPECIAL PROJECTS members get big discounts on everything in the SP Shop. And shipping for an order with multiple items is a significantly better deal than single items (just the way DHL works; the first kilogram is the most expensive). Orders ship next business day from my warehouse in Osaka, and arrive almost everywhere around the world in (usually) 2-3 days. It’s very efficient! These all make good presents.

We just — finally! — sold the last Tomato Farmer’s print. Thank you to everyone who bought one over the years. One of my goals for next year is to do more printing (working with local high-end photo shops doing C-prints?). Maybe even do a show at some point? I have a huge back catalogue of shots (many now with negatives) and should probably do something with some of them.

items.body:
Life as I knew it quietly began to unravel on a drizzly January morning in 2022.

I was standing at the kitchen sink in a puffer jacket, staring out at my favorite persimmon tree, now bare. Only weeks before, the tree had been so full of persimmons that we collected them in huge plastic garbage cans for our neighbors to take by the grocery bagful. Our Labrador-ish mutt, Buster, was fat from persimmon overconsumption.

Back then, the kitchen was loud, warm, and colorful. Our four kids were home for the holidays, bringing hungry friends and favorite songs, their late-night cookie-baking leaving sugar dust and dirty dishes everywhere.

Now that the kids were gone, my husband Mark and I conserved energy by leaving the downstairs heat off, telling each other we couldn’t justify heating the whole house just to keep the kitchen warm. We were real empty-nesters, ready to downsize.

Within weeks, we stripped our house of everything personal. We took down family photos, scraped butterfly stickers from hidden corners, and painted over the teal walls preteen girls had decorated. All traces of our family life vanished. We put our home on the market. It was the end of an era.

In December, my seemingly super-fit mom was diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Our house still hadn’t sold—by the time we put it on the market, mortgage rates had started climbing for the first time in two decades—but I moved into my childhood bedroom at my parents’ home to help my dad care for my mom. She passed away four months later.

A week before my mom’s memorial, I myself was diagnosed with invasive breast cancer. And a few days after my first cancer-related surgery, a close cousin died of an accidental overdose just after his 50th birthday.

Also during that time, a dear college friend, a fit, athletic doctor, had a fatal heart attack. And while I was having radiation for my breast cancer, our beloved dog Buster was diagnosed with lymphoma and needed to be put down.

Other losses were expected and even positive. Our house finally sold, and so we said goodbye to the home where we had raised our four kids. I packed up that house through tears—for my mom, for my health, for my beloved dog and cousin and college friend, sobbing as I threw away things that marked my kids’ childhoods: boxes of ribbons from horse shows and swim meets, SAT score reports, so many old shoes and backpacks, homemade Harry Potter wands.

Mark and I put our stuff in storage and moved in with my dad for real while we renovated a new house in Berkeley. I loved this time with my dad; it made my cancer treatment and everything else bearable. He had always been my person, and now I got to cry and laugh with him every day, with no space between us.

About a year after my mom died, we finally moved into our new house. The first morning I woke up there and looked out the window at the whole Bay Area, I was astonished to see not one, but four rainbows touching down on the water of the San Francisco Bay. I felt welcomed and reassured that I was right where I was meant to be.

But then my brother-in-law Brian was diagnosed with a malignant brain tumor, the kind that doesn’t usually respond to chemo or radiation. They did everything anyway—brain surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, experimental drugs, an electromagnetic cap, expensive immunotherapy from Germany—but less than nine months later, he too passed away. I’ve never known a man with a bigger heart than Brian; when he died, we lost the emotional center on Mark’s side of the family.

Our family was devastated. Again.

With each of these losses and life changes, I picked myself up and told my friends that at least it wasn’t my dad. When my dad dies, I’m going to stay in bed for a year, I said. When my dad dies, expect my complete collapse. I started believing that I could bear anything except for losing my father, my oldest and dearest friend. The loss of my father would leave a hole in my heart I knew I could never fill.

And then, in April of 2025, one month to the day after we lost Brian, my 84-year-old dad passed away.

items.body:
When Siddhartha Gautama gave his first teaching after enlightenment, it was to five friends in the deer park at Sarnath, not far from Varanasi in the Ganges Valley. Wanting to transmit to them the essence of his breakthrough, he crystallized his insights into what would become known as the four noble truths. These include the truth of the way out of suffering, known as the noble eightfold path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

The eightfold path offers a way to touch awakening as Gautama did. These insights were not the result of thinking or study, nor were they a creed or philosophical doctrine. They were the fruit of Gautama’s own direct experience and meditative realization, and they conveyed a path that traced a “middle way” between the two extremes of asceticism and indulgence. It was a way, he believed, that could lead anyone to realize understanding, liberation, and peace.

#### “You don’t hurry to get the dishes done quickly so you can get on with something else. You encounter the miracle of life that includes dishes.”

As a species we’re still struggling to find a middle way, to steer a wise course through the extremes of fanaticism, greed, nihilism, rage, and despair. The ancient wisdom of the eightfold path offers eight matrixes that are powerfully relevant today as a guide to help us navigate these extremes and bring a meaningful direction to our daily lives, actions, and relationships.

All elements of the eightfold path inter-are. You cannot extract any of them from the context of the path. So, for example, if you take mindfulness out of the ethical context of the path, it is no longer right mindfulness. All eight elements are interrelated and interdependent. They enhance each other. When practiced deeply, each element of the path contains the other seven within it, and they complement each other to create a complete path to liberation.

My teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, taught that right mindfulness is at the heart of the eightfold path. So, with the energy of right mindfulness as the foundation, we’re able to develop right concentration. This gives rise to insight or “right view,” which Thich Nhat Hanh described as the “insight of interbeing.” It is this deep view of the world that guides us to an ethical and beneficial life through right thinking, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort. So, when you generate the energy of mindfulness, you are naturally concentrated on the object of your mindfulness, whether it’s your breathing, your body, the sunset, or the presence of the person in front of you.

Photo © Noumae | Dreamstime.com

The energies of mindfulness and concentration naturally give rise to insight, right view. You touch the insight of interbeing between your breath and the earth, or between your body and your ancestors and descendants, or between your heart and the sun in the sky. You realize that you inter-are with the person in front of you.
Already, this insight of interbeing helps us touch peace, joy, and freedom.

Now, with the energy of mindfulness, concentration, and insight, your thinking will naturally be right thinking.

It will be free from discrimination and separation, and on the basis of that thinking, your speech will be right speech and your action right action.

Cultivating right diligence (or effort) in that moment, you’ll be able to see and calm any unwholesome seeds that may get triggered in your consciousness, such as anger or despair, and identify and activate positive seeds, such as gratitude and compassion. With all those energies alive in you, the way you spend your time, energy, and labor—your livelihood—will be “right.” It will be beneficial for you and everyone around you.

items.body:
# The human voice

This is a post from Robin Sloan’s lab blog & notebook. You can visit the blog’s homepage, or learn more about me.

## The human voice

November 20, 2026

I encourage you to open Levent Alpöge’s PDF note announcing his proof of the Rie­mann Hypoth­esis with the help of AI — because although the work was AI-assisted, this note is so clearly and beau­ti­fully human. It’s fabulous.

I have noticed the steady creep of AI-generated text into the pub­li­ca­tions of the big AI com­pa­nies themselves, and while it tends not to be on the level of “egregious slop”, it does lend every­thing a … smoothness. I note also that these pub­li­ca­tions are very rarely signed; they come from The Blob. Who wrote this?Who wrote this? I know it’s cus­tomary for big com­pa­nies to speak Blob-like, but/and I still find it jarring.

Coun­ter­point Alpöge: his note is not only better than a smooth, AI-generated summation, it’s also better than an aca­d­emic paper, because his passion — his appre­ci­a­tion of sur­prise and beauty — is so clear on the page. It seems almost to rise off the screen, a 3D layer of sparkling energy.

Tell you what, you can use all the AI you want in your project, if you write about it like this, in your real human voice.

P.S. And then there’s this, the absolute sig­na­ture of our new era: “The Rie­mann Hypoth­esis is proven, but not yet understood.”

items.body:
Next up in Dezeen's [20x20](https://www.dezeen.com/20x20/) project in partnership with [Kohler](https://www.studiokohler.com/home?id=paid-media_dezeen_studiokohler_Global-20x20_2026_Editorial-Series_version-1), which marks 20 years of Dezeen, is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by [Kelly Wearstler](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/kelly-wearstler/) for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship.

Goti has experienced a remarkable rise since presenting [a furniture collection made from salvaged foam insulation](https://www.dezeen.com/2023/05/05/kiki-goti-neo-vanity-dressing-room-furniture/) during the 2023 edition of [Milan design week](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/milan-design-week/).

Her conceptual, research-led work typically explores heritage, identity and craftsmanship, resulting in playful objects and spaces that reexamine the cultural codes embedded in design.

Goti was nominated as an emerging talent to watch by American designer [Wearstler](https://www.kellywearstler.com/), who praised how Goti “approaches ornament with the precision of an engineer and the instincts of a sculptor”.

“That refusal to treat craft and technology as opposites is going to matter more over the next 20 years,” Wearstler added.

Kelly Wearstler (above) has picked Kiki Goti (right) for Dezeen's 20x20 project. Photo courtesy of H&M Home

Goti recently relocated from New York to Paris. Photo by Liz Carababas

As well as a shared love of ornament and the decorative arts, Wearstler also picked up on how Goti's practice is informed by her background in robotics and machine learning.

“It's amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail,” Goti told Dezeen.

> It's amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail

Goti added that she was pleased to be recognised by a leading female designer, as her creative muses are mostly women and femininity plays a major role in her own practice.

“My work is very personal so of course there are a lot of references to being a woman,” she said, adding that she draws inspiration from well-known artists and designers such as [Louise Bourgeois](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/louise-bourgeois/) and [Faye Toogood](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/faye-toogood/).

Goti spoke to Dezeen from Paris, where she currently lives with her partner, French filmmaker Vincent Staropoli, having recently relocated there from New York.

She was raised in Thessaloniki and received a diploma in architecture from the local AUTh university before completing a masters degree in Integrative Technologies and Architectural Design Research at Stuttgart’s Institute of Computational Design.

Goti is known for her highly crafted, decorative pieces, including glassware, which was presented at Alcova. Photos by Matthew Gordon Photography

The move to New York came after accepting a research position at Pratt Institute, but during the Covid pandemic Goti realised that she missed making her own work, so began experimenting with found materials.

“I really didn’t know what I wanted to do,” she recalled. “But through my research at the university and the New York design community I realised there were other people working in a similar way, which encouraged me to stick with it.”

The initial collection was followed by projects made with glass, marble and, most recently, [a series of furniture pieces featuring lacquered wooden surfaces that contrast with bell-like aluminium elements](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/09/11/collectible-design-fair-new-york-2025/).

> The outcomes are very unpredictable. Because the collections all look different there isn’t anything people can point to and say ‘that’s clearly made by Kiki’

Goti explained that her work usually starts with research into a specific technique or a material that interests her, before she then applies her findings to the design of an object.

She said she finds this approach creatively fulfilling as it offers endless opportunities, though as someone early in her career it means there is no identifiable style associated with her work.

# Let's Play with Hardcaml! - Metasepi

## Let's Play with Hardcaml!

Posted on November 28, 2026 / Tags: takibi, fpga, ocaml, hardcaml

### Table of contents

I prepared a five-minute lightning talk for the 8th Homebrew CPU Meetup on November 28, 2026. The slides are below.

Open slides in a new tab · Download PDF · View Markdown source

This talk is a gentle introduction to Hardcaml, an RTL design library embedded in OCaml. Rather than discussing advanced verification techniques, I wanted to share the fun of building digital circuits in an interactive programming environment.

We start with a simple 5-bit counter and do everything inside utop, an OCaml REPL:

- Describe a digital circuit using ordinary OCaml functions.
- Generate Verilog from the circuit.
- Simulate the circuit cycle by cycle using an ordinary OCaml for loop.
- Display the recorded waveforms directly in the terminal.
No FPGA, external Verilog simulator, or even a separate OCaml project is needed to try this example. I tested the installation steps and the REPL session in a Docker environment, so you can follow along with the slides.

And what happens if we keep playing with Hardcaml?

With the help of AI coding agents, I ended up building a dual-core RISC-V SoC that boots Linux 6.18 with SMP on a Colorlight i9 FPGA board.

I hope this talk encourages more people to give Hardcaml a try and enjoy building their own digital circuits.

items.title: Going by; Laughing; Living.
items.subtitle: The sky is pink, and orange, and yellow all washed-out by the grey of the clouds.
items.feedText: Do you hear all this noise? It's frightening. A group of people is going by, they are laughing, they are living. And I wonder how. I'm trying to understand, how can I go by? How can I laugh? How can I live? Why aren't they walking alone? The room is getting dark, the colors have faded. I can't hear the people anymore, but they are still walking around my brain. They are going by, they are laughing, they are living. Getting my head through the window, I am looking at the trees. Looking right in their eyes. "I'm s…
items.body:
Do you hear all this noise? It's frightening.

The sky is pink, and orange, and yellow all washed-out by the grey of the clouds.

A group of people is going by, they are laughing, they are living.

And I wonder how.

I'm trying to understand, how can I go by? How can I laugh? How can I live?

Why aren't they walking alone?

The room is getting dark, the colors have faded.

I can't hear the people anymore, but they are still walking around my brain.

They are going by, they are laughing, they are living.

Getting my head through the window, I am looking at the trees. Looking right in their eyes.

"I'm sorry", I tell them.

You didn't deserve this.

"You are precious", I tell them.

And I wonder why I don't hear it coming from everywhere.

Why is there only this scary noise?

The noise of life going on, of people going by.

As if it was all ok. As if all around us wasn't screaming.

But the noise is too loud, too loud to listen with our ears.

I wonder if people can listen with their hearts.

I wonder if people can look at trees right in their eyes.

Just like they can go by,

Just like they can laugh,

Just like they can live.

I hope they can look at trees right in their eyes.

And tell them they are sorry.

Stop going by.

Stop laughing.

Stop living if just for a moment.

And tell them they are sorry.

I hope people can be alone and look at themselves.

At the sky full of pink, and orange, and yellow.

Hear all this scary noise they are making. Hear it with their hearts.

Then maybe they can all be silent, we can all be silent.

Be silent while all around it's getting dark.
And wait the night out.

Wait alongside the trees, the rivers, the critters running under our feet.

Tell them all they are precious,

That we never meant it and that we are sorry.

Maybe then I can go by.

Maybe then I can laugh.

Maybe then I can live.

## The Contents of Perception

In contemporary philosophy, the phrase ’the contents of perception’ means, roughly, what is conveyed to the subject by her perceptual experience. For example, suppose you are looking into a piano at the array of hammers and strings. There will be a way these things look to you when you see them: they will look to have a certain shape, color, texture, and arrangement relative to one another, among other things. Your visual experience conveys to you that the piano has these features. If your experience is illusory in some respect then the piano won’t really have all those features. But even then, there will still be something conveyed to you by your experience. Three main questions will be addressed in this entry. First (Sections 1–2), what are contents and what is their relation to experiences? Second (Sections 3–7), which contents are contents of experience? Finally (Section 8), in virtue of what do experiences have contents, when they do?

## 1. What are Perceptual Experiences?

This entry will focus exclusively on the contents of perceptual experiences . It is definitional of experience, as the term is used here, that they have some phenomenal character, or more briefly, some phenomenology. The phenomenology of an experience is what it is like for the subject to have it. At any given waking moment, one normally has experiences in some (perhaps all) of the five sense modalities, along with proprioceptive experience of some sort. Like occurrent emotions and background moods, these contribute to one’s overall experience . Each of five sense modalities seems to be accompanied by a distinctive kind of phenomenology. Sometimes the boundaries between them can be hard to draw, for example between olfactory and gustatory phenomenology, kinesthetic experience and haptic-tactile experience (that is, tactile experiences involving movement rather than just pressure sensation), and perhaps, in some cases, between the latter two and visual experience (on the last point see Press et al . 2004, Kennett et al . 2001, Fotopoulou et al . 2009; on distinguishing the senses, see Stokes, Matthen and Briggs 2014, Wilson and Macpherson 2018). In general, it is an open question how holistic perceptual experiences, and to what extent it can be viewed as an aggregate of separable experiences in distinct modalities. Despite these difficulties, some rough distinctions can be drawn: the difference between seeing red and seeing blue is not a difference in how things sound, or in how one’s body feels.

items.body:
How does an artist sustain five decades of artistic production while remaining faithful to her cultural heritage? For Batima Zaurbekova, one of Kazakhstan’s most respected artists, the answer seems to be an unrelenting commitment to her craft. “You can’t be lazy,” the 80-year-old artist told me during a recent conversation.

That maxim is borne out in “Threads of Heritage,” a retrospective of more than 80 works at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Her largest exhibition to date, it features the textiles she is known for as well as drawings and paintings. Curated by Alina Fedorovich, a curator at the Museum of Moscow, the exhibition traces a career in which tapestry becomes both a repository of cultural memory and a vehicle for artistic reinvention.

Rooted in traditional Kazakh textiles, her practice is also shaped by the influences of modernist painting and music, moving fluidly between abstraction and figuration and in turn, defying easy categorization. Her tapestries hold seemingly disparate influences, transforming traditional motifs into a distinct visual language. Ornamental Rug (1969), for example, revives motifs associated with horses, spiritual symbolism, and petroglyphs depicting mountain goats. Completed just after her graduation and the earliest work in the exhibition, Ornamental Rug provides a recognizable reference to the country’s landscape via the distinctive horns of the wild argali, a local mountain goat, while distilling these forms into rhythmic, stylized arrangements. The work’s title foregrounds the relationship between ornament and abstraction, suggesting how decorative forms can become a vehicle for modernist experimentation.

Zaurbekova grew up in the mountainous Zhambyl region of Kazakhstan, where textile-making was part of everyday life. She remembers watching older women create syrmak, traditional felt rugs, and kurak-korpe, patchwork quilts meaning “stitched from scraps.” Neighbors gathered to work, sing, cook, and share food, embodying the Kazakh tradition of asar, in which a community joins forces to help a household undertake a task, be it making a carpet or building a home.

Installation view of “Batima Zaurbekova: Threads of Heritage,” 2026, at Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts, Almaty, showing In the Yurt (1985).

Photo KIRILL FEDOROV

Textile-making was as much a social practice as a technical one, transmitting skills and cultural knowledge across generations. This collective spirit is evoked in In the Yurt (1985), a weaving in which a maternal figure presides over the dastarkhan, the table prepared for guests. The yurt, a traditional felt dwelling associated with Kazakh nomadic life, becomes a symbol of hospitality, family, and belonging. Its ornaments merge with the surrounding figures, establishing a visual language equally rooted in the formal and the domestic.

In her youth, Zaurbekova had alternative ambitions for herself. “I really loved music, so I wanted to become a musician,” she recalled. However, her seamstress mother encouraged her to pursue painting instead. She is equally accomplished in oil painting and tapestry, and occasionally the same image is translated in both mediums.

Nevertheless, music has remained central to Zaurbekova’s life and practice, in which her visual compositions are animated by repetition, variation, and rhythm—the basic structure of music. This way of working is best observed in one gallery showing three works, each titled Composition and made in 1980, 2019, and 2024. Their stained-glass aesthetic, contrasting color planes, and rhythmic linear forms evoke Henri Matisse’s celebrated “Jazz” series. Undulating figures and vegetal motifs merge within an ornamental field, dissolving the distinction between figure and ground.

Installation view of “Batima Zaurbekova: Threads of Heritage,” 2026, at Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts, Almaty.

Photo Kirill Fedorov

## Keep tabs on Parliament.

### What we’re doing

Finding out what your representatives in Ottawa are up to can be tough.We’re trying to make it easy.

Find your MP by entering your postal code above. See what your representatives are saying, and what laws they’re proposing. Poke around.

### What they’re talking about

The latest House transcript is from Wednesday, November 25th, when the word of the day was seniors. The House is sitting today; transcripts are usually available the next morning. These are the topics that were discussed.

This summary is computer-generated. Usually it’s accurate, but every now and then it’ll contain inaccuracies or total fabrications.

Statements by Members

Tony Bennett's democratic legacyNicholas Herring wins Giller PrizeSt. Thomas curling championshipsRemembering Robert CarloRemembering Carl LefebvreHolodomor anniversary and UkraineAdvent and Christmas messageRemembering Satinder Kaur BahiaImmigration levels and hospital capacityAgricultural award winnersCanada by Canoe expeditionImmigration levels and affordabilityWelcoming Tibetan leader Penpa TseringAlto project and alleged Liberal favouritismMen's Shed community initiativesAlto project property rightsCanada by Canoe and nature access

Question Period

The Conservatives criticize high immigration levels, linking them to strained health care and housing and questioning the government’s ability to track newcomers. They allege Telesat favouritism and other insider dealings, oppose the Alto rail project’s land powers, blame spending and the industrial carbon tax for affordability and job pressures, and warn that cuts are weakening military reserves. The Liberals defend a controlled immigration plan, including pathways for workers already in Canada and retaining immigrant health-care professionals. They promote Alto high-speed rail, Telesat Lightspeed, auto-sector investment and economic growth, while highlighting marine conservation, affordable child care and defence readiness. The Bloc condemn Alto’s expropriation powers, warning they threaten Quebeckers’ property rights and farmers. They also defend the legitimacy of Quebec’s elected MNAs and their right to resume work, criticizing federal silence over attacks on the National Assembly. The NDP condemn cuts to Parks Canada search-and-rescue capacity, warning park warden closures endanger public safety.

International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women Members mark the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women and the start of 16 days of activism, calling for year-round action to prevent violence, support survivors and improve justice-system responses. Speakers discuss femicide, coercive control, technology-facilitated abuse, barriers to safety and the disproportionate risks faced by Indigenous women and girls. They differ on government policies and funding, while emphasizing collective responsibility. 3600 words, 25 minutes.

Scoliosis Awareness Act First reading of Bill C-298. The bill designates June as Scoliosis Awareness Month and June 26 as Canadian Scoliosis Screening Day to encourage early recognition and screening of scoliosis in children. 100 words.

Canadian Space Launch Act Second reading of Bill C-28. The bill establishes a licensing, safety, environmental, liability and oversight framework for commercial space launches in Canada. Liberals argue it will foster investment, jobs and innovation while strengthening satellite access, communications and national security, including for rural regions. A Conservative raises concerns about prioritizing space investment while cellular service remains unreliable in parts of the country. 2600 words, 20 minutes in 2 segments: 12.

items.body:
Die Gouverneurin des US-Bundesstaats New York macht sich bei den Automobilherstellern keine Freunde. [Ein neues Gesetz](https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/money-your-pockets-governor-hochul-signs-bill-restricting-exploitative-vehicle-subscription) verbietet es künftig, bereits im Fahrzeug verbaute Funktionen im Nachhinein gegen Abo-Gebühren freizuschalten, sofern mit deren Nutzung keine laufenden Kosten für den Anbieter verbunden sind. Dergleichen hatte hierzulande bereits vor ein paar Jahren im Zusammenhang mit den Sitzheizungs-Abos von BMW für heftige Diskussionen gesorgt.

Die Regelung tritt am 27. Februar 2027 in Kraft und richtet sich gleichermaßen an Automobilhersteller, Händler und externe Dienstleister. Die Regierung des Bundesstaats will damit verhindern, dass sich die nachträgliche Vermarktung bereits vorhandener Fahrzeugfunktionen als Geschäftsmodell in der Automobilbranche etabliert.

## Keine Abos für bereits verbaute Technik

Das Gesetz beschränkt sich nicht auf klassische Ausstattungsmerkmale wie Sitzheizungen. Auch die Nutzung von Navigations- und Unterhaltungssystemen oder Fahrassistenzfunktionen fällt unter die Neuregelung, sofern die dafür benötigte Technik bereits im Fahrzeug vorhanden ist und deren Nutzung keine laufenden Kosten aufseiten des Anbieters verursacht.

#### Mercedes bietet sogar Drosselung als Abo an

Abonnements für Dienste, deren Bereitstellung tatsächlich laufende Kosten verursacht, bleiben dagegen zulässig. Hierzu dürften beispielsweise Mobilfunkanbindungen oder die Bereitstellung aktueller Verkehrsinformationen zählen.

## Deutsche Autobauer halten an Abo-Modellen fest

BMW hatte sich zwar nach massiver Kundenkritik wieder von seinem Sitzheizungs-Abo verabschiedet, hält grundsätzlich aber [weiterhin](https://www.ifun.de/bmw-haelt-an-abo-modellen-fest-und-setzt-weiter-auf-connecteddrive-274036/) an der Vermarktung zusätzlicher Fahrzeugfunktionen im Abo fest.

#### Parking Assistant: Eine der Abo-Optionen bei BMW

Auch bei anderen Automobilherstellern wie Mercedes-Benz und Audi haben wir in der Vergangenheit über vergleichbare Angebote berichtet. Selbst die Nutzung von Apple CarPlay war bei BMW zeitweise mit wiederkehrenden Gebühren verbunden.

Dass die jetzt in New York beschlossene Regelung auch andernorts als Vorlage für vergleichbare Verbraucherschutzgesetze dient, halten wir allerdings für wenig wahrscheinlich.

[★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=iphone-ticker.de)

Der Beitrag [Erstes Verbot für Abo-Modelle in Autos](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/erstes-verbot-fuer-abo-modelle-in-autos-291589/) Wurde zuerst auf [iphone-ticker.de](https://www.iphone-ticker.de) veröffentlicht.
